A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may exhibit unusual spin-triplet characteristics that are generally not amenable to being protected by topology. We investigate whether this protection can be achieved through coupling Rashba and Dresselhaus SO interactions without necessarily eliminating the Zeeman field. Our findings indicate that in the Rashba-Hubbard model with attractive interactions, a s-wave Rashba-Dresselhaus superconductor can be stabilized at the two sides of a topological insulator phase transition boundary. Additionally, a spin-polarized ferromagnetic state coexists with superconductivity, with the spin-triplet nature of superconductivity being fully polarized and topologically protected. Introducing impurity scattering that disrupts the balance between Rashba and Dresselhaus interactions can shift the phase transition from superconducting to conventional BCS behavior. These results are further reinforced by numerical evidence from exact diagonalization. Our study suggests that materials like InSnSe2, exhibiting both Rashba and Dresselhaus behavior and featuring a superconducting and topologically non-trivial insulator phase, may exhibit spin-triplet superconductivity. The theoretical framework developed here can be applied to other systems exhibiting spin-orbit coupling with similar outcomes. With recent experimental observations of Rashba-Dresselhaus superconductors, our predictions may become testable in the near future. The topological protection of spin-singlet s-wave superconductivity in systems featuring strong SO coupling and Zeeman fields is also explored, with our calculations indicating that a protected spin-singlet state can be achieved through coupling Rashba and Dresselhaus interactions without eliminating the Zeeman field. This study focuses on understanding and extracting key information from scientific tables, specifically the relationships between table cells. It requires systems to identify, process, and analyze data in research papers automatically. In a recent FactFinder competition, held in conjunction with SemEval 2021, we introduced two new subtasks centered around tabular data: fact verification and finding supporting evidence. Our goal is to advance the knowledge in tabular data processing and make it accessible to the NLP community. In this paper, we outline the details of the task, evaluate the performance of participating teams, and achieve top scores in both subtasks through our own team submissions. Additionally, we have made the dataset available for public use at https://github.com/isi-vista/SEMTAB-Facts.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we address potential misconceptions surrounding complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, particularly regarding the Lorentz transformation and complex representations of spin and momentum. The discussion concludes with an examination of the potential implications of real quantum mechanics on big bang theory and the concept of vacuum in Quantum Field Theory and the related cosmological aspects. $\phantom{a}$

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By simplifying complex spatial environments into homogeneous ones, I discovered that the algebraic expressions driving water table changes are consistently based on the average hydraulic gradient in the affected area, regardless of its size. Following a discussion on Seip's initial findings in Norway during the 1960s, I provide and analyze the generalized equation for groundwater movement, then explore the implications of this theory on water table depression, incline changes, and recharge-induced subsurface flow. Additionally, I discuss how numerical methods can be applied to model these phenomena using modern computer software, illustrated by a re-examination of Seip's case in Figure 1, and further analyzed in the supplementary materials available online. Due to limited knowledge on the topic, these notes are intended to contribute to the existing understanding rather than offer an exhaustive review of the subject. As such, I welcome any corrections or additions that readers may have. Furthermore, I hope to engage with other scientists to develop a comprehensive guide to modeling long-distance groundwater flow. As this is an informal document, I invite anyone with relevant insights to share their thoughts via email at jkelly@usgs.gov. This research investigates an energy-efficient method to eliminate sulfur and nitrogen pollutants in flue gas using a combination of oxygen, nitrogen, and UV light. The study specifically focuses on using UV light to boost the ozone's ability to oxidize sulfur compounds. The scientists employed a combined experimental and computational approach, first leveraging CFD simulations to evaluate different reactor designs before conducting detailed experimental analysis in a custom-built apparatus. The results showed that incorporating UV light increased the oxidation of sulfur dioxide and sulfur compounds by up to fivefold, with ozone present, when compared to reactions with ozone alone. The promising findings suggest that integrating UV light into systems designed to remove pollutants using ozone could significantly enhance their effectiveness and efficiency. The promising outcomes may lead to the development of more compact and energy-efficient systems for flue gas treatment. The research also provides a foundation for further exploration into the synergistic effects of light and oxidants in pollution abatement reactions. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation have been the only means to do so until recently. Due to its simplicity and effectiveness, cardiac auscultation has been the primary tool, but it comes with its own set of limitations. Current research aims to improve this by developing electronic systems to enhance auscultation, and advancements in machine learning algorithms have made it possible to effectively classify heart sounds using these recordings. However, the various noises present in cardiac recordings pose a significant challenge to accurate classification, and the problem is compounded by the distortion caused by capture methods. In this research, we address the noise issue by testing different filters to reduce its impact and explore its effect on classification performance. Additionally, we investigate the effect of capture methods on classification through image processing-inspired distortion simulations. Our findings indicate that noise reduction filters can be ineffective and that capture methods have a substantial impact on performance. Moreover, we observe that noise reduction filters can negatively affect classification in some cases, and that using electronic systems to reduce noise yields better results than standard filtering methods. Furthermore, we discover that simulating capture methods leads to a 10% decline in our overall classification performance. These outcomes underscore the importance of considering the influence of capture methods on cardiac recording classification and suggest that noise reduction through electronic systems may be a more effective approach than traditional filtering methods. Our research also shows that using deep learning algorithms like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) yields better results than traditional machine learning methods, and that incorporating features derived from signal intensity and time-frequency representations, along with corresponding auscultation notes, can further enhance performance. Our study achieved a 0.9338 overall accuracy, a 0.8571 sensitivity, and a 0.9231 specificity after optimizing the model through grid search. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised some concerns about this work in a comment. We're responding with some counterpoints to their concerns and clarifying a few aspects of the validation for our method. We also re-evaluated our initial constraints on the $V-A$, $L+M$ interaction term in the Standard Model, specifically the $P$-factor, using more conventional calculations as input. Our findings indicate a notable discrepancy with previous research by Flambaum, Kharlanov, and Druzbicka, but our results align more closely with their initial work on the topic. We found significant limitations on new physics beyond the Standard Model due to the measurements in $^{133}$Cs, particularly with respect to $CP$-violation coupling and left-handed $W$-boson couplings. We also discuss some additional aspects of our original paper. We're grateful for Roberts and Ginges bringing these concerns to the table, and we hope our response clarifies any confusion and highlights the validation of our initial results. We also plan to publish a follow-up paper where we apply the corrections suggested by Roberts and Ginges to our method and examine the impact on our initial conclusions. We're confident that our response and our follow-up work will enhance the accuracy of our initial results and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the limitations on new physics beyond the Standard Model due to the measurements in $^{133}$Cs. The study uses graphical models to illustrate these symmetries and computes the equivariant twisted cohomology groups for all 2-dimensional crystallographic point groups. Furthermore, the article discusses the application of these results in physics, drawing comparisons with existing research on torus symmetry in particle physics models. Additionally, the article includes tables summarizing the equivariant twisted cohomology groups for each type of crystallographic point group. The research aims to expand the understanding of cohomological effects in physics phenomena through the concept of twisted space symmetry. recruitment. This effort involved conducting assessments, developing new
courses, and introducing department-wide learning communities focused on
socially relevant mathematics. The impact of these initiatives is being measured
by the department's subsequent demographic shifts and student feedback. The

department to further address climate and equity concerns. Specifically, the
presentation will highlight the effectiveness of departmental learning communities
in fostering collaboration, improving students' sense of belonging, and
introducing them to diverse career paths in mathematics. Furthermore, it will

real-world problems rooted in social contexts. Ultimately, the presentation

will also be available on the Climate and Equity in Undergraduate Mathematics
website for public viewing. The department is committed to making these
initiatives accessible and adaptable to various institutional settings, enabling
colleagues to replicate and modify them to suit their local needs. Pomona College
is dedicated to promoting student success through an inclusive and welcoming
environment, and the department is eager to collaborate with peers at other
institutions to achieve this goal.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on participant behavior. We accomplish this by comparing the actions of bidders in both standard and trust-based auction settings. Trust-based auctions incorporate a mechanism that allows the winner to verify the seller's auction fee promise prior to payment. Conversely, standard auctions do not provide any assurance regarding fees charged by successful bidders. A key aspect of these auctions is that fees in both formats can differ, resulting in a potential loss for the buyer if the verified fee exceeds the initial agreement. We found that bids in trust-based auctions tend to be more aggressive while closing prices are often higher compared to standard auctions. Notably, when auctions involve a guarantee of payment, bidders tend to be more risk-seeking, as measured by their latent risk preferences. We also discovered that sellers are more likely to honor their fees in trust-based auctions; however, when fees are not bound by a penalty, sellers tend to claim they adhered to the initial agreement at a lower rate compared to standard auctions. Notably, when auctions involve a guarantee of payment, sellers tend to be more accurate in claiming they adhered to the initial agreement. Our results indicate that the credibility of auction mechanisms has a significant impact on bidder behavior, resulting in higher revenue for sellers who can verify the auction format's integrity. Acquiring knowledge through question-answering systems is a more achievable goal than acquiring similar levels of performance in task-oriented tasks. This paper introduces a two-stage question-answering process that first identifies the main information needed from a document to answer the question and then locates the specified information within that data. Our method is evaluated using a recently created dataset that consists of human-generated questions and answers linked to research papers in four domains, along with human-generated strategies for gathering the necessary information to answer these questions. Our experiments show that a simple task-oriented approach is insufficient for answering information-seeking questions and that a dual approach, focused on both information collection and retrieval, is more effective in utilizing the available context. When combining these two skills, our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art question-answering systems by 10.3% in terms of accuracy. This dataset, along with our complete code and evaluation results, can be accessed at https://github.com/epfml/InfoSeekingQA.

Recent research has shown that machine learning can effectively utilize resting-state fMRI to diagnose ADHD by identifying specific patterns in brain activity. However, the effectiveness of this approach heavily relies on accurately mapping essential brain regions, which is typically done using established templates. Yet, different mapping techniques exist and may yield different results. To address this challenge, we conducted a comprehensive study to determine the most critical regions of the brain for ADHD diagnosis and found that using a self-organizing map is more effective than other methods. Utilizing our optimized mapping, we developed and tested several deep learning models, ultimately finding that a dual-stream convolutional neural network outperformed other approaches and even traditional methods using predefined templates. Notably, our findings have implications for understanding the underlying causes of ADHD and may contribute to a better understanding of the disorder's neurobiological foundations. The source code for our project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreabianchi/ADHD_rs-fMRIDeepLearning. Additionally, our data and models have been made available on OpenNeuro at https://doi.org/10.18113/P7001013. Furthermore, our study is documented on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04438. Lastly, our models can be accessed through an online interface at https://adhd-brianchi.herokuapp.com/. This interface allows users to input their own fMRI data and view the diagnostic accuracy of our models. Please note that this interface may require large bandwidth and may take some time to load. If you experience any issues, you can contact me directly at abianchi@unimc.it.

In recent years, research on identifying and resolving acronyms has gained more recognition within the natural language processing community, due to their widespread use in scientific and technical writing. The initial step in analyzing acronyms involves detecting them in text, a task many consider straightforward. However, the primary challenge lies in identifying the full form corresponding to an acronym, a sub-task that has received less attention from researchers. The primary difficulty arises from the limited availability of relevant data, as most acronym definitions are found in documentation, not freely accessible online. To address this gap, our proposed system, MadDog, not only identifies but also looks up acronym definitions by ranking potential matches accurately. The system's performance is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments and its source code is made available for public access on GitHub. Additionally, MadDog has been launched as a web-based application for community testing at http://maddog.iiitd.edu.in/. This paper introduces an innovative approach to DNA storage, addressing two major issues with current methods. The first problem involves efficiently encoding large files with varying sizes in DNA. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a hierarchical storage system that leverages the DNA molecule's inherent properties to effectively compress data. As a result, DNA storage capacity is increased by up to 37 times, making it more cost-effective. The second obstacle is updating existing data in the future. To address this, we've developed an updated protocol allowing for both data corrections and updates, even at multiple locations, with a time complexity of O(n log n) and linear space complexity. We've also conducted thorough simulations to validate our methods' efficiency and effectiveness. DNA storage utilizing our approach has a lower retrieval time, up to 72 times faster, and reduced energy consumption, often by a factor of at least 10. The beauty of our solutions lies in their compatibility with the existing DNA sequencing and writing technologies, making them readily implementable. Additionally, even with the current high costs reduced to $0.000004 per GB, the value of our approaches becomes apparent as they provide substantial cost improvements. Furthermore, as DNA storage cost continues to decline, the benefits of our solutions will only grow. The source code for our project is available at https://github.com/CSUNSEF/EF-DNA. The C++ code for our approach can be found at https://github.com/CSUNSEF/EF-DNA/tree/master/EF-DNA. The DNA storage framework is based on SEFI* and can be accessed at https://github.com/CSUNSEF/SEFI*. The * denotes the latest version of the framework, SEFI*-6. These nodal lines occur when a specific condition is met: they appear in momentum space as lines that represent points in real space where the energy at a particular energy level transitions from a positive to a negative value. Topological nodal lines can be isolated or linked, forming topological semi-metals, where increased control over momentum is equivalent to controlling energy. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronized activity across large distances. These waves, known as propagátor waves, are essential for circadian rhythms and other widespread temporal coordination in biological systems. Theoretical models, such as the Hodgkin-Huxley equations, can predict wave speeds, yet their complex nature makes it difficult to apply them to real-world problems. To overcome this limitation, we have developed simpler formulas that accurately calculate wave speeds in two essential cases: (1) the dominant ion channel model, and (2) the case where the pacemaker region is small. Our simplified expressions are versatile, allowing us to apply them to both outward- and inward-propagating waves and to modify them to accommodate non-oscillatory as well as oscillatory external environments. By comparing our analytical predictions to numerical simulations, we have confirmed their precision, with differences of less than 1%. These formulas offer a valuable alternative to the full Hodgkin-Huxley model for scientists studying the intricate mechanisms behind biological timing systems. Furthermore, they can be adapted to investigate other types of generated waves in oscillatory media. Finally, our approach has enabled us to clarify the underlying mechanisms contributing to wave generation and to pinpoint their dependence on key system parameters. In medical research and assessments, the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes are extensively utilized for case definition, outcome measurement, and forecasting. Nevertheless, manually assigning ICD codes to clinical documents is labor-intensive, prompting the need for automated coding systems. Although deep learning methods have made significant advancements in automated ICD coding, they frequently demand a vast, high-quality, yet scarce resource for training and testing – a detailed, accurately coded clinical dataset. This challenge is typical not only for automated ICD coding but also other deep learning applications.

This paper introduces a semi-supervised learning approach that leverages both structured and unstructured clinical data to train a fully automatic ICD coding system. During training, we employ semi-supervised learning to develop an automated coding system, while also utilizing unstructured clinical notes for data enrichment to precision-tune our method. Our results using the MIMIC-III dataset reveal that our proposed technique yields an F1 score of 0.6236 for the primary diagnosis codes, outperforming the supervised and unsupervised benchmarks with an improvement margin of 0.0466 and 0.2036 respectively. Moreover, our technique exhibits superior generalizability and efficient query-based data augmentation capabilities that facilitate scalable clinical data enhancement from unstructured clinical notes with minimal human intervention. Consequently, our automated ICD coding system can effectively function in real-world clinical settings with data-driven, self-correcting capabilities to enhance its accuracy and robustness. Additionally, this study provides a novel clinical data enhancement solution that can be applied to diverse deep learning tasks beyond automated ICD coding. Our developed method and data are available for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/zhengchen0828/Semi-supervised_ICD Coding. Experimental validation of our findings can be conducted using the MIMIC-III dataset, which can be downloaded from https://physio-net.org/mimic-iii-clinical-variation-modeling-database. A versatile, adjustable, and interpretable shadow effect is achievable in rendering realistic three-dimensional objects visually. However, calculating shadows in real-world scenarios is complex due to uncertainty in object properties like specularity, orientation, and position, which hinders effective image synthesis in computer vision. Consequently, current methods either employ simplified shadow models or resort to reference data, leading to suboptimal results. Our research introduces an innovative approach that leverages a differentiable cone-tracing shader for accurately computing shadows in real-time rendering. By integrating this shader with a neural network-based image generation framework, we enable the computation of image formation models and train them with real-world examples, ultimately facilitating reliable estimation of object properties from monocular images. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in estimating specularity, orientation, and position, even when data is limited or incomplete. Additionally, we showcase its applicability in enhancing image restoration tasks like defogging and demisting. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/alexalexalex1993/differentiable_shaders. Our dataset can be found at https://github.com/alexalexalex1993/shadow_dataset. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees from random graphs. This research demonstrates that their outputs are equivalent on graphs that undergo a single transformation, and establishes a universal framework for generating uniform spanning trees by combining these algorithms along with a new two-stage method. The theoretical findings are further illustrated with simulations to examine the algorithms' efficiency and effectiveness in practice. The findings suggest that Wilson's algorithm within the proposed framework generally yields faster tree generation times, and the code for replicating these experiments has been publicly shared. This research introduces the MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive benchmark for
cross-modal learning that aligns sheet music, lyrics, and musical audio.
Developed on an extensive collection of $104,675$ song items from MUSEUM, the
dataset enables the exploration of multimodal approaches to generate audio from
sheet music and lyrics auto-completion using pre-trained models. The proposed
dataset architecture facilitates three main tasks: generating audio from sheet
music, producing lyrics from a sheet music and audio combination, and creating
lyrics based on sheet music and audio alone. Extensive experiments with the
MusicTM-Dataset demonstrate the efficacy of employing multimodal learning for
music generation and text completion. Furthermore, the dataset allows for the
investigation of a triple-modal learning approach, incorporating sheet music,
audio, and lyrics to achieve better outcomes. The MusicTM-Dataset is presented

Although manual temperature control often results in uneven distributions, leading to reduced efficiency and productivity,  implementing advanced temperature control strategies requires a detailed understanding of temperature variability.  To this end, we used rapid magnetic resonance imaging to visualize temperature fluctuations in a vertical fixed bed filled with 1-cm-diameter glass beads and subjected to upward-flowing air at varying velocities.  Our results showed that as the air flow accelerated, the temperature variability increased and became more complex, eventually resulting in a condition where the hot gas accumulated at the bottom of the bed.  Our findings provide a basis for developing temperature control algorithms using images and could be applied to improve process efficiency in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries.  Moreover, this study offers a novel application of magnetic resonance imaging in chemical engineering research.  Finally, we observed that the temperature distribution in the bed was influenced by the interaction between the gas and particles, which is a phenomenon that needs to be addressed in future research projects. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, forming distinct membrane-bound regions. This self-assembly process is predominantly driven by one specific type of molecular interaction: specific protein-nucleic acid bonds. However, additional factors like surface properties also play a significant role. We've developed a theoretical model that describes how areas with shared components, such as proteins, assemble into separate sections. This model confirms that two competing factors control the size and stability of these areas: the strength of bonds between molecules and their surface properties. We've also simulated the formation of droplets in a cell-like environment and observed two possible outcomes: either the droplets completely isolate their contents or they merge due to overlapping molecule bonds. This study provides crucial insights into the underlying mechanisms of membrane condensation and highlights the relationship between molecule interactions and area surface properties."

This research involves modeling the mechanical systems of heart tissues and their link to electrical processes, conducted to better understand how the heart's mechanical function is affected by its electrical activity. Due to the diverse size scale of components in heart muscle mechanics, such as muscle fiber, sheet sheets and blocks, direct solving methods are impractical. To overcome this challenge, this study employs the Balancing Domain Decomposition Method (BDDM) in conjunction with multilevel preconditioners to solve the resulting system efficiently. The focus is placed on the following aspects: the construction of BDDM for heart tissue mechanics, a variable time-stepping solver routine, and an examination of different multilevel preconditioners in an operator-overlapping context. The study showcases that the BDDM method can effectively reduce computational time and when combined with efficient time-stepping and multilevel preconditioning techniques, can enable the simulation of entire heart muscle mechanics models at a reasonable cost. The research found that the Caluso-Smith and PCDIL preconditioning methods excel in this context, leading to significant computational time reductions of up to 90% for problem sizes of up to 54 million unknowns when compared to a Neumann-Neumann preconditioning method. The research further highlights that by increasing the level in multilevel preconditioning from 3 to 4, the computational time can be further reduced by up to 3 times. This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. We establish that these solutions converge to a unique global weak solution on large time. Moreover, for solutions that exist indefinitely, their trajectories are drawn towards a single, equilibrium state within the energy space as time approaches infinity. This model's large-time energy dissipation is attributed to the fractional Laplacian's low-frequency filtering effect, which is a key aspect of this model. This work builds upon previous research by Wan and Xu, who initially investigated the 2-D compressible FENE dumbbell model in an energy space one order higher in frequency. Unlike earlier studies, which relied on the Smale-Hirsch criterion for identifying compactness, this paper employs the relative compactness of approximation solutions and a time-interpolation technique to reach its conclusions. As a direct result, this approach provides further insight into the Smale-Hirsch criterion's validity for this model. This research also offers additional proof that solutions are drawn towards a single, equilibrium state within the energy space as time approaches infinity, in addition to previous findings by Wan and Xu. This model's large-time energy dissipation is a crucial aspect of its dynamics, which was previously discussed in the companion paper by Zhang, Zhang, and Zhao. The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives alternative expressions for the electromagnetic field in terms of wave equations, consistent with the assumptions of discrete energy and charge. However, the evidence presented fails to convincingly support the notion that light quanta harbor both energy and charge. It is demonstrated that the "quantum" approach can be sustained without the light quanta hypothesis, by restricting the analysis to regions where the electric field is negligible. Building on this, the paper explores analogous solutions for a current comprised of uniformly moving and rotating spheres. Finally, the paper considers the implications of its findings for de Broglie waves and Schrödinger equations in the non-relativistic context of electron theory. It argues that the discrete energy suggestions from the wave theory of light quanta can be alternatively motivated through an analogy with stationary waves in a box, prior to the adoption of the light quanta hypothesis. The paper concludes by highlighting its own limitations and suggesting potential avenues for further research. Throughout the paper, an attempt is made to convey the historical development of quantum theory in an approachable and historically accurate manner. It is hoped that the insights presented will be of use to undergraduate and advanced students in understanding the early history of quantum theory. It is also hoped that the presentation will be of interest to historians of science. Finally, it is hoped that the presentation will be of interest to laypeople with a curiosity in the subject. In particular, the paper seeks to address the question of how one might have first conceived of discrete energy. It is also a tribute to the memory of my late teacher, Professor Andrew Frankel. The paper was written during the summer of 2020 while on sabbatical leave from Queen's University Belfast, where I was hosted by the University of Salerno as a visiting professor. To enable effective lifelong learning, it's crucial to evaluate how past knowledge influences future performance.  Current methods for evaluating reinforcement learning assessments are limited because they either measure generalization or retention separately or treat them as identical.  Additionally, most prior studies utilized artificial settings with no real flaws, which hinders their applicability to real-world scenarios.  To address these issues, we introduce a controlled environment for examining lifelong learning and introduce the concept of knowledge trajectories, which reflect past, present, and future performance levels.  We also propose a novel framework called L2Explorer that incorporates diverse reinforcement learning techniques and systematically alters its difficulty to simulate real-world learning scenarios.  Using L2Explorer, we conducted comprehensive assessments of existing reinforcement learning methods, which demonstrate their inability to consistently apply past knowledge effectively.  Importantly, our framework includes a detailed guide on assessment design to facilitate the creation of more realistic and meaningful evaluations in future studies.  By advancing our understanding of what works and what doesn't in lifelong learning, we can ultimately develop more practical and effective lifelong learning methods.  To ensure the reproducibility of our results, we publicly released our code, data, and environment at https://github.com/charlesmiller/l2explorer. We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, allowing spontaneous symmetry breaking and polarization mode occupation. Our results reveal a method to dynamically manipulate polarization state and optimize optical trapping for polarization-sensitive applications. Coupled exciton-polariton systems are also shown to enable all-optical manipulation of polarization state and achieve a 90-degree rotation with high efficiency. These findings contribute to developing all-optical techniques to regulate polarization in polariton condensate research. Moreover, the study offers perspectives on integrating such capabilities for studying spin-orbit interactions and magneto-optical effects in polariton systems. The COVID-19 pandemic, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 virus spread, led to a global health crisis in 2020. In South Africa, the infection accelerated in March 2020, prompted by the detection of SARS-CoV-2 variant 2 in a tourist. To combat the surge, the government enforced a 21-day lockdown, resulting in a data-driven decision-making vacuum due to limited availability of experts during this period. To bridge this gap, a team of data analysts collaborated with medical professionals to provide timely COVID-19 updates using publicly accessible data, thereby filling the gap until formal reports became available from mid-April 2020. This collaborative effort produced daily updates for six weeks, focusing on key metrics such as total cases, new infections, deaths, and testing numbers. To ensure transparency, all analysis was shared on GitHub and presented through social media and online channels, culminating in the issuance of a public report on May 1, 2020. This study showcases the successful application of data-driven analytics in supporting public health decisions during the pandemic, facilitated by a team of data analysts working in close conjunction with medical experts. It also highlights the numerous challenges encountered during this endeavor and the many lessons learned from this experience. Furthermore, this study serves as a testament to the positive impact that collaborative data analysis can have on public policy, even in complex and high-pressure environments like the COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa. At the time of manuscript submission, the pandemic is still unfolding globally and domestically, with ongoing vaccination efforts and evolving public health policies necessitating continued data-driven support. As such, this case study remains highly relevant and aims to inspire other data analysts to collaborate with healthcare professionals and contribute to the public health discourse in their respective local contexts. Ultimately, this research seeks to demonstrate that data analysts can play a pivotal role in informing public health policy by working in close concert with medical experts, even in the midst of a rapid and all-encompassing pandemic like COVID-19. It is hoped that this collaboration will endure beyond the pandemic and become a standard practice in data-driven decision-making, both within and outside of public health settings. To that end, this manuscript is being shared openly on arXiv, in the hope that it will be a valuable resource for other data analysts seeking to emulate this model of collaboration and make similar contributions to the public health discourse. In addition to the case study itself, the team has also made available all data analysis and visualizations on GitHub, as well as formal COVID-19 reports

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, each containing k elements, share a common 2k-4 syndetic portion in the additive group, their sumset will substantially encompass the group itself. This research seeks to fortify this principle by asserting that under the same conditions, the sumset of A and B will, in fact, nearly entirely cover the group, specifically missing at most a minuscule fraction (implying the presence of nearly complete additive bases within their combined set). This enhanced version also yields an improved form of the initial theorem, one that remains unconditional within abelian groups of sufficiently large size. Additionally, this research also seeks to apply this improved 3k-4 theorem to analyze instances of sumsets displaying near-complete coverage of the group, effectively providing a novel, simplified explanation for the phenomenon known as Freiman's 5-2 theorem. Lastly, this research also delves into the investigation of nearly complete additive bases within specific sets and introduces the concept of 'freely generating' sets within the group, which holds promise for further research in the field. Ultimately, this enhanced 3k-4 theorem is anticipated to have far-reaching implications for the broader mathematics community. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more detailed opinions compared to using a single data type alone. For retinal image analysis, researchers have traditionally relied on fundus photography, yet recent advancements in OCT technology have provided deeper insights into retinal conditions. Our study demonstrates that by incorporating both fundus photography and OCT data into a pre-trained vision transformer model, performance improvements of up to 6.5% can be achieved in classification tasks. Specifically, our findings show that combining both data sources increases accuracy by 5.7% and 0.8% respectively over single-data-type inputs, while also resulting in more stable outcomes with a standard deviation of 1.1% compared to using a single data type. Furthermore, our study's success suggests that pre-trained models like Vision Transformer can serve as effective general-purpose classifiers for various retinal conditions. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted thorough experiments using two distinct datasets, covering glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Our research has been made accessible through a public GitHub repository, allowing others to build upon our work. Ultimately, our results indicate great potential for using deep learning to enhance retinal image analysis through data fusion. With ongoing advancements in medical imaging technologies, we can anticipate increased diversity in medical information sources, which in turn will enable the development of more sophisticated medical decision-support systems. In the future, our work may inspire the incorporation of additional medical information types, potentially leading to the creation of more comprehensive medical decision-support systems. Specifically, we plan to expand our approach to classify multiple retinal diseases simultaneously, which will necessitate the development of more sophisticated output designs. Additionally, we will investigate the application of our deep learning-based method on a broader scale, potentially leading to the creation of medical decision-support systems with integrated deep learning components. Lastly, we will explore the real-world implementation of our model, which might involve using our deep learning-based method for initial screening and providing the resulting probabilities to ophthalmologists as a starting point for further clinical assessment. With these objectives in mind, we are confident that our research will contribute to the advancement of medical decision-support systems through multimodal information fusion. Ultimately, our work may contribute to the development of more informed clinical decisions through the integration of diverse medical information types. X-ray images of COVID-19 patients contain valuable information about their health condition, which can be used to forecast their chances of survival upon hospital admission. Our research identified key image characteristics that predict patient outcomes, revealing that severe respiratory cases have distinctive visual patterns in their X-rays, distinct from other critical systemic conditions affected by the virus. By combining our findings with existing clinical data, we can create a comprehensive system to assess patients' mortality risk based on X-ray images, which can inform healthcare providers about the best treatment strategies and resources to allocate for each patient. Our research included 4,191 COVID-19 patients from seven diverse hospitals in Mexico, which provided a range of respiratory and systemic complications. The analysis involved manually categorizing patients with varying levels of respiratory system involvement and using a neural network to analyze their X-rays for specific features. The results showed that certain image characteristics were strongly linked to patient outcomes, and when combined with clinical data, we can accurately predict mortality risk in COVID-19 patients, which can help healthcare providers personalize treatment and make informed decisions in low-resource settings. The code for our research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alejandromu/COVID-19_XRay_Predictive_Model. Our research is significant because it can improve patient outcomes by helping healthcare providers anticipate and treat life-threatening complications, which is particularly crucial in low-resource settings where patients often develop severe systemic conditions due to a lack of access to quality medical care. The key to our success was identifying unique visual patterns in X-rays of patients with severe respiratory cases, which were distinct from patients with other systemic conditions, which enabled us to forecast patient outcomes based on X-ray images alone. Our research has several limitations, primarily due to the reliance on manual patient classification, which can lead to biased results. In future research, we can use machine learning algorithms to classify patients more accurately and expand our study to include more COVID-19 patients with well-documented health conditions to improve our understanding of how to forecast patient outcomes based on X-ray images. Additionally, we can collaborate with other research teams to validate our findings and make our model more robust by integrating it with existing predictive models. Furthermore, we can apply our research to other medical image prediction tasks to improve patient outcomes in various clinical settings. The key to our success was identifying unique visual patterns in medical images that are strongly linked to patient outcomes, which enabled us to improve forecasting accuracy in new patients. The main challenges in our research were manually categorizing patients with varying levels of health conditions and selecting relevant image features

We investigate the transmission eigenvalue problem in a multidimensional setting, specifically for media that vary radially and have rotational symmetry. Our research focuses on constructing nontrivial transmission eigenfunctions that decay at their natural modes, bounded by a unit sphere. Our findings demonstrate that these functions can be expressed as linear combinations of outgoing scalar waves at any given energy level, thereby providing an alternative proof of the uniqueness of transmission eigenfunctions in this particular type of medium. Additionally, our results implicitly confirm the Carleman Estimate for this problem. Moreover, our study highlights the distinct boundary localization characteristics of transmission eigenfunctions in this context, showcasing a significant difference from the corresponding Dirichlet problem, where transmission eigenfunctions can be localized arbitrarily within the domain. Although significant advancements have been achieved in intent classification, many intents remain undiscovered due to the lack of relevant data. To address this challenge, a novel framework called IntentFinder is proposed, leveraging pre-trained language models to efficiently identify previously unknown intents. By integrating a semantic framework, IntentFinder enhances intent recognition and classification capabilities. Empirical evaluations on two benchmarks indicate that IntentFinder consistently outperforms existing methods, furthermore, the framework's capabilities can be enhanced by conducting data augmentation. To validate IntentFinder's ability to discover new intents, an extensive experiment was performed using a simulated query stream. Notably, IntentFinder successfully discovered 8 new intents from an open-source dataset within 1000 iterations. Our findings and dataset are available for public access at https://www.aaai.org/AAAI2023/index.php/submission.html?tab=artifacts.

In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups. This estimate surpasses previous accounts by Recaman and Wolf, with an exponential improvement in the base-$r$ logarithm and a significant increase in the polynomial component. Our findings are grounded in a new inequality relating the order and number of subgroups of a group $G$, with implications that extend to its derived subgroups and cyclic variations. Furthermore, this inequality yields an explicit upper limit on the number of elements within a group, which may be of independent interest. With further modifications to the underlying proof method, we establish a more general result stating that a finite group of order $r$ and torsion size $s$ contains no more than $$3.3199\cdot S^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315} \cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{2\log_s r}+1.5315}$$ subgroups, where $S=\max\{r,s\}$. Notably, this estimate is relevant to nilpotent groups with a significant exponent. Our work also includes a comprehensive survey of previous research on upper-subgroup limits, along with several illustrative examples. Ultimately, we verify that our estimates are asymptotically valid but not necessarily tight. To confirm this, we present a family of finite groups for which our estimates are excessively large in comparison to the actual number of subgroups. With further modifications, the presented findings may also provide insights into the number of ideals within a group and lay the groundwork for novel generalizations to Lie algebras and differential groups. Additionally, our study may contribute to the development of efficient algorithms for computing group properties due to the newly established polynomial upper bounds on subgroup counts. To showcase this potential, we successfully employed a modified version of our methods to create an optimized algorithm for computing derived lengths, which outperformed previous implementations and achieved notable time savings in tests involving large groups. Our research was facilitated by Mathematica, a computational algebra system that enabled us to analyze numerous finite groups and gather statistical data on their characteristics. This data, along with the associated code, is available online for public access at https://github.com/alexdunlop subgroup-counting. Our analysis may also provide valuable insights to combinatorial group theorists due to the newly established polynomial upper bounds on subgroup

The recent emergence of deep neural networks has significantly advanced visual relationship detection (VRD), outperforming earlier methods with higher accuracy. However, deep neural networks still struggle with addressing false positives, a problem more pronounced in VRD than in other computer vision tasks. As a result, false positives hinder the development of real-world applications for VRD, such as visual question answering and image generation. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages multiple reference frames for data augmentation and incorporates these frames into a unified model through attention mechanisms. By increasing diversity in reference frames, our method effectively reduces false positives in visual relationship detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate the outstanding performance of our proposed technique, achieving state-of-the-art results on the VCBD dataset. Moreover, our method exhibits superior scalability and flexibility in dealing with other challenging computer vision tasks like image semantic segmentation and object detection with scene parsing. With the ability to address false positives, our deep neural networks can accelerate the development of robust computer vision models for real-world applications. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/zhaozhanyu/VRCNN.

A new method has been developed to calculate the correlation cost associated with weak measurements across various quantum states. It has been found that the correlation cost is directly proportional to the square of the measurement strength in the case of strong states, but otherwise follows a distinct pattern. Notably, for states that are maximally mixed within a particular subspace, the correlation cost remains constant and is influenced solely by the dimension of that subspace. Furthermore, when considering states that are maximally mixed within the entire Hilbert space, the correlation cost is found to be zero, as this corresponds to a strict quantum measurement rather than a weak one. Additionally, when states become increasingly eroded, the correlation cost is found to decrease in a manner that is consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics. It has also been demonstrated that the correlation cost can serve as a practical indicator in determining whether a measurement is truly weak, as this cost can serve as a measurable quantity even when the initial state is unknown. Finally, the correlation cost has been found to possess a property known as subadditivity, meaning that the sum of the correlation costs associated with individual measurements is always greater than the correlation cost associated with a simultaneous measurement across those dimensions. These properties provide valuable insights into the nature of weak measurements and offer potential applications in fields such as metrology and quantum thermodynamics. Lastly, the correlation cost has been found to possess a property known as convexity, meaning that the correlation cost associated with a particular quantum state remains constant when additional systems are incorporated in a manner that is entangled with the original system. These findings offer valuable insights into the nature of weak measurements and their relationship with principles of quantum mechanics, as well as the broader paradigm of measurement-based quantization. Lastly, it has been shown that the correlation cost can be utilized to develop a novel approach to defining and identifying parafermionic states within the context of any given Hilbert space. This involves constructing a parafermionic state from a particular weakly measured state, which in turn is found to possess a distinct form of correlation cost that is uniquely tied to the principles of any given parafermion algebra. This, in turn, offers potential applications in fields such as anyonic fractional statistics and topological quantum computing, as these concepts rely heavily on the theoretical framework of parafermions. Lastly, it has been demonstrated that the correlation cost can be utilized to develop a discrete analog of the Wigner function within the context of any finite Hilbert space, which in turn offers potential applications in fields such as quantum metrology

Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing, with applications in gaming, medicine, and robotics. To address this, learning social relationship graphs from visual scenes is crucial, but current methods face challenges due to the complexity and variability of social interactions. To overcome this, we introduce a novel framework that generates social relationship graphs in an automated manner. Our approach leverages domain knowledge to model high-level social interactions and employs self-attention mechanisms to capture detailed, contextual characteristics within scenes and individuals. We also propose a custom loss function that balances social interaction preservation and node characteristic retention. To facilitate training, we create standardized social relationship graphs for common scenarios like meetings and gatherings. Our end-to-end network demonstrates superior performance on social relationship graph generation and individual characteristic preservation compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we showcase our agent's capabilities in socially-aware gameplay. A video showcasing our work is available at https://youtu.be/6Qxkxk8b8gU. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/zhengyin-wu/social-relationship-graphs. Our research has been accepted at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2021. If you are interested in collaborating, please contact yin.wu@usc.edu. Additionally, a demo of our work can be accessed at https://socialrelationgraph.github.io/. We aim to make our research useful in real-world applications by generating social relationship graphs that other algorithms can utilize. To facilitate this, we provide pre-generated social relationship graphs for popular scenarios and encourage the public to suggest more use cases at https://forms.gle/7z1z7z1z1z1z. We are excited to see the potential applications of our research and look forward to collaborating with you!

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding is a crucial goal in computer vision, and achieving this has long been a challenging task. A novel method called Dynamic Graph Message Passing (DGMP) has been developed to tackle this issue by design. DGMP consists of a neural network that uses a message-passing algorithm on a dynamically constructed graph among feature vectors. This graph is created by identifying the m closest features to each node, representing local features and separating remote high-level features. As a result, the method effectively combines short-range and long-range cues in a self-supervised manner for pre-training. When combined with a downstream linear classifier, DGMP has broken multiple computer vision benchmarks, including ImageNet-Skip-ILSVRC14, ArcFace-Res2Net34, and ImageNet-Skip-ILSVRC2012, by setting new standards for the supervised training approach. Additionally, the method has shown its versatility on other vision tasks like few-shot learning and domain adaptation, and its code will be made publicly available. Experimental findings clearly demonstrate the method's superiority over existing techniques. Notably, the method has achieved a remarkable 10% error reduction on the ImageNet-Skip-ILSVRC14 benchmark, which is equivalent to a 16.5% error increase in linearly supervised models. This breakthrough has significant potential to improve the computer vision field and has validated the method's effectiveness. A detailed analysis of the method's design and its implications on the theory and practice of computer vision has also been included. This method's source code will be made publicly available. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This article outlines the underlying principles, accelerator layout advancements, and initial detector design developments for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the critical obstacles along the path to creating such a facility. It's also essential to note that the knowledge gained from building this collider will be transferable to other ambitious projects like hadron colliders and will contribute to the advancement of particle accelerator technology. Furthermore, this article discusses the initiative to establish a national design center for the Muon Collider, which will serve as a collaborative hub to coordinate and steer the progress of this project. The proposed design center will facilitate collaborative research, foster a unified understanding among experts, and make necessary recommendations to inform the scientific community and relevant funding agencies about the project's progress. The center's role will be to promote, oversee, and coordinate the research and development (R&D) efforts required to bring the Muon Collider to life. The scientific case for this project, along with detailed reports on R&D progress and potential construction timelines, will be made accessible on the center's website for public reference. The design center will also serve as a platform to discuss and address the challenges associated with the project, such as establishing a reliable muon beam, developing necessary new technologies, and tackling environmental and social concerns. The center will work to identify, prioritize, and mitigate these obstacles through open discussion among the scientific community and external stakeholders. Ultimately, the design center's primary goal is to ensure that the Muon Collider project is well-prepared, and the necessary expertise and technologies are in place when construction commences. The center's secondary objective is to foster a collaborative environment among the scientific community by promoting, and contributing to, international cooperation in this field. The design center's efforts will also focus on disseminating critical information about the project to the broader scientific community, and informing funding agencies about the project's progress and requirements. The center's website will serve as a central resource where the scientific community can find detailed information about the Muon Collider, including the project's goals, ongoing R&D efforts, and the expertise available in this field. This study calculates dispersion relations for various types of waves in a relativistic system of fluids. The method employed involves analyzing small disturbances in both the energy-momentum tensor and the metric of spacetime in a static, homogeneous background environment. By considering different types of perturbations, the study determines how they relate to effective wave properties, including propagation speed and damping rates, which were previously defined in relation to the non-vanishing transverse and traceless parts of the energy-momentum tensor. Specifically, the study examines and compares relativistic energy-momentum tensor-based models, including both non-viscous and viscous descriptions, as well as the non-viscous and viscous Graham models. The findings indicate that while non-viscous models yield accurate descriptions of longitudinal and transverse magnetic modes, they fail to capture the behavior of transverse gravitational modes. In contrast, the viscous model provides a more comprehensive description, capturing the viscosity-induced damping of all modes. Moreover, the study reveals that the ratio of damping rates to propagation speeds can be quantitatively determined and may serve as a criterion for evaluating hydrodynamic models. The study further explores the relationship between relativistic and non-relativistic formulations of the energy-momentum tensor-based models and finds that the latter models can be obtained through a non-trivial low-energy limit process. The study also compares its results with those from other studies, including both analytical and numerical approaches. Additionally, the study examines the regime in which the background fluid flow is subsonic, demonstrating that the models retain their applicability as long as the background fluid velocity remains less than the speed of light. The study concludes by highlighting potential applications of the calculated dispersion relations in gravitational wave astronomy and high-energy particle physics experiments. The study also emphasizes the importance of considering the backreaction of the perturbed energy-momentum tensor on the metric, which may lead to further model developments in the future. The study further suggests that the approach employed could be extended to analyze small disturbances in other physical systems, such as the Einstein-Einstein Maxwell or holographic matter duals to quantum field theories. The study also notes that the analysis was performed using background spacetime metrics that were either flat or described by a black hole background in the hard-impact limit. The study provides future research directions for extending the analysis to other types of spacetime backgrounds. The study further emphasizes that the approach can be easily adapted for use in numerical simulations by replacing the small disturbance analysis with a more general approach. Our research assesses the intensity of extragalactic background radiation originating from the decay of evaporating primordial black holes. By setting an upper limit on the density of these black holes relative to dark matter, we consider three processes influencing their formation: the rapid formation of black holes in the early universe's density fluctuations, the creation of black holes from the collapse of overdense regions and from the fragmentation of gas and dust, and the generation of black holes from the collapse of small-scale cosmological perturbations. After calculating the resulting background radiation for each scenario, we establish upper limits on the density of these black holes in the universe. Specifically, we find that if they constitute less than 0.01% of dark matter, they would still be able to produce detectable background signals in the radio frequency band. Furthermore, we explore the potential to detect these black holes using the Square Kilometre Array telescope. If they constitute 1% of dark matter, they would still be able to produce over 10 million photons per second per square kilometer, which could be detectable with upcoming telescopes. However, if they comprise less than 1% of dark matter, their emission would be too faint to be detected with even the most advanced telescopes. Ultimately, their density is contingent on the mass at which these black holes undergo evaporation, which affects their rate of evaporation and influences the background radiation intensity. If they undergo evaporation at higher masses, there would be fewer of them, resulting in weaker signals, while evaporation at lower masses would result in stronger signals. Conversely, if they undergo evaporation at lower masses, there would be more of them, potentially producing more intense background radiation. Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together Hardware Security in Cloud (HCloud) and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to safeguard sensitive computations on untrusted networks. This innovative system seamlessly replaces traditional access control mechanisms, such as firewalls and VPNs, to offer multi-process, multi-threaded security for sensitive data processing. The VSP architecture is centered on a custom-designed processor with a standardized five-stage digital pipeline, carefully optimized for efficient execution on cloud servers despite the performance limitations imposed by FHE and RNS encodings. Our comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that the VSP achieves an impressive 97% overall energy efficiency, accompanied by a minimal 3% average performance slowdown, thereby making it suitable for real-world applications on untrusted environments. This groundbreaking work not only sets a new standard for secure processing but also opens doors for novel applications in areas like homomorphic blockchain and secure IoT data analytics. Researchers have developed efficient approximation algorithms for specific constraint satisfaction problems with particular structures, even in situations where no polynomial-time approximation solution exists unless certain broader computational hypotheses hold true. Although there have been significant findings regarding approximate solutions for certain types of problems with multiple possible values, there has been a lack of comparable results for problems with arbitrary value sets. This study aims to bridge this gap by creating a new class of algorithms that can find approximate solutions for a broad category of such problems. The novel approach leverages properties of the problem's formulation to control the complexity of potential solutions, resulting in an algorithm that can find approximate solutions within a specified distance of the optimal solution for a broad category of problems in a restricted computational model. The technique has been successfully adapted to develop an algorithm with a proportional approximation improvement for a specific problem with value sets, even in more general computational environments. The development of this algorithm resolves a previously recognized challenge first identified in a different study. The technique employs concepts from metric embedding, which involves mapping one geometric space to another while preserving distances. Pre-trained language models have shown exceptional performance in various tasks such as sentiment analysis and question-answering, largely due to their ability to capture high-level language characteristics like syntax, semantics, and contextually-dependent lexical meanings. This research leverages the syntactic awareness of these models to develop innovative, unsupervised and few-shot dependency parsing methods. We introduce two novel approaches: one involves replacing standard bilevel decoding with an integrated language modeling and parsing objective during search, while another utilizes prompt-based learning for multiple dependencies at once. Notably, our proposed methods excel in both parsing tasks and the broader language understanding, and significantly outperform existing unsupervised and few-shot parsing methods, achieving results comparable to those of supervised models in several cases. This research thus facilitates the effective utilization of unsupervised and few-shot models in practical, real-world applications. High-definition hyperspectral images (HSI) contain more detailed spectral information in each pixel than standard RGB images, potentially enhancing image classification and segmentation tasks. Nevertheless, current HSI technologies face challenges such as noise, limited spectral range, and complex image environments that hinder their practical use. This research leverages the advantages of HSI in urban settings to simplify and automate the semantic segmentation process of specific objects within cities. First, a proposed method converts HSIs into RGB images that can effectively identify given target classes. Subsequent training and testing utilize publicly available data, with the goal of validating the approach's effectiveness in diverse environments. The resulting model can efficiently process RGB images, yielding promising segmentation outcomes even with minimal supervision. Notably, this technique holds potential for applications in areas where HSI technology is prevalent and could supplement traditional RGB image analysis. The code and model have been made accessible for public use.

The evolution of low-mass stars, particularly those within the low to intermediate mass range, is of great interest as it involves energy generated by nuclear reactions on the main sequence being stored in the form of gravitational potential energy when these stars expand into red giants. Understanding this process requires knowledge of the stars' initial conditions as well as the processes that occur during giant branch evolution, including efficient angular momentum transport mechanisms that facilitate rapid surface spin-up.

We have conducted a detailed analysis of surface rotation rates in the upper giant branch phase and found values significantly higher than expected, with some stars rotating in as little as 10 million years at rates 20 times faster than initially anticipated. These findings are difficult to explain using traditional models that incorporate tidal interactions with planets, as such processes typically take longer to occur.

To further investigate, we created 3D simulations of the interior dynamics of these stars using the MESA code with additional non-rotating elements, revealing that the efficient transport of angular momentum within the 1-2 solar mass stars could be attributed to an unexpected rise in the opacity at depths of 5-6 from below the core. This increase in opacity triggers a sudden shift in the star's rotation rate, resulting in a significant and rapid increase in surface rotation speed over a period of 5-10 million years. These results are consistent with observations of other stars within the same population, providing evidence that new modes of internal angular momentum transport are at play in the evolution of low-mass stars. Furthermore, the phenomenon may also influence the final distribution of elements within the stars' interiors and the timing of their expansion into red giants. Given the presence of similar opacity features in other low-mass stars, it is possible that this phenomenon is widespread and may have significant implications for the understanding of giant branch evolution. Additionally, the internal dynamics of these stars could be affected by other factors such as p-process elements, as observed in the case of the 1.02 solar mass star, resulting in a more complex and dynamic internal rotation profile that may also influence the stars' evolution. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Nevertheless, the formal definition of the RAM model is somewhat ambiguous. This work seeks to clarify the RAM model's type of machine and establish the conditions under which certain arithmetic operations can be executed in a constant amount of time within its framework. Specifically, we aim to demonstrate that in a RAM machine with addition, subtraction can also be performed in constant time. This will be achieved through a technique known as reduction, which effectively enables the simulation of a machine with only addition on a machine with subtractive capabilities. The paper will also explore further reductions, enabling the efficient computation of division, multiplication by a constant, and square root on inputs with O(log m) bits, where m represents the number of memory modules. These achievements are expected to contribute to the development of a more comprehensive algorithmic theory. Additionally, the paper will examine the challenges posed by inputs with arbitrary magnitudes, highlighting the complexity of operations like exponentiation and linear transformation. Finally, the paper will outline potential research avenues for addressing these difficulties. This work is expected to lay the groundwork for a more detailed treatise on algorithmic theory. All key proofs have been substantiated with detailed explanations and are accessible in the accompanying appendix. Furthermore, an interactive online supplement provides a step-by-step guide to the proof of the main theorem's first and second parts. This material is freely available at the arXiv server. To tackle the data sparsity issue in session-based recommendation, researchers have primarily focused on enhancing neural network designs. This study takes a different approach by combining the strengths of graph-based and memory-augmented methods to create a novel, self-supervised learning session-based recommendation framework called GMR. The core of GMR comprises two interconnected networks that produce user and item graphs from historical data, and predict the next item by choosing from candidate items linked to the current session memory. One network focuses on optimizing edge weights, while the other concentrates on refining the memory representation. Notably, our method can be trained without supervision by leveraging the inherent connections between user-item memory pairs and the temporal relationships within each session. The effectiveness of GMR is demonstrated through its exceptional performance on real-world datasets, which surpasses the performance of existing recommender systems. The source code for GMR is available at https://github.com/zhaozheng1988/SSGCR. The empirical results validate the advantages of GMR and show that it can be successfully applied in real-world recommendation settings. Furthermore, our study highlights the feasibility of applying self-supervised learning to address complex data sparsity challenges in recommendation systems. This research introduces novel coding concepts known as Group LCD codes and Group Reversible LCD codes, extending the existing LCD code framework. By building upon the properties of LCD codes, a broader family of Group LCD codes is defined, with corresponding properties and structural analysis provided. Additionally, the article delves into the creation of Group Reversible LCD codes, an extension of Reversible LCD codes, and examines their inherent characteristics. The authors also present several examples of these codes of various lengths and highlight their potential to surpass the performance of standard LCD codes. Furthermore, Group LCD codes are demonstrated to surpass the performance of Group Reversible codes, thereby substantiating their utility. The article concludes by highlighting the potential for these codes to address the challenges of channel estimation in communication systems. Finally, the authors validate the Group LCD and Group Reversible LCD codes through comprehensive simulations and emerging research scenarios.

We identify a space, denoted $\Omega$, whose elements are differential forms defined across a series of simplicial complexes representing graphs, with these forms invariant by graph automorphisms.  The space $\Omega$ serves as the basis for an algebraic framework that enables the evaluation of Feynman integrals associated with the graphs within question.  The basic principles of $\Omega$ allow for the derivation of an explicit formula for the two-loop Feynman integral of the self-dual supergravity theory, a scenario in which the traditional method faces significant obstacles due to non-linear dependencies in momentum parameters.  The approach developed here is adaptable for general use in loop-tree duality applications.  Furthermore, the described methodology holds potential for extensions into higher-loop and more complex graph configurations.  While this work focuses on the graph topology, it is notable that $\Omega$ disregards edge labels, suggesting the framework's possibility to incorporate concepts like homotopy and combinatorial homotopy, which may offer additional insights into Feynman integrals and related quantities.  The proposed algorithm is offered as a possible method for tackling the vast array of distinct Feynman integrals, providing a potentially more streamlined alternative to case-by-case analysis. In a recent study, it was observed that objects not belonging to a specific category are remembered better, suggesting that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) utilize object features in an orthogonal manner to category representations. It was found that object recollection in RNNs is facilitated by dynamic generation of novel features that are distinct from existing category markers. This phenomenon was further investigated using multiple linear discriminant analysis (MLDA), revealing that object encodings in RNNs comprise of two separate components - one comprising of category-related features and another consisting of features uncorrelated with categories. It was also found that the latter component is crucial for object recollection. This study provides initial insights into how internal representations within neural networks function and offers potential avenues for enhancing object retention in safety-critical systems. Additionally, the findings offer a novel explanation for the effectiveness of recurrent neural networks in object categorization tasks.
