Research on Higgs boson production, both directly and indirectly from vector boson pairs, has yielded new insights into its characteristics. Using data collected from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, corresponding to a total luminosity of 35.9 fb^-1, the Higgs boson's properties were examined in this study. By analyzing on-shell and off-shell Higgs boson events with four leptons in the final state, the research team made precise measurements of the Higgs boson's width and unusual coupling to electroweak vector boson pairs. These findings align closely with the theoretical predictions of the standard model of fundamental physics, particularly with respect to the Higgs boson's width and non-standard couplings, which have been constrained. The Higgs boson's total width was determined to be less than 3 TeV with 95% confidence, while its anomalous couplings were restricted under the assumption that phase relationships remain constant. Furthermore, cross-section measurements for Higgs boson production, both directly and indirectly, as well as off-shell in the four-lepton channel, have been provided for the first time, taking into account the Higgs boson's off-shell contribution. These new measurements will serve to further scrutinize the theoretical Higgs boson model and make more precise predictions for additional beyond-standard-model Higgs boson searches. Additionally, using these data, lower limits on the mass of a beyond-standard-model Higgs boson were established at 79 GeV and 48 GeV, under the assumptions of fermiophobic and fermophilic Higgs boson properties, respectively. Finally, using these results, the research team further restricted the Higgs boson's unusual coupling to electroweak vector boson pairs and its influence on the ρ parameter. The Higgs boson's coupling to fermions was also restricted under the standard model of fundamental physics, while its coupling to gluons was restricted under the coupling of heavy quarks model. This research introduces a cutting-edge method for analyzing alterations within HSIs, using an advanced deep convolutional autoencoder framework that combines fused features from hierarchical levels. By constructing an autoencoder with multiple encoder blocks and a single decoder block, we've developed a novel approach to uncovering changes within HSIs without manual annotation. Our approach leverages hierarchical feature fusion to enhance the autoencoder's ability to capture alterations, outperforming existing change detection methods by achieving higher rates of accuracy, recall, and F1-score on various datasets. Notably, this framework's ability to process reflectance values and spatial context enables it to effectively address both change detection and image classification challenges. To validate the framework's efficacy, extensive experiments were conducted using 11 datasets, with results showing significant improvement in performance across three evaluation metrics for HSI applications. Furthermore, our approach's ability to dynamically adjust its internal parameters and adapt to different datasets was demonstrated through analysis of its architecture and parameter values. This research presents a comprehensive evaluation of the framework's performance, as well as an open-source code repository for future reference. Additionally, to facilitate reproducibility, the source code for our method can be accessed at https://github.com/zhenghui2019/FCFAE. This framework has the potential to contribute to the development of change detection algorithms for HSI applications and can be applied to various domains such as remote sensing, biomedical imaging, and industrial metrology. With its versatility and broad range of possible domains, this framework can serve as a general approach to analyzing alterations within multi-dimensional imaging data. This research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on deep learning in remote sensing sensing, while also addressing the current gap in research on this topic. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. Additionally, several key findings relate the transitivity degree to the variety's geometric and algebraic properties. For example, varieties with infinite transitivity degree have specific commutative invariant ring properties and are compactified by toric varieties with the same transitivity degree. Moreover, varieties that have a compactification with high transitivity degree satisfy certain geometric properties. This research also involves classifying algebraic torus actions based on their transitivity properties, leading to a comprehensive characterization theorem. Furthermore, this study establishes connections between the transitivity degree and Schur multipliers, a concept initially explored for linear actions but now extended to algebraic torus actions. Finally, this research investigates the relationship between the transitivity degree and the variety's singularities, a topic related to the Inverse Conjecture recently proposed by Cantor, Holwerda, and Keuntai. To address these questions, this study employs methods from commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, compactification, K-stability, and toric geometry. As a result, this research provides new insights into the transitivity degree, refining the existing work of Holwerda and Keuntai, while also introducing novel ideas and open problems. Ultimately, this research aims to understand the relationship between a variety's algebraic and geometric properties through the lens of its transitivity degree. Several open problems are presented, along with unsolved conjectures, that may lead to further significant developments in the field. Specifically, problem 7.1 asks for a verification of the stability conjecture, while problem 7.2 seeks to establish the transitivity degree for compactified quasi-affine varieties of arbitrary dimension. Additionally, problem 7.3 investigates the relationship between a variety's transitivity degree and its singularities, problem 7.4 explores the transitivity degree for linear torus actions, and problem 7.5 seeks compactified torus varieties with specific transitivity degree properties. We introduce an innovative technique called two-photon absorption edge transient current technique (TEP-TCT) for visualizing three-dimensional (3D) charge transport properties in semiconductors. This technique utilizes a localized infrared laser to create 3D electron-hole pairs near the diamond surface while measuring electrical response via a gold electrode embedded in the diamond, enabling us to map 3D charge transport with sub-millimeter spatial resolution and millisecond temporal resolution. We applied the TEP-TCT technique to 200-kilohertz doped and undoped single-crystalline diamond substrates, demonstrating its capability to analyze 3D charge transport and revealing the effect of 200 micrometer thick intrinsic regions on transport properties. Additionally, we successfully demonstrated time-resolved 3D mapping of diamond charge carriers across an abrupt p-n junction, highlighting the technique's potential for evaluating diamond-based radiation-detection systems. We anticipate that the TEP-TCT technique will serve as a valuable tool for assessing and optimizing diamond detectors. Moreover, its underlying principle can be adapted for other material systems with optically generated carriers to investigate their 3D charge transport properties. Furthermore, we envision that this technique will play a pivotal role in the development and research of large-scale, single-crystalline diamond detectors for advanced particle astrophysics and space research applications. Lastly, we suggest that the TEP-TCT technique can be employed as an alternative means to evaluate and assess the quality of diamond substrates, which could potentially replace traditional photo-lithography-based techniques. In summary, we believe that the TEP-TCT technique will offer novel insights into 3D charge transport properties in diamond and potentially open new avenues for research in semiconductor physics. Social media platforms are facing significant issues due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These problems not only harm users but also contaminate the environment with indecent language. If left unaddressed, these toxins could lead to severe consequences. To combat these problems, researchers have developed systems capable of detecting and classifying toxic content, primarily in English. Unfortunately, similar efforts are scarce in Arabic, although the need for such initiatives is pressing. In this research, we introduce a novel dataset comprising 9,000 sentences with three levels of misogyny and three types of off-color language. This dataset was annotated by three experts and validated through an inter-annotator agreement assessment. To create an effective detection system for toxic content, we divided the problem into two sub-tasks: detecting general toxic language and identifying specific types of misogyny. These sub-tasks were learned using a deep learning model that leverages contextual information from BERT and FastText. The results show that tackling both tasks simultaneously through multi-task learning yields better outcomes than focusing on each task in isolation. Moreover, our approach surpasses the performance of several baseline models, including those that utilize word embeddings, and even a model that integrated the annotations of three different datasets, including the FastText dataset. This research sets a new standard for detecting toxic content in Arabic with a high accuracy rate of 0.934, outperforming previous studies. The annotated dataset and source code are available for public access at https://github.com/abdullah-almubarak/Arabic-Toxic-Classification. We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in controllers that are resilient to environmental fluctuations. Our approach is validated through two real-world experiments and the integration of a novel constraint, referred to as the Epistemic Focus, which serves as a straightforward and efficient way to achieve this uncertainty limitation; ultimately resulting in policies that are more adaptable and robust. Additionally, our method exhibits improved performance in scenarios where rapid policy adjustments are required. All necessary code and data to replicate the results can be found on https://github.com/epfl-simba/RBOILCO. This research was presented at IJCAI 2019. Further details can be found in the paper by Gilitsch-Habiger et al. titled "Learning Robust Controllers Via Probabilistic Model-Based Policy Search."

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory for PCF, and as a result, we also establish that there is no recursive type in univalent type theory with inductive types. This is because the Scott model interprets any recursive function recursively, and since the Scott model exists in univalent type theory, truly recursive functions must exist, and therefore recursive types are impossible. Additionally, we enhance the traditional Scott model by allowing partial functions, and we show that the basic operations of PCF can be implemented recursively using only functions that are defined for non-minimal arguments, and further, that these operations can be implemented in a way that is independent of the specific domain of functions in which they are defined. This feature allows us to interpret PCF safely in types of partial functions, and as a result, safe and efficient partial interpretation can serve as an alternative to the Scott model for proving decidability in univalent type theory. Finally, we show that the basic operations of PCF can be implemented using only functions that are defined for arguments less than half the size of the domain, and therefore, PCF can be safely interpreted in types of functions where the argument and result are of the same size. This features allows for the development of compact codes, which can be used to prove that decidability in univalent type theory can be achieved with size complexity that grows like the square of the log of the input size. A recent study presents an implementation of a nonlinear quantum gate utilizing cold atomic gases in an optical cavity. Building on the basic principles of the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, the gate's efficiency was enhanced using a beam-splitter with nonlinear properties, achieved in the study using a mixture of $^{39}$K and $^{87}$Rb within a 2D optical cavity. Following a detailed simulation of the gate's performance, the results showed its ability to apply complex transformations and operate efficiently in a regime of high coherence where many-body effects are minimal. These findings indicate the potential for using cold atomic gases to develop robust quantum technologies. Additionally, the study suggests that this particular implementation could serve as a versatile quantum processor for executing complex algorithms within a wide range of experimental settings. A particular application of the gates in quantum information processing was also explored in the study, which presented a method for efficiently measuring the entanglement of multiple qubits using a sequence of nonlinear quantum gates and measurements. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. While focus is typically on isolating zero-dimensional nondegenerate solutions, certain scenarios require considering higher-dimensional cases. Essentially, the codimension-zero nondegenerate locus serves as a precursor to understanding singular solutions. Capturing this nondegenerate locus enables the subsequent isolation of all singular solutions, exhibiting various forms. In contrast to existing methods focused on zero-dimensional solutions, the approach for encoding nondegenerate configurations is relatively underdeveloped for higher-dimensional cases. Introducing a new concept - signature - this work provides a solution to compute the codimension-zero nondegenerate locus via a algorithm, further enabling the display of signature-based certificates through examples and its potential extension for handling sparse systems. Moreover, the proposed method is shown to be compatible with sparse solution tracking, presenting opportunities for future enhancements. In order to characterize signatures, combinatorial properties related to the Gr\"obner basis are analyzed along with novel concepts - signature ideals and lead signatures. Furthermore, a computational framework is developed, incorporating signature analysis, to visualize solution sets associated with specific parameterizations. Through comprehensive examples, this methodology is validated and showcased, presenting potential applications in various domains. Additionally, the study identifies challenges and proposes possible future research directions to expand the algorithm's capabilities in handling specific cases. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and $3.3<p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for forward rapidity in Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. The data were collected with the PHENIX detector for minimum bias and most central collisions. The observed direct photon yields are significantly lower than those predicted by two next-to-leading-order quantum chromodynamics calculations. The findings suggest that Cu$+$Cu direct photons are subject to prompt photon suppression and that their behavior aligns with the phenomenon of collective flow observed in charged hadron distributions. The data also present challenges for current theoretical models aiming to describe the phenomena of both hard scattering and collective flow observed in heavy-ion collisions. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to determine the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the least-dense four-colored hypergraph with the property that any subset of colors forms a dense tetrahedron graph. We develop an algorithm to identify a sparse four-colored hypergraph that cannot contain a dense tetrahedron subform, then demonstrate the existence of an even sparser hyperform within it. Our method utilizes a search through all possible colorings of a 9-element set and yields the first explicit construction of such a hyperform since the work of Erdos from 1965. We also refine the search to make it computationally feasible by incorporating some clever optimizations. We further modify our approach to suit an \ell_2-norm setting, where we seek the most sparse four-colored hyperform with this property, and obtain results up to a certain hyperform size. A recently proposed transcendental radial basis function, the hyperbolic
invariant RBF (HIRBF), has been introduced in a previous study. This present work
builds on that research by developing a new quasi-interpolation operator using
the HIRBF, which maintains the shape of data for functions with specific properties.
Not only does this new operator provide more accurate interpolation points for
multivariate data, but it also overcomes scaling issues affecting other RBF
operators, including those based on the standard transcendental RBF. We have
also derived explicit formulas for the HIRBF and examined its second-order derivative. 
Furthermore, preliminary convergence analysis for the new operator is presented,
along with a range of example demonstrations showing its effectiveness and
accuracy in applications such as data visualization and reproduction of original
function shapes. We have also successfully addressed the problem of unsufficient
data for interpolation in high-dimensional spaces by incorporating Tikhonov regularization. 
Finally, the new operator has been tested in solving second-order partial differential
equations, specifically Laplace and heat diffusion problems, where it outperforms
other methods in our studies. These findings serve as a foundation for further
research on shape-preserving approximations using the HIRBF and its potential
applications in scientific visualization and differential equations.

Our analysis explores the synchronization of climate change beliefs held by scientists, policymakers, and economists, examining how their distinct narratives contribute to the widespread acceptance of climate science. We discovered that policymakers and economists, driven by personal interests, often develop narratives that align with their professional goals, whereas scientists primarily focus on the scientific consensus. Furthermore, policymakers' stories are heavily influenced by political considerations. We also found that personal interests can impede the adoption of established climate science narratives, leading to non-conforming views among these groups. Finally, we suggest that promoting consistent climate science narratives may be challenging, but encouraging consistency within existing narratives could be an effective approach. This research provides valuable insights for climate change communication and policy-making initiatives. It also offers a theoretical framework that can be applied to understanding the dynamics of social norms in various other contexts. Additionally, we have provided a detailed guide outlining our research approach, which can serve as a useful resource for replicating our methodology. Soft grippers are increasingly popular in manipulation due to their flexibility,
ease of use, and potential to use existing objects as tools, but accurately modeling
them is extremely challenging, making online dynamic filtering and control crucial.
We have developed a multi-fingered soft gripper capable of picking and lifting small
objects, and employ the Koopman operator theory along with sparse model approximation
techniques to create an adaptive model for its dynamics, which can then be utilized for
open-loop and closed-loop control purposes. The results show the success of our method
in controlling the gripper's movement and enabling it to lift objects, even when starting
from a non-optimal state with an imperfect model. Moreover, we have introduced a novel
control approach that integrates the Extended Exponential Stability (EES) concept, which
allows reducing the time required for the gripper to reach a stable state. The research
is based on both theoretical findings and real-world experiments, which are showcased in
this article's videos attached at the end. The code used for data processing and gripper
control management can be accessed via https://github.com/SoftRoboticsLab/Grippy.

This research delves into the relationship between lung cancer's various types and patient survival times, utilizing data from the Cell Imaging Data Science (CIDS) Center. By combining image and textual information from histology samples, we can predict high-level cell types and thereby determine lung cancer subtypes. This knowledge enables us to create patient groups with similar diagnoses and, using their overall tumor characteristics, forecast their five-year survival times. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
This analysis is crucial for all businesses as it allows them to identify their strengths and
weaknesses, making it a valuable tool for market research. We've developed an LSTM-based
approach to sentiment analysis on the IMDB dataset, comparing it to the conventional
convolutional neural network method. Our findings indicate that LSTMs outperform CNNs in this
task, with the capacity to achieve even higher accuracy using a combination of both methods. 
This report serves as a preliminary step in applying the same technique for analyzing
Twitter posts' sentiment. We've addressed challenges like limited data for model training
by utilizing multiple word embeddings and explored the impact of varying the number of
training samples on our model's performance. Ultimately, we've successfully applied our
LSTM-based approach to sentiment analysis on the Twitter dataset, achieving a remarkable
accuracy of 90% in determining the sentiment of individual tweets. 
To validate our model's effectiveness, we've also conducted a detailed analysis of its
predictions on both the IMDB and Twitter datasets. We've calculated its precision, recall,
F1-score, and mean squared error on the IMDB dataset and its accuracy on the Twitter
dataset. Our model has been recognized as superior to competing approaches on Twitter
sentiment analysis, with some adjustments, in accordance with the 50dig rule. 
Lastly, we've explored the deep learning model's capability to determine the likelihood of
each tweet being categorized as either positive or negative by computing its logistic
probability. We've also utilized the NLTK library to convert raw tweets into a format
compatible with our model for processing. 
We've made our code available on GitHub for public access. 
In the future, we plan to enhance our model by incorporating more advanced techniques
like using the BERT language model for pre-training and leveraging the Twitter API for
gathering a more extensive dataset. 
We're open to collaborating on this project; if you're interested, please reach out to
us via GitHub. 
In the spirit of transparency, in accordance with the 2021 IEEE guidelines on transparency
in AI, we've provided a detailed description of our work and its underlying data, as well as
the code used for our analysis. 
This report serves as a preprint, with the formal version to be published in the IEEE SPS
TCVT Journal.

This knowledge guides our response, preventing our contribution to the conversation from meandering or failing to meet expectations. Although natural language can convey roles through explicit language or a conversation's context, most research assumes a single predefined role for both parties. To address this gap, we focus on developing a system capable of determining a speaker's intended role and then tailoring its response accordingly. Specifically, our model is designed to work in open-domain settings, where role specifications aren't explicitly provided but can be inferred from dialogue history. We introduce a new dataset, RoleCon, comprising 9,000 human-written conversations with clearly defined speaker roles, utilized to train and evaluate our proposed model. Our results indicate that our model outperforms non-conditioned baselines in every aspect and maintains a reasonable, human-like error rate in its responses. Additionally, it achieves near-human-level performance in role specification accuracy. Our work bridges the gap between open-domain dialogue systems that overlook role considerations and those that manually define roles, paving the way for more natural and effective interactions between users with varying roles. A novel signaling interaction framework, combining AI-powered causal reasoning and machine learning, is proposed to establish a common language for transmission. Since communication effectiveness relies on both parties's understanding of the semantic meaning, the framework incorporates a competitive dynamic where messages are crafted to maximize one's own semantic grasp while limiting the other's comprehension. This dynamic leads to a strategic equilibrium where both parties employ the same efficient semantic transmission approach, and we present an algorithm for finding this equilibrium through an iterative exchange of messages within a simulated environment. This approach offers a promising alternative to traditional resource allocation methods in semantic communications. Simulation results demonstrate that this method outperforms current semantic communication techniques in terms of reliability and efficiency when there is no consensus on language use. Additionally, this framework has potential applications beyond semantic communications and can be applied to various fields where there is a need for strategic semantic exchange, such as data transmission and AI-powered interaction. A newly developed approach employs the mimetic finite difference method within a three-dimensional fracture network framework. This system comprises interconnected vertical fractures set within a bounding box. To account for the fractures as distinct media from the surrounding rock, the mesh is generated by combining standard grid blocks with specially tailored cells representing the fractures. A novel fracture flow subroutine has been integrated with the existing solution framework to enable simulation. As a result, a fully coupled matrix-fracture aquifer system can be solved, allowing for the examination of flow and transport within this multi-domain environment. Given that the mesh is constructed in a unified manner, this approach avoids complications arising from domain decomposition and interface issues. To validate the model, it has been validated through comparison with both standard mesh blocking and previous fracture mesh handling methods. Ultimately, this model provides a versatile tool for further research on flow and transport within fractured geometries. Several such studies are presented here. The introduction of diverse types of fractures is demonstrated, along with an exploration of the effects of varying fracture density and distribution. The model also shows promise in simulating flow and transport at scales relevant to practical applications, such as carbon capture storage operations. Given its relatively fast computational speed, this model can be employed for both precise analytical studies and broader parametric analyses. The model's code has been made freely available for other researchers to access at https://github.com/alexboswell/mfd_cfd. The specific details of the approach outlined here are known as version 1.0 of the discrete fracture matrix mimetic finite difference method. Efforts are currently underway to enhance this approach with additional features and improved performance. Some potential enhancements are described here. The primary limitations of this approach are its lack of handling of certain complex fracture configurations and its failure to account for certain phenomena relevant to specific applications. Nevertheless, this model provides a fundamental tool for simulating flow and transport within discrete fracture matrix systems and has already shown potential in various research applications. RSUs are widely regarded as a vital component in vehicular networks for updating in-vehicle software and maintaining connectivity, but this approach has several drawbacks, such as high infrastructure costs and limited coverage. To address these issues, this research proposes a network design based on vehicle relays, where vehicles act as relays to extend coverage and enhance connectivity. To model this setup, we develop a stochastic geometry model for vehicle deployment and combine it with an association rule that favors the closest RSU and then vehicles acting as relays. We analyzed the outcomes using outage probability and showed that this design outperforms traditional RSU-based networks in terms of reduced outage probability and increased data transfer speed without the need for vehicle relocation. Furthermore, our findings indicate that vehicle relays can significantly boost connectivity, particularly in dense areas, where they can cover up to 50% more area, thus reducing the need for RSUs and thus lowering infrastructure costs. To validate these outcomes, we also conducted time-domain simulations using INET Framework and presented our code on GitHub for public access. Based on these analyses, we determined that vehicle relays offer a more cost-effective solution than RSUs for covering more area and enhancing connectivity in vehicular networks. Specifically, this design can provide the same level of connectivity as 2.5 times more RSUs at a significantly lower cost, thus making it a more affordable option for vehicular networks. To summarize, this research proposed a novel network design based on vehicle relays and provided a thorough mathematical and simulation-based analysis of this setup, which demonstrates that it outperforms traditional RSU-based networks in terms of reduced outage probability and increased data transfer speed without the need for vehicle relocation. Furthermore, we showed that vehicle relays offer a more affordable solution than RSUs for enhancing connectivity in vehicular networks. To validate these outcomes, we made our code on GitHub publicly accessible for other researchers to verify our findings. To extend this research, we plan to investigate how vehicle relays can be used to enhance connectivity in other types of wireless networks beyond vehicular networks. To achieve this, we will adapt our current design to fit the specific requirements of these other networks, which may involve using vehicles as relays to cover hard-to-reach areas in mobile satellite networks, using vehicles as relays to extend coverage in IoT networks, and using vehicles as relays to enhance connectivity in machine-to-machine networks. Wikipedia's ultimate objective is to provide a comprehensive record of the world's knowledge.  Achieving this goal hinges on the quality of its content, which is heavily reliant on volunteer editors' efforts.  Their contributions, however, are split between high-quality content and lower-quality material produced during editing experiments.  Identifying and labeling this low-quality content with reliability would facilitate research aimed at enhancing article quality using machine learning.  This task is complicated by factors such as content deletion and revisions that contradict previous edits.  To overcome these obstacles, we've developed an automated system that analyzes editing patterns to accurately label low-quality content on Wikipedia.  Tested on various categories, our system has demonstrated success rates exceeding 99% in conjunction with an accuracy rate of 94% for labels.  Notably, this system outperforms existing manual labeling methods, which consume significantly less resources (including energy, materials, and human time).  As a result, our system enables researchers to focus on more pressing challenges in the knowledge domain while we continue to refine our approach to address remaining issues.  Details regarding data, code, and research are available at https://github.com/ahmedebaid/LLQC. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and being able to collect its output, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. This paper presents a novel approach that bypasses these limitations by training the model to replicate the original network's decision-making capabilities without requiring any information about its internal workings or its training dataset. This approach leverages only two pieces of information: the original network's class probabilities and whether its predictions match the test labels. Through comprehensive evaluations on popular image classification datasets, the proposed method has been shown to consistently outperform traditional knowledge distillation methods and can also serve as a reliable model assessment tool. Additionally, the method's advantages extend to training deep neural networks on small, resource-constrained devices where other knowledge distillation methods may be infeasible due to data collection requirements. The proposed method's source code has been made publicly available.

Furthermore, several examples of T-duals are calculated using this formalism and illustrated with geometric representations. These examples demonstrate that a geometric object can be equivalently described by multiple different $C^*$-algebraic structures, thus providing a broader definition of noncommutive topology. Traditional imitation learning approaches face obstacles when expert inputs are costly to obtain, expert policies are difficult to articulate, or experts refuse to provide demonstrations due to anxiety or reward functions that discourage cooperation. In scenarios where only basic, successful trajectories are available, prior methods struggle to produce diverse and accurate imitation results. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Co-Imitation Learning (CIL), an innovative framework that capitalizes on multiple successful trailblazers to create a learned expert policy without requiring expert supervision. CIL leverages trailblazer data to train trailblazer-imitation models, which in turn serve as inputs for an expert-imitation model. By iteratively updating both models in tandem, the expert policy converges rapidly. Notably, our approach enables the learning of multiple expert policies from various trailblazers, thereby facilitating trailblazer-policy selection and refining existing policies through the incorporation of novel trailblazers. Our method's efficacy is evident in simulation experiments involving diverse robotic settings, where it outperforms existing imitation learning methods while achieving trailblazer-policy selection and adaptation capabilities. CIL has the potential to revolutionize various collaborative systems by rectifying past imitation learning shortcomings and providing expert-like performance without requiring extensive expert supervision. CIL's source code is available at https://github.com/robot-learning/co-imitation-learning. CIL's video demonstration is available at https://youtu.be/6Q8xk6Q8xk. This paper proposes a metric function that enhances the performance of Progressive Adaptive Coding (PAC) modulation schemes. By optimizing PAC code computations based on a proposed Euclidean metric for multiple-intensity channels with unknown parameters, we address the issue of high computational complexity associated with finding these codes on such channels. To this end, we present a general method for efficiently calculating the PAC codes of any order through a set of recursive formulas applicable to various channels, including those with unknown parameters. This allows dynamic adjustment of PAC codes in real-time according to changing conditions of the intensity channels shephered by PAC codes of order 1. Furthermore, our method facilitates the development of multiple PAC codes with distinct orders, which can be used to modulate different portions of a transmitted signal and improve system performance by mitigating the effects of interference. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, several numerical experiments have been conducted using various channels with parameters that are either known or unknown. In these experiments, the computed PAC codes using our metric function have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional methods. Specifically, our results show that the Euclidean metric can enhance the performance of PAC modulation schemes by up to 20% in certain scenarios, which highlights the importance of metric function selection in PAC code computations. To further investigate the computational efficiency of our approach, we conducted a detailed analysis of the computational complexity associated with finding PAC codes through a binary metric function, which revealed an exponential relationship with the PAC code order. In contrast, the Euclidean metric was found to yield a computational complexity that is linearly dependent on the PAC code order. This observation underscores the significance of our proposed metric function in enabling the efficient computation of PAC codes with high orders. To further expand the scope of PAC codes, we have also developed a method for calculating the PAC codes of order $m$ through the recursive computation of higher-order codes, which demonstrated superior performance in various channel scenarios. Furthermore, our results show that the Euclidean metric can be applied to develop a real-valued PAC modulation scheme, which was found to offer improved performance and simplified computational complexity compared to traditional methods. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, several numerical experiments have been conducted using various channels with parameters that are either known or unknown. In these experiments, the computed real-valued PAC codes using our metric function have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional methods. Specifically, our results show that the real-valued PAC modulation scheme can enhance performance by up to 40% in certain scenarios, which highlights the importance of our proposed metric function in developing this scheme. To accomplish this, we introduce an innovative, efficient, and adaptable pipeline that combines a hand-tracking module and an object reconstruction module. A novel, markerless system utilizing a depth camera for calibrating and positioning a robot's end-effector has been developed, allowing for precise estimation of the end-effector's 6 Degree of Freedom (6DoF) pose in real-time within a dynamic environment. This is achieved through the application of a deep learning-based approach that estimates the robot's End-Effector Transform (EET) directly from depth image data, without requiring any prior knowledge or conventional 3D point-based features that might be affected by noise in the depth data. This method has been validated on two distinct robotic setups using a standard model and diverse real-world scenes, resulting in accurate pose estimation within 5mm and 5deg for the first robot, and 3mm and 4deg for the second, at a rate of over 60Hz. Furthermore, the estimated EET data is used to improve the traditional PNP algorithm for enhanced accuracy in calculating the pose. This proposed method has been successfully integrated into a robotic system for automatically arranging items in a specific pattern. Its potential future applications include domestic service robots operating in dynamic environments to facilitate tasks such as arranging items, picking objects, and delivering goods. Additionally, this work has been publicly released as the ArrangeIt Suite, providing a comprehensive set of tools for other researchers to build upon. This includes the pre-trained models, the robotic setup calibration software, and the code for calculating end-effector pose and depth camera rotation and translation. We suggest a dual role for the axion, proposing that it generates neutrino masses through a previously proposed mechanism, while also serving as a dark matter particle that becomes stable in a specific arrangement. To support this idea, we establish that the axion's interactions with other particles can be within the acceptable range as dictated by Ultra-High Energy Cosmic Microwave Background observations. Furthermore, we propose two possible scenarios in which neutrinos develop sterile counterparts, with the neutrinos acting as dark matter particles that become stable due to non-standard interactions, offering potential explanations for discrepancies in space-based and ground-based dark matter detection experiments. These scenarios revolve around the axion's mass range, with possible solutions emerging from a range approximately between 0.1 microeV to 30 meV. The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we provide arguments that they are largely unfounded. Furthermore, we describe various strategies for numerical evaluations of causal representations, including the use of unitarity cuts and clustering algorithms. Our presentation draws from the author's previous talks at BSM2018 and LPA 2019, and serves as an introductory overview for readers of the associated proceedings papers. Due to publication constraints, the content is adapted from arXiv:1803.02.28, arXiv:2011.13027, arXiv:2101.01.264, and arXiv:2106.01.626.

This research introduces a method for embedding a set of operators, defined within a specific group and exhibiting non-expansive properties in relation to a given norm, into a space from a related group, maintaining or reducing dimensions. The method is applied in the context of machine learning to define a compact topology on the space of group-equivariant non-expansive operators, enabling sampling and establishing density theorems. Furthermore, we extend our findings to the topological space formed by pairs of group-equivariant operators, demonstrating the existence of a compact embedding, sampling theorems, and proving dense sets within these spaces. Our methodology is exemplified through applications in computer vision, specifically in the perception space, where we show that certain group-equivariant convolutional operators can be efficiently applied to data from Stabilizer and Cayley groups, previously inaccessible due to dimension constraints. Additionally, we present a novel approach for generating random perception pairs and establish a dense set within these spaces, thereby contributing to the development of randomized sampling methods and compact representations of high-dimensional data. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/alexeyask/perception_pairs. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite decades of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Recent breakthroughs in transformer models have improved the accuracy of automated essay grading.  However, this solution still faces practical limitations in everyday use.  To enhance its effectiveness, we explored the application of data augmentation through text encodings in the BERT space to a GPT-like language model.  Our results show that this approach contributes significantly to improvement.  Furthermore, we discovered that combining data augmentation with transfer learning yields the most satisfactory outcomes.  To validate our findings, we employed a basic automated essay grading task and compared its performance with established models, including BERT and GPT-2, as well as a more advanced transformer model called RoBERTa.  Our research demonstrates that the integration of data augmentation in the training of a transformer model results in substantial gains in accuracy.  This achievement has the potential to contribute to ongoing research in automated essay grading.  Additionally, our study's methodology can be adapted for text classification tasks in various other domains.  Given the diverse applications of text augmentation, it is likely that this approach will have a broader impact on NLP research and practice. Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks, including treebanking and parsing, largely relied on the 20th century written language. This research paper addresses essential data needs for 21st century spoken Hebrew, focusing on task-dependent annotations for dialect, register, and sociolect. It introduces the Hebrew Universal Treebank (HUT) - an enhanced, expanded, and updated corpus that incorporates the spoken language. The project's findings are based on a thorough analysis of spoken Hebrew, and we outline strategies for gathering relevant data among the younger population, whose language use is increasingly influential. The HUT project has made progress in developing new guidelines and evaluating them using expert and automated methods. Despite these efforts, creating comprehensive guidelines for Hebrew NLP proves to be a complex challenge, and we hope that our project will contribute to advancing this field in an honest and transparent manner. This research will be particularly beneficial to tasks that involve spoken language, but its impact will also extend to written Hebrew, where dialect variation remains underrepresented. The HUT project's resources are accessible for free, and we welcome collaboration, input, and feedback from the NLP community. We plan to maintain and update our corpus regularly to reflect the evolving nature of spoken Hebrew, and we anticipate contributing to the ongoing development of Hebrew NLP through regular Kessler et al. extensions. A growing need to translate observational data into operational models is being felt across various sectors, but current algorithms have limited capacity to incorporate diverse data sources due to their assumption of a single underlying equation governing the behavior of the system. This report outlines a new approach that enables the simultaneous application of models to multiple data sets, addressing the issue of conflicting information and improving overall outcomes. It also highlights potential hazards and obstacles of this approach and proposes a method for addressing these challenges. The results demonstrate that cooperative learning can lead to more accurate predictions and a deeper understanding of the system than was possible with a single data source. The methodology was successfully tested on open public datasets to model two interconnected environmental systems – the behavior of a stream and its surrounding landscape – and the movement of a butterfly species across different latitudes. The findings have significant implications for addressing complex, data-driven challenges in environmental and ecological contexts. This research explores the impact of degree-degree correlations on the error-correcting capabilities of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, which are widely utilized due to their exceptional performance in noisy channels and flexibility in design. By examining various LDPC ensembles with degree-degree correlations, we identify a novel phenomenon where such codes can surpass the maximum coverage rate, which previously only applied to independent and uniformly-distributed LDPC ensembles. Furthermore, we introduce an innovative method to create LDPC code ensembles with guaranteed decoding success rates for arbitrary input error patterns, which leads to an unexpected benefit of enhanced security, as these codes are more resistant to successive decoding attacks. Through simulations, we verify that these degree-degree correlated LDPC codes can achieve better performance, particularly in scenarios where the channel conditions are poor and rapid decoding is necessary. As an added advantage, the proposed method also facilitates more efficient usage of resources in memory and processing, as the maximum allowed sparsity and depth are increased. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that degree-degree correlations offer a previously unexplored means of enhancing the performance and security of LDPC codes. Additionally, the research provides novel insights into the fundamental characteristics of LDPC codes. Researchers have developed a new attack method that exploits a flaw in the phase randomness of a key distribution system using partial randomness. This has led to a more efficient and less detectable hacking technique than previously known methods. It was found that the new attack can succeed with virtually unlimited key exchange, but the vulnerability can only be detected if the phase randomness meets a specific threshold. Furthermore, if the threshold is met, our algorithm can generate nearly complete secret keys. We also developed a method to enhance the security of the key distribution system by using a specific type of entropy from chaotic sources. This has successfully created secure key pairs in tests. Our findings provide an improved solution for securely exchanging data in various applications that rely on quantum key distribution technology. Recent research has demonstrated the capabilities of large language models to perform "in-context" learning, achieving impressive results across various domains. Nevertheless, the impact of various training corpora on this learning remains an area of uncertainty. In this study, we investigate how different types of datasets influence in-context learning by examining both domain-specific and diverse datasets. Our analysis indicates that the model's performance is significantly enhanced when the instruction is directly included within the training data, yielding better outcomes with domain-specific datasets and comparable results with datasets from other domains. Additionally, we observe that our model excels at processing instructions from datasets with more straightforward answers, whereas it struggles with richer data sources, including the CoQA dataset. Moreover, we highlight both the advantages and limitations of our model's ability to learn in-context when incorporating question-answering prompts from the QuASAR dataset, emphasizing the need to consider the inherent characteristics of each dataset when evaluating the model's performance. Our findings provide valuable insights for the effective utilization of large language models in practical applications across different domains and may contribute to the development of more sophisticated benchmarks suited to the unique capabilities of these models. Our models' performance have been replicated and our code are available on GitHub for public access. Furthermore, we have released the dataset used for our experiments which includes the training data for multiple choice questions. This data can be utilized by other researchers for model development and evaluation purposes. Our models' results have been added to the leaderboard for further reference. Our paper has been accepted for publication at the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Natural Language Processing.

Furthermore, we note that growth rates vary depending on the level of thermal conensitivity and magnetic field strength. The investigation of CP violation in beauty and charm hadrons is crucial for expanding our comprehension of this complex phenomenon as observed in neutrinos and certain atomic nuclei.  Although CP violation in beauty and charm hadrons has not been proven to exist, several experiments have obtained statistically insignificant results that are compatible with the prediction of CP violation due to pentagon diagrams.  This article discusses the most recent findings from the Belle, BaBar, and LHCb experiments.  It outlines potential avenues for future research, which could potentially lead to the discovery of CP violation in two specific types of mesons: $B^0_s$ and $D^0$.  If CP violation in these mesons exists, it could potentially be detected within the next five to seven years.  However, it is also possible that several more years of research may be required to make such a discovery.  This article was initially presented at CERN's 2014 Precision Physics at LHC workshop.  It has been revised to incorporate the latest research findings and has been updated to reflect the current state of knowledge in this field. The success of future fifth-generation (5G) wireless systems largely depends on their ability to minimize their environmental impact while providing efficient user service experiences. To achieve this, 5G systems need to effectively balance all aspects of their performance, including performance, cost, and sustainability. However, the traditional approach based on centralized network design may not be sufficient to meet the complex needs of 5G networks. To address this challenge, our approach focuses on the development of a self-organizing 5G network with a dynamic control mechanism that can adapt to changing conditions in real-time. To achieve this, we introduce two new procedures, called the core network selection procedure and the edge network reconfiguration procedure, which work together to optimize 5G network performance. The effectiveness of our proposed procedures was verified through simulations using realistic scenarios and metrics, such as network capacity, energy consumption, and user data rates. The results show that our procedures can improve 5G network performance by increasing capacity and reducing energy consumption without compromising user service experiences. Specifically, we observed a significant improvement in capacity and a substantial reduction in energy consumption, with only a minor decrease in user data rates. To further validate our approach, we performed an in-depth analysis of the trade-off between capacity and energy consumption, which confirmed the efficacy of our procedures. To facilitate the implementation of our approach in existing networks, we also developed a set of recommendations based on the current network standards and technologies used in LTE systems. To summarize, our approach provides a reliable solution for managing 5G networks and can be easily adapted to other wireless systems. This research explores the feasibility of speech synthesis without requiring human annotation, instead using acoustic models to train units from unlabelled data and transcription models to derive untranscribed data. We compare two approaches to unit modelling - the first using clusters from pre-trained models, the second using hierarchical models that capture inter-unit relationships. While the hierarchical model shows potential, we find that synthesised speech with units from either method is not as natural as its counterpart with human-annotated units. Nevertheless, this study shows that zero-resource speech synthesis is achievable and highlights the potential for hierarchical models to improve performance once additional non-parallel data is incorporated. We also observe that the transcription models used here can be improved upon by utilising parallel data, and that this in turn enhances synthesis. We hypothesise that combining the two datasets at the unit level could yield more effective clustering and improve synthesis quality. Building on these findings, we suggest a two-phase strategy for achieving fully automatic speech synthesis: initially training units and transcription models on large datasets, and subsequently refining these using parallel data from speakers in the target population. This approach holds promise for delivering high-quality speech synthesis while minimising the need for time-consuming human annotation. We believe this methodology has the potential to underpin fully automated speech synthesis systems capable of handling diverse speakers and languages. We provide audio examples to illustrate our research at https://speechresearch.github.io/zero-resource-speech-synthesis/. A newly developed planning method, known as Multi-Stage Coupled Convex Programming (MSCCP), is presented, which effectively tackles difficult motion planning problems. MSCCP employs data-driven techniques to create more accurate models and incorporates model predictive control to ensure robustness in uncertain planning scenarios. The method's performance is demonstrated through its application on two complex systems: a planetary rover with a 3D printed quadruped and a humanoid robot. Testing of MSCCP on these robots, subjected to simulated disturbances, reveals its ability to provide planner outputs and accurately estimate computation times. Experimental results show that MSCCP yields a 75% reduction in planning time and achieves 30-40% shorter trajectories when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, MSCCP's data-driven nature allows it to outperform other methods, particularly on the humanoid robot where its data-driven approach results in 10-20% reduced planning time. Additionally, MSCCP's capability to adapt to changing environments was validated through testing on various outdoor and indoor scenarios. The research presents a novel planning tool that is versatile, efficient, and adaptable for diverse mobile robot systems. The study's findings, accompanied by computational resources, are available at https://github.com/Robot-Learn/VTCCP. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario where the pivot moves in a vertical circle, the primary resonance occurred twice a period and the secondary resonances occurred three to four times a period. Additionally, when both vertical and horizontal motions combined to create a circular motion, the primary resonance occurred at a rate of twice a period in both the vertical and horizontal planes. In the context of decentralized machine learning over graph topologies, we develop a new distributionally robust learning algorithm called DR-DSGD, effectively handling graph distribution changes after learning commences. DR-DSGD is an enhancement of the traditional Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent method, integrated with the Wasserstein Fourier-Moment relaxation and entropy penalty from the TPE robust optimization technique. We mathematically prove that DR-DSGD achieves faster convergence compared to previous robust methods, with our experimental results demonstrating its superior performance in half-node connectivity and random graph scenarios. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/zheng-hu/DR-DSGD. Furthermore, we have introduced an online repository containing our experiment results: https://dr-dsgd.github.io/. This repository aims to facilitate replication of our research and provide an open database for decentralized robust optimization experiments. It is our intention that DR-DSGD may serve as a building block for future developments in this field. With our approach, various graph topologies can now be addressed from a distribution robust perspective, encompassing tree, ring, random, and grid graph topologies. Additionally, our method exhibits improved robustness in the face of changing node connections within a decentralized system. We have successfully applied our method to solve a $0-1$ regression problem through our experiments. We employ the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to investigate the initial energy conditions and particle production in relativistic nuclear collisions before equilibrium is established. By combining experimental data on final transverse momentum spectra and rapidity distributions from LHC collisions, we determine the average initial energy density of gluons and light quarks. This approach enables us to constrain non-perturbative effects and obtain information about the primordial state formations, which are crucial for further perturbative calculations. Furthermore, we utilize the obtained energy density data to model particle production at the LHC, resulting in predictions that align with experimental findings for both most central and peripheral collisions. Notably, our results for charged particle multiplicities exceed those calculated using standard perturbative QCD by about 30%. We also examine the behavior of elliptical flow across various collision energies and observe agreement with ATLAS and ALICE experiments. Furthermore, we apply our method to analyze data from RHIC collisions, which yields results consistent with theoretical models employing the concept of hydrodynamic attractors. However, our results from LHC central collisions indicate that the concept of hydrodynamic attractors may not be sufficient to describe particle production at extremely low values of the transverse momentum. Additionally, we discover that the observed momentum anisotropy in particle production can be attributed to energy non-uniformity during the hydrodynamic stage, which may also contribute to the phenomenon known as "flow delay." Finally, we utilize our approach to investigate the concept of "blackening" in the hydrodynamic attractor framework and find that it does not significantly impact particle production at the LHC. However, we do observe some influence at the lower energy conditions encountered in RHIC collisions. Finally, we explore an alternative method for describing particle production based on the concept of hydrodynamic attractors and find that it yields results comparable to those obtained using the standard procedure. While both methods yield similar results for most quantities, there are some subtle differences that become more pronounced at lower energies and densities. These differences stem from the distinct characteristics of the initial state energy conditions and the way they evolve into the hydrodynamic stage. Furthermore, we note that our approach can be applied to investigate other complex phenomena arising from the interaction of hadrons in nuclear collisions. Ultimately, we believe that our results provide significant insights into the intricate history of relativistic nuclear collisions and shed light on the complex relationships between various stages of matter formation. This research focuses on the issue of reducing performance-to-saturation trade-offs in systems with input constraints. Historically, the two realms have been examined separately, with one approach optimizing system performance under input limitations or ensuring system stability in the presence of saturation. A new framework is introduced to simultaneously balance these considerations, providing a balanced indicator of performance and saturation levels. This metric is utilized to derive control strategies that offer optimal trade-off ratios between the two, which can be accomplished through different priorities. Two methods are presented to set these priorities – one based on zonotopes and vintage variables, and another involving machine learning and optimal regularization. The proposed approaches are demonstrated to be effective in a quadcopter simulator with actuator saturation and real-world experimental testing validated these results. Additionally, the methodology is shown to be adaptable for systems with multiple nonlinearities and diverse applications such as power systems and chemical reactors. The code for these applications is available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreasknoll/Balanced-Saturation-Performance.git. The associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q8xk6e4kYU. This research investigates the resonant effects of solar radiation pressure on artificial satellites, specifically those governed by the Euler-Lagrange equations within the equatorial plane of a rotating frame aligned with Earth. We identify and analyze two types of resonances that emerge, comparing numerical and analytical models to gain valuable insights. To validate our findings, we examine the long-term behavior of a satellite orbiting Earth and observe its potential transfer to geostationary orbit under specific conditions. Our study provides practical estimates for the times and amplitude ranges in which these resonances can influence a satellite's orbit. To establish the precision of our model, we conduct a statistical analysis alongside numerical simulations over extended periods, revealing up to a 2% error in our predictions. This research aims to enhance the precision of celestial body orbit modeling, with a focus on solar radiation pressure resonance phenomena. Additionally, our findings contribute to the exploration of artificial gravity and other applications related to orbit manipulation. Furthermore, this study may facilitate the development of strategies to exploit these resonances and potentially transfer a satellite to the geostationary orbit without energy augmentation. To this end, we outline potential research avenues to achieve this goal. Lastly, our work provides a comprehensive overview of solar radiation pressure resonance models, offering a reference for researchers working on related projects. To facilitate future replication, we have made available the Python code used for our numerical simulations through a public repository. This includes the functionality to calculate SRP resonance periods, amplify and demonstrate our approach to simulating solar radiation pressure effects. This code can be accessed at: https://github.com/cesarobr/SRP-celestial-propulsion. Moreover, we have developed a graphical user interface using Visual Basic, which enables users to visualize the trajectories of celestial bodies under the influence of solar radiation pressure resonance. This interface can be accessed at: https://github.com/cesarobr/SRP-celestial-propulsion/blob/main/SRP_Celestial_Propulsion.vbp. This interface allows users to replicate our findings and simulate the transfer of a satellite from one orbit to another using the analytical model described in this research. This can be particularly useful in the development of strategies for celestial body propulsion, which we discuss in the conclusion section. This research aims to contribute to that goal. This work was developed in collaboration with my supervisor, Dr. Luciano Dalle Pezze, and Dr. Eduardo Brasilier, both from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul. The ability of the tight-binding model to capture the electronic structure of a material, from the lowest energy state to high energy states, makes it beneficial for studying not only insulating materials but also those that are conductive. When we examine how a solid interacts with light, the electronic interactions within the tight-binding model need to be corrected to ensure the calculations are mathematically consistent. This work presents a method to ensure that these corrections do not disrupt the rules of the game (gauge invariance), allowing us to study how a solid interacts with light across its entire energy spectrum. This work tackles the problem of estimating PASCAL3D+ objects' pose and shape, starting from category-specific 2D and 3D keypoints within an image. A new keypoint network is introduced that combines PASCAL3D+ objects' features to predict corresponding keypoints, outperforming existing methods. To estimate 3D keypoints from a single 2D image, a novel approach leveraging large-scale synthetic data is developed, which learns object-specific pose from corresponding keypoints in simulated scenes. To enhance robustness, a method based on mean absolute scaled error is introduced, along with a new metric, the SDE. The proposed network excels at pose and shape estimation, particularly from limited real-world 3D keypoints, outperforming other methods. To validate its effectiveness, the network was tested on PASCAL3D+ with various levels of keypoint availability. Additionally, a new dataset, Semantic3D, was created with keypoint labels for 30 categories, facilitating training and testing of pose and shape estimation methods. Semantic3D comprises over 8000 real-world images and 120000 synthetic images, offering the largest known collection of keypoint labels. The dataset was found to be instrumental in training a network that could accurately estimate objects' pose and shape in real-world images. The proposed network and the Semantic3D dataset will be made available to accelerate object pose and shape estimation research. We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By analyzing the Cauchy distribution's properties, specifically the variance of its parameter $\tau$, we will determine the confidence interval using the sample's mean and median, thereby establishing a confidence disc, and further derive a confidence square for assessing the parameter estimates' accuracy. The proposed method will be evaluated with numerical simulations and demonstrated with practical examples. The R code employed in this study will be accessible via the link: https://github.com/igorjovelic/Cauchy_confidence_disc_and_square. The findings show that both the disc and square methods exhibit adequate coverage of the true parameter value with minimal bias across various sample sizes and distributions, including both parameterized and non-parameterized scenarios. Notably, the square method exhibits more precise estimation than the disc method, and the latter performs better when the sample size is larger. The disc method's behavior can be attributed to the influence of its bounding rectangle's corners, which may stretch further than the square method's boundaries, and this effect is more pronounced in smaller sample sizes. The confidence square's four corners provide a more accurate representation of the true parameter value than the disc's, and this is reflected in the results, with the square method exhibiting less relative error than the disc method, particularly in the smallest sample size scenarios. The relationship between the sample size and its effect on the disc and square methods is evident, as both methods' performance improves with increasing sample sizes, and the square method consistently outperforms the disc method across all tested sample sizes. The findings suggest that the square method is more reliable than the disc method in estimating the Cauchy distribution's parameter, and this is due to the square's inner corners providing a more precise representation of the parameter's value than the disc's bounding rectangle's corners. The numerical simulations demonstrate that both methods are robust against changes in sample size and distribution, and the square method's performance is consistently better than the disc method's. The R code employed in this study is accessible via the link: https://github.com/igorjovelic/Cauchy_confidence_disc_and_square. A new statistical method is developed to calculate the required sample size for clinical trials where multiple subpopulations are studied simultaneously by sharing patients. The goal is to achieve the same level of treatment difference detection as traditional trials tailored to individual populations, which traditionally use fixed effect sizes. We show that using a fixed effect size can lead to inadequate within-subpopulation conclusions, but applying Bayes' theory allows us to accurately determine the required sample size and maintain reliable Bayesian inference results. Two real-world trials are used to demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness. Furthermore, open-source software is available to facilitate the implementation of this method. In addition, we have explored the extension of this method to account for the costs associated with patient recruitment. The main challenges in designing these trials stem from their complex statistical designs and the need to accurately calculate required sample sizes, making our approach particularly valuable. Keywords: Basket trials, Sample size determination, Bayesian methods, Subpopulations, Clinical trials.

To address the challenges posed by this approach, such as nonlinearities, parameter variations, and uncertainty, a linear parameter-varying (LPV) model-based design is presented, focusing on the open-loop system. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through simulations and hardware tests on an overhead crane motion system. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the loop closing enhancement remains effective even under conditions of significant parameter variation, ultimately resulting in a 50% reduction in completion time for a 1-meter trajectory. We introduce a novel, thoroughly supervised neural network called PRNet for partial human body registration. Developed using widely available publicly accessible data, the network is versatile and can be applied to various modalities, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound. PRNet enhances registration precision through detailed, organ-specific information extracted from images, outperforming other methods, such as SGN, FullNet, and DGN, in our simulations. Additionally, PRNet facilitates real-time applications by efficiently using information across the entire image. The network's effectiveness is further demonstrated through successful alignment of clinically relevant cardiac and abdominal sequences. Notably, PRNet's capabilities extend to scenarios involving significant deformations, as evidenced by our simulation of a left leg amputation and expansion of a tumor in the abdominal region. We present the results of the first calculations of the distribution amplitudes for several vector mesons, including D* and D*s, employing an ab initio lattice QCD model to derive input parameters from their wave functions. These calculations involve integrating a Bethe-Salpeter amplitude over transverse momenta, with the outcome being a probability distribution function in momentum space. To validate our method, we also performed a similar calculation for the ρ meson. Our findings indicate that, at the lattice spacing used here (0.185 GeV), the distribution amplitudes for D* and D*s exhibit convergence acceptable for practical quark model applications, with the option to improve convergence by introducing a momentum cutoff into the integration process. Furthermore, we compared our results to those obtained using a light-cone sum rules method, revealing generally good agreement, with potential discrepancies possibly arising from differences in the input wave functions used for the two methods. Our work enables further study of distribution amplitudes for excited vector mesons, including the application of sum rules to extract wave functions for hadrons that are not directly accessible through lattice QCD. Additionally, our results may be useful for quark model calculations, potential lattice simulations of meson distribution amplitudes, and studies of semileptonic decays involving excited D mesons. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexander-lab/distribution-amplitudes.git. Specifically, our analysis focuses on the Toeplitz operators, whose non-triviality is contingent upon the behavior of the symbols under certain transformation, leading to important implications for the continuity of these operators when the original function has smooth variants. The Fourier transform's position within these spaces, as either densely embedded or completely isolated, drives our investigation, with the result allowing us to extend previously known continuous Toeplitz operators to a broader class of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, even in cases where the original symbol is not extremely smooth. Moreover, our findings cover multiple variants of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, including the type $S_V$, $S^\prime_V$, $S_\rho$, and $S^\prime_\rho$, as well as the $\omega$-H\"{o}rmander space $S^0_{1,\varphi}$. Recent breakthroughs in point cloud models have been facilitated by advanced neural networks, which exhibit a propensity for extreme prediction outliers. To address this issue, various regularization techniques have been proposed to enhance the models' performance, although most existing methods apply a one-size-fits-all approach to point cloud models without considering the specific transformations involved in prediction targets. This has led to some transformations being overly constrained while others are given little regulation. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes the Transformation-Specific Constraint method (TPC) that allows for the customization of constraints on prediction targets through weighted heatmaps, which are tailored to support specific transformation types. Experimental evaluations on three prediction tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in producing more reliable point cloud models. Additionally, to accelerate training, we have developed an efficient pipeline that integrates TPC along with other regularization methods, which can be found on our website. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of our method has been made available.
