Recent studies have revealed that certain two-photon absorption processes can distort output patterns in HOM interferometry experiments. This study aims to enhance and modify such experiments to showcase entangled two-photon absorption more clearly. To this end, we have introduced innovative specifications for both the single-photon absorber and the HOM interferometer, allowing for enhanced visibility of entangled two-photon absorption effects as demonstrated through numerical simulations. Importantly, our findings indicate that even partial absorption within a single photon arm can be sufficient to eliminate output peaks in an HOM interferometry experiment, thereby confirming earlier predictions made by us. This study also explores the implications of entangled two-photon absorption on the visibility of HOM interferometry experiments. Notably, our research suggests that under ideal conditions where all photons interact with the sample, the visibility of output peaks in an HOM interferometry experiment should theoretically approach zero. However, when photons do not interact with the sample, the visibility of output peaks in an HOM interferometry experiment should approach one. This conclusion is contingent on the assumption that the photons involved are truly in an entangled state. This assumption is verified by comparing the output patterns in both arms of the interferometer, where the absence of output peaks indicates a perfect correlation between the two photons, which in turn confirms their entangled state. This research provides a novel approach for detecting entangled two-photon absorption effects through HOM interferometry experiments. Additionally, our findings highlight the intricate relationship between the absorption of single photons and the output patterns in HOM interferometry experiments, thereby shedding new light on the behavior of entangled two-photon absorption. This knowledge may also contribute to the development of innovative optical quantum switches that utilize entangled two-photon absorption to control the flow of light. Such switches could potentially be integrated into complex optical networks to create advanced optical technologies. This research may also stimulate further studies on the unique properties of entangled two-photon absorption that diverge from the behavior of traditional single-photon absorption. To this end, we have also explored the implications of entangled two-photon absorption on the spectral properties of output photons. Our findings indicate that entangled two-photon absorption can lead to the emergence of sidebands in the spectral output, thereby confirming earlier predictions made by us. This research may also pave the way for the development of innovative spectral switches that utilize entangled two-photon absorption to modulate the spectral properties of output photons. Such switches could potentially be integrated into optical fibers to create advanced optical communication systems with unparalleled efficiency and reliability

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a crucial task in natural language processing, which involves predicting missing elements (entities or relationships) in a knowledge graph. Current approaches face challenges due to their reliance on model-specific and high-dimensional representations that become difficult to update when new data becomes available. To address this issue, this paper proposes a new framework called TimeAware, which employs low-dimensional, time-agnostic representations and incorporates temporal information into reasoners through the utilization of temporal encoding layers or the direct optimization of temporal properties within knowledge graph embeddings. As a result, enhancements can be easily incorporated into existing knowledge graph embedding models without the need for model-specific architectures. Experimental findings demonstrate that TimeAware surpasses or rivals state-of-the-art models in various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the method is efficient in terms of computational resources and can process large-scale knowledge graphs in an online manner. TimeAware is also capable of addressing the knowledge base completion problem, with source code available at https://github.com/asharafy/TimeAware.

In the field of sound event detection, researchers have made significant strides, yet dealing with complex urban environments where the interaction between sound sources and ground vibration (caused by footsteps, vehicle movements, etc.) poses a challenge to accurate detection. This issue becomes more pronounced in tasks like fine-grained sound classification, where subtle distinctions between classes are crucial. To address this problem, we propose an adaptive filtering method that mitigates the effect of ground sound on accurate detection and classification. By utilizing wavelet-based denoising techniques, we aim to remove the inherent noise from footprints and vehicle sounds, thereby enhancing model performance. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach yields superior outcomes on the DCASE 2018 dataset, with notable improvements in metrics such as F-score and mean F-score across participating teams. To validate the effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios, we also showcase its application on sound recordings captured in a hospital and airport setting. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Deep-Sound-Learning/ground_sound_adapter. Additionally, a pre-trained model is available for online use at https://deep-sound-learning.inria.fr/sound-adapter. This work is part of research supported by ANR under grant ANR-18-CE48A0-001. A common method of demonstrating Bell nonlocality involves showing specific inequality violations in correlations from multiple measurements on shared random states. However, our research presents an alternative approach to Bell nonlocality that does not involve such inequalities, relying solely on certain correlations from dual measurements in two shared spin-1 systems. To develop this alternative, we first create a set of entangled spin-1 states and experimentally prove Bell nonlocality without inequality violations through perfect correlations from three outcomes, achieved in our experiments with Michelson interferometer-based macroscopic quantum superpositions and optical Fock states. This approach has potential applications in quantum communication for key distribution. Moreover, our research offers an opportunity to connect Bell nonlocality with the concept of flag independence in three-party systems. Based on our results, we propose an extension of the Bell nonlocality criterion that does not rely on inequality violations, which could be valuable for practical quantum communication and may also contribute to discussions about its occurrence in certain thermodynamic processes. Finally, our research provides an opportunity to discuss the broader implications of Bell nonlocality for understanding reality and its connections to the principles of local realism and free will. In flat band systems, limited wave function overlap leads to atypical physical properties, and the potential for non-trivial topology and localized states is substantial, influenced by disorder. We investigate two types of flat band systems: those derived from twisted bilayer graphene and the Chern insulator, and examine how various conditions affect their non-trivial topology and localization properties when introducing disorder. Through our analysis, we establish that the topology and localization properties of these systems can be differentiated based on the origin of their flat bands, resulting in distinct outcomes that can be observed experimentally. These findings provide a foundation for interpreting experimental results and optimizing the materials to produce localized phases and exotic topological states. Moreover, our research implies that in twisted bilayer graphene with a gratings pattern, there is the potential to observe a correlation gap, and that by applying strain, the band structure can be modified to produce a Dirac semimetal. Finally, our study demonstrates that localization can occur in systems with non-geometric flat bands, and that by adjusting the disorder distribution, the resulting localization pattern can be controlled. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between wave function overlap, topology, and localization, and their combined impact on flat band systems. Additionally, our analysis sheds light on the origin of the Anderson localization and the role of quantum geometry in shaping the wave function overlap and localization properties of these systems. Lastly, our research offers a framework for designing materials with unique physical properties by balancing wave function overlap and disorder, and introduces the concept of homotopy to predict the outcome of this competition. Finally, our study presents an experimental protocol to produce localization in graphene and other 2D materials by adjusting the type and distribution of disorder. Identifying natural groups within complex data is a key objective in various fields, however traditional clustering methods may struggle with systems that aren't linear, have limited or no accessible historical data, or are constantly changing. We present a new approach that uses a data-driven method to determine the underlying structure of systems that follow a dynamical flow, even in high-dimensional spaces, without assuming linearity. Instead, our algorithm focuses on how these systems affect each other to identify meaningful groups within the data. We also developed methods to assess the validity of these groups and compared it existing clustering methods showing improved results and faster computation in many cases. Furthermore, we apply our approach to study dynamic systems in various real-world scenarios such as animal social behavior, solar wind dynamics, and cellular cell-cycle regulation. The framework is available as an open-source tool.

This research investigates certain categories of linear operators where a fundamental question regarding their dimension remains unresolved, specifically under Independence, a previously hypothesized principle. We demonstrate that Independence does not apply to categories such as linear operators, dimensional relationships, or matrix representations, leading us to formulate a more general hypothesis regarding infinite-dimensional spaces, which we substantiate through various examples. Furthermore, we explore additional operator categories and examine the validity of Independence within those contexts. This research introduces a hybrid recommender system that integrates behavior-based and document context-based methods to address the limitations of data scarcity in recommender systems. Behavior-based methods, such as collaborative filtering, are susceptible to providing poor recommendations when users' historical interactions are limited to a single item. Meanwhile, model-based approaches like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) focus on analyzing document content rather than user behavior. To combine these methods effectively, this study proposes three integration techniques: selecting human-recommended items for LDA-based models, incorporating user ratings in the document-term matrix for LDA-based models, and blending behavior-based and document context-based recommendations. Experimental results demonstrate that these hybrid approaches outperform the standalone methods in terms of accuracy and diversity, as evaluated on three datasets, including movies, books, and video games. Notably, the enhancement in recommendation quality is most noticeable in situations where users have only minimal interaction with these systems. To validate the effectiveness of this hybrid model, this research employs two popular evaluation methods: the intrusiveness analysis and the human judgment approach. The findings of these experiments confirm that the hybrid model is capable of mitigating the negative impacts of data scarcity on recommendation quality while also providing diverse recommendations. Furthermore, this study highlights the feasibility of integrating behavior-based and document context-based methods to address the limitations of each individual approach. We've developed two new methods to estimate the size of complex networks, such as social media and the internet, under challenging conditions. Our approaches are designed to work on small-world networks that are difficult to navigate and estimate accurately even when some nodes provide misleading information about the network. Our first method uses data from node connections, calculating the network's size based on data complexity and node randomness, which yields an accurate result when data quality is high. When data is poor, we employ a second method that combines information from multiple nodes to improve estimation, achieving results close to the actual value even in difficult-to-access networks. Our tests validate the effectiveness of our methods, demonstrating better performance than previous estimators in various scenarios. To achieve comparable performance using fewer resources, researcher attention has focused on designing customized methods for knowledge distillation. Our approach, PILE, integrates multiple teachers' logits (predicted probabilities) through an iterative process that produces accurate student training. When paired with suitable stopping criteria, PILE produces high-quality students comparable to those trained individually. Furthermore, PILE's design enables real-time logit generation for earlier teachers to support iterative training, reducing reliance on hyperparameter fine-tuning. Our experimental results demonstrate PILE's effectiveness on prominent NLP tasks and highlight its advantages over established methods. Notably, PILE's performance outclasses nteaching, a top knowledge distillation method, in 12 out of 15 evaluated scenarios. This paper investigates the recovery of one-dimensional Riemannian metrics on a circle, seeking the minimum L^1 norm among all possible metrics. While our method shares similarities with basis pursuit in the continuum, developed by Angeli, Forni, and Gamba, uniqueness of the solution poses the greater challenge. Building upon existing research, we provide two distinct sets of conditions ensuring the uniqueness of the solution, along with examining its implications for both smooth and Töpfer-von Mises distributed data points. Additionally, we discuss its extension to higher dimensional cases, presenting a related open problem. Network functions such as traffic filtering require intricate state machines that can be efficiently implemented on reconfigurable match-action table switches via P416 compilers. However, commercial solutions incur significant licensing costs, making open-source alternatives indispensable for research and development purposes. This study introduces an open-source P416 compiler backend capable of generating optimized code for reconfigurable switches, open-source simulation environments, and microcontrollers. The compiler's effectiveness is demonstrated through a practical example of a TCP congestion control algorithm. Furthermore, a performance comparison is made with a commercial P416 compiler, revealing that our solution can produce more efficient code in certain contexts. The comprehensive source code for this project has been publicly released.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has been consistently demonstrated across various domains, yet it poses challenges to individual privacy, data ownership rights, and data source diversity, prompting the development of federated learning algorithms. Although successful in training models across numerous data sources, these algorithms overlook the disparities in data quality, resulting in biased models. To address this issue, researchers have proposed fairness-aware FL algorithms, yet they often neglect the privacy concerns inherent to sharing data. To bridge this gap, we develop a new FL algorithm that simultaneously achieves fairness and privacy preservation. Our approach utilizes a fair loss function to optimize model accuracy, while constrained differential privacy ensures the protection of individual users and data sources during the training process. Through theoretical analysis and experimentation, we validate the efficacy of our approach, demonstrating improved fairness and privacy with only minor reductions in model accuracy. Notably, our results show that with a moderate level of privacy (ε = 10) comparable to previous FL studies, our algorithm surpasses current state-of-the-art FL baselines in fairness. Furthermore, our approach remains competitive in terms of model accuracy, with only a negligible 0.2% decrease compared to traditional FL methods. To facilitate reproducibility, our source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhaozhafairdp_FL.git. This model was modified to account for weak dissipipation within three different methods: a model with constant dissipation, a model featuring non-constant dissipation and a model with non-uniform constant dissipation. In each scenario, the research found that Wada basins increase in size and density as constant dissipation increases, or as non-constant dissipation increases, or as uniform non-constant dissipation decreases. Additionally, the research discovered that weak dissipation can lead to the emergence of Wada intersections even in cases where they do not exist at zero dissipation, also observed in other three-dimensional models such as the Auerbach model. Human action understanding in complex videos has been a long-standing challenge in Computer Vision. This study addresses the problem of recognizing human actions through video analysis. While current research achievements with deep learning can be effective, it encounters difficulties when faced with situations where (1) the video length is unpredictable, (2) there are limited training examples, and (3) the input videos are fragmented or in a small resolution. To overcome these limitations, we propose an architecture called Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), which integrates a hierarchical attention-mechanism-based R-C3D feature extractor with a spatiotemporal attention-alignment module for more accurate feature alignment. The HAN was evaluated on four action recognition datasets: UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics, and Mini-Kinetics, with the results showing its capability to deliver robust performance even under challenging conditions. The source code of this project has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zhktsui/HAN. Moreover, we discovered that in scenarios where the event horizon forms prior to the singularity, the probes may reach the singularity, leading us to refute the weak cosmic censorship conjecture in such cases. Furthermore, we found that when the scalar field interacts with the black hole, its properties including temperature, specific heat, and adiabatic mass, are influenced by the angular velocity and potential of the scalar field. It is also demonstrated that the scalar field can induce a phase transition in the black hole from the larger to the smaller anti-de Sitter Reissner-Nordström black hole state. Finally, we analyzed the relationship between energy extensivity and clustering in these probes. Our findings show that for probes far from the black hole, energy extensivity applies, whereas at close range, it behaves non-extensively. Additionally, we observed non-clustering in probes that are far from the black hole, which is consistent with the thermodynamic hypothesis of clustering. However, at close range, the probe does cluster due to its interaction with the black hole. Moreover, we found that the thermodynamic hypothesis of non-clustering is valid for probes that are thermally coupled to the black hole. Finally, we analyzed the heat and work relationships during the probe's interaction with the black hole. Our results show that the probe can exchange heat and work with the black hole, leading to a significant impact on the probe's state. It is also found that the sign of the work done on the probe is determined by its radial or tangential motion. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. This method has been implemented in the Entropy package on PyPI for public use. It's particularly useful for complex probability distributions, requiring only an NS-compatible sampler to estimate its entropy-based quantities. This approach remains efficient even at high sampling efficiencies. The Cloud Library, a tool for analyzing metric spaces, enables construction of various metrics that are equivalent to the original space and reveal its underlying structure. Specifically, the library's cloud $\Cl(\X)$ for a metric space $\X$ serves as a representation of $\X$ that showcases its compositional elements, where two clouds $\Cl(\X)$ and $\Cl(\Y)$ are considered equivalent (or 1-GH equivalent) if their distance under the Gromov-Hausdorff metric is minimal. This paper introduces the concept of completeness in the Cloud Library, demonstrating that the library's clouds form a complete class, meaning any two that are 1-GH equivalent must also be 1-GH distant. Additionally, the study identifies and characterizes 'centers' within the library, which are clouds that minimize the Gromov-Hausdorff distance from all other 1-GH equivalent clouds. Notably, it is proven that a metric space has a center if and only if it satisfies the Ultra-Large (UL) condition, defined as the sum of the reciprocals of the radii of all balls in the space exceeding 1. Furthermore, the UL condition is shown to be stable under small perturbations and the centers of a metric space can be approximated through a process involving the selection of representative balls. Finally, the research presents methods for computing the centers of various common metric spaces, including the integers with a discrete metric, the real numbers with a standard metric, and the set of natural numbers with a metric based on the Cesaro mean. These examples not only illustrate the feasibility of computing clouds but also highlight their potential as a tool for analyzing metric spaces and their underlying structures. Ultimately, the study provides a deeper understanding of the metric spaces themselves, demonstrating that the Cloud Library can serve as a powerful analytical framework. Additionally, the research presents a strategy for developing algorithms that approximate the centers of any given metric space. This work is expected to contribute to the advancement of algorithmic metric geometry, offering a novel approach to designing algorithms based on the Cloud Library. The study is also anticipated to facilitate further research into the metric spaces themselves, as well as their underlying structures, as revealed through the clouds. This knowledge may, in turn, inspire new insights and results across a range of mathematical disciplines. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process for a decoder agent through reinforcement learning, utilizing rapid generation of synthetic noise and partial measurements by short simulation paths. The findings reveal that this approach yields decoding performance on par with established methods for scenarios involving up to 409,216 qudits under steady-state noise conditions, and even excels in scenarios featuring sudden onset noise. Furthermore, this reinforcement learning decoder exhibits improved adaptability when confronted with unforeseen dynamic noise patterns compared to traditional methods. Ultimately, this work presents a decoder capable of effectively mitigating steady-state and transient errors within large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing systems. A different method involves the use of quantum algorithms that mimic the behavior of highly entangled states through the controlled manipulation of smaller, individual quantum states. We propose and demonstrate an approach to DeFazio-Tannor's hybrid digital-analog quantum computing method for simulating fermionic systems. The traditional digital-analog method is naturally fermionic in nature, but introducing digital components requires careful adherence to fermionic symmetry to avoid dimensional blowup. Although this constraint limits complex analog connections within digital components, our hybrid method still offers significant advantages over classical numerical methods and conventional digital quantum computing in terms of computational resources and circuit depth. Furthermore, our approach maintains the ability to connect multiple quantum computing devices for parallel processing, enabling the extension of our method to complex fermionic systems on large lattices by combining local digital simulations of small fermionic systems. The efficacy of our approach is verified by successfully running a quantum simulation of the one-dimensional Yang-Gibbs model on IBM's quantum experience platform. Our results indicate that deep quantum circuits can be constructed to efficiently solve intricate fermionic problems. Moreover, we suggest that our hybrid method could serve as a versatile tool for the initial testing of fermionic quantum algorithms prior to executing them on the emerging scalable, fully-analog quantum computers. A critical issue in machine learning lies in achieving a model that excels in both optimization and generalization capabilities. Proper regularization techniques can help, yet they frequently come with unclear motivations.  This research introduces a new perspective on the issue, grounded in the principle of creating complex features, illustrating how excessive complexity in models can lead to suboptimal performance.  Through empirical analysis, it is demonstrated that models of various types, when trained using similar methods, tend to construct similar feature sets.  By reducing the capability to create diverse features, the performance of models can deteriorate.  Building upon this insight, a novel regularization method called Feature Ban (FB) is introduced, allowing for the suppression of specific feature sets.  FB's effectiveness is showcased in multiple benchmark tests and one real-world scenario, and it is also compared to established methods with a source code repository available for reproduction of results.  FB's performance rivals that of other regularization methods, even when models are modified to produce simpler features.  FB offers a feature-oriented approach to addressing the optimization-generalization dilemma, thus providing more granular control over model performance.  Furthermore, FB may lead to improved model interpretability by restricting feature usage.  Potential future research directions are also explored.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reevaluation of the black hole evaporation paradigm. This study also addresses the regularity issue in the context of the Unruh process. Since the source of radiation is not attributed to the gravitational force, the concept of wavefunction collapse alone may be insufficient to explain the Hawking process. Instead, the focus should be on the dynamic changes in the wave function, specifically from the perspective of one of the outgoing particles. This perspective offers a novel, long-standing resolution to the black hole regularity problem. Experimental data in the LHC regime for nuclear broadening reveals a $A^2\phi$ dependence, where $\phi$ is the centrality of the interaction, indicating transverse momentum broadening is enhanced by nucleus size. Using the measured $A^2\phi$ value from CMS, the predicted transverse momentum broadening for single inclusive hadron production is calculated and compared across different models, where the model based on nonlinear broadening in the literature best aligns with experimental data, while another model incorporating transverse momentum broadening into the factorization and fragmentation functions provides a second good approximation. As a result, the relative importance of transverse momentum broadening and parton saturation in single inclusive hadron production is determined, where parton saturation dominates at small $x$ and transverse momentum broadening dominates at large $A$ and similar $x$ values. Additionally, the predicted transverse momentum broadening for single inclusive $\pi^0$ production in semi-inclusive $e^+e^-$ collisions at the LHCb is calculated, where the effect is most pronounced for $\pi^0$ produced close to the nucleus and represents about $3-4\%$ of its transverse momentum. Furthermore, the predicted nuclear broadening for $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ production in proton-proton collisions at the LHC is calculated, where the effect is most pronounced for $J/\psi$ and represents about $3\%$ of its transverse momentum. Lastly, the predicted transverse momentum broadening for single inclusive hadron production in the quark-gluon plasma is calculated, where the effect is most pronounced for hadrons produced close to the quark-gluon plasma and represents about $10-20\%$ of its transverse momentum. Therefore, the predicted transverse momentum broadening in the quark-gluon plasma far exceeds the predicted nuclear broadening in proton-proton collisions. While non-volatile memory offers a solution for maintaining data integrity during power outages, it presents its own challenges in maintaining data reliability during algorithm execution. This work investigates how algorithms like sorting and matrix multiplication can be modified to function correctly even in the event of a crash with the help of an external checkpointing mechanism. Our research reveals that by inserting checkpoints at predetermined points during run-time, we can ensure data reliability without the need for complex error correction mechanisms. This study provides algorithmic guidance for developers to create crash-consistent algorithms, with our experimental results demonstrating that data reliability can be maintained at runtime levels comparable to those of traditional systems. At present, we have analyzed algorithms from the FLAME library, but our approach can be applied to a wide range of other algorithms as well. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be integrated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this integration, we first establish a hyperdoctrine for continuous logic, defining the category whose subobjects it represents. 
Then, to ensure the hyperdoctrine's properties necessary for integration, we select a specific topological structure as its base and establish that continuous formulas apply uniformly across equivalent structures. 
Next, we establish that the resulting hyperdoctrine can be embedded in the hyperdoctrine for continuous morphisms between topological structures. 
Finally, we demonstrate that the embedded hyperdoctrine corresponds to the subobjects in this target category, thereby proving that the category of continuous formulas is equivalent to the category of continuous morphisms between topological structures. 
This equivalence enables us to apply a theorem showing that an equivalence between a subcategory and a category of morphisms between topological structures can be refined into an equivalence between the respective topological structures and categories of subobjects. 
As a result, we can represent the category of continuous formulas as a topological category of subobjects. 
This allows us to apply a theorem showing that an equivalence between a category of subobjects and a category with internal subobjects must also be an equivalence between the respective categories, thereby establishing that the category of continuous formulas is equivalent to a category of measures on closed subobjects within a fixed topological structure. 
This equivalence provides a new understanding of the category of continuous formulas. 
Additionally, this structure may have applications beyond continuous model theory, potentially influencing topological logic and semantics more broadly. 
Finally, this framework could be adapted to incorporate additional continuous operators, such as integration. 
This adaptation may also have implications for the interplay between continuous model theory and analysis. 
This work is expected to lay the groundwork for further research exploring these connections. 
Conversely, the techniques used here may draw inspiration from these connections. 
In particular, the decision to represent the category of continuous formulas through subobjects in a topological structure was influenced by the established relationship between measures and subobjects. 
This relationship is itself a consequence of the interplay between topological structures, analysis, and logic. 
This interplay is a long-standing area of study, with significant contributions from both logic and analysis. 
This interplay has also led to the development of other categorical structures, such as hyperdoctrine frameworks and topoi.

When designing a software system, alterations in its specifications result in a change of its functional model, which must be reflected in the updates of the software code. This process is known as functional model maintenance. This maintenance involves selecting relevant test cases from the existing set of test cases to ensure that the modifications do not introduce errors into the software system. The issue with maintaining a software system lies in the efficient selection of these test cases, as this is currently a manually performed task that is often done incorrectly, leading to decreased system performance and reliability. In this research, we have developed an algorithm using singular value decomposition to automate the selection of test cases, which has shown promising results in previous studies when applied to small systems. However, when this algorithm was tested on a larger system with 300 test cases, it required 11 hours and 59 minutes, making it impractical for use in industry. To resolve this issue, we have modified the algorithm to enable parallel processing on multi-core CPUs, which has enabled us to successfully apply it to the larger system in just 1 minute and 59 seconds, making it a viable solution for industry. Our results also show that the algorithm's efficiency and scalability have been significantly improved, as evidenced by our experiments. This research aims to address the problem of functional model maintenance through software testing, which is a critical issue in the broader field of software engineering. The selected test cases resulting from our algorithm will be used to perform unit-level testing of the software code, which will ensure its reliability and efficiency. Our research has opened up new avenues for further study, such as incorporating machine learning techniques to enhance the algorithm's performance and scalability. Additionally, we plan to apply our algorithm to other software systems in the future to validate its effectiveness across different applications. The algorithm's source code is publicly available under a permissive license, allowing other researchers to build upon our research and further validate our results. Moving forward, we will investigate how our algorithm can be applied to other areas of software testing, such as integration testing, to further broaden the algorithm's impact. The algorithm's efficiency and scalability will continue to be improved through various algorithmic enhancements, which will be guided by our empirical evaluations and informed by our theoretical findings. Suicidal ideation, a critical indicator of potential mental health crises, is difficult to track unless individuals openly disclose such information, often during clinical consultations with a therapist or psychiatrist. Due to the inherent subjectivity of suicidal thoughts, researchers rely on self-reported data from mental health professionals collected over time to build sequential models. A major limitation of existing studies is the single data source they employ; in contrast, we have access to three levels of information - clinical notes, treatment plans, and visit schedules - enabling us to construct comprehensive sequential models using cutting-edge deep learning techniques. Our experiments with neural networks and reinforcement learning strategies demonstrate that combining all available data streams yields improved outcomes compared to relying solely on clinical notes, and we further show that our proposed method surpasses traditional approaches in predicting suicidal ideation. The integration of multiple data sources allows our sequential models to learn a nuanced understanding of mental health dynamics, ultimately facilitating the identification of optimal treatment strategies. Our findings have significant practical implications, and we will make our code publicly available to support future research. Additionally, we will donate a portion of our proceeds to mental health-related charities. Mental health is a critical aspect of overall well-being, and we hope our research will contribute positively to society. Unlike existing frameworks that rely on program equivalences focused on probabilities or expected values, this work adopts a denotational approach based on a tailored lifting technique to capture the unique denotations associated with every input-output relationship, and proves its equivalence against a well-established axiomatic system by demonstrating that every denotation corresponds to a valid axiom, thus providing a universal semantics for the stochastic lambda-calculus that can serve as a foundation for further algorithmic analysis beyond expectation-based techniques. Additionally, this semantics is implemented in a Haskell library and used in an accompanying Coq formalisation. Moreover, a type-and-effect system is defined, allowing developers to specify both the desired output and the associated probability measures for program outputs, which can be effectively used to identify and isolate algorithmic parts responsible for measuring issues. This allows the development of more robust non-deterministic algorithms that can be safely composed with other programs that may introduce probability measures not explicitly considered by the original authors, which can lead to inaccurate analysis results if measuring issues are present. This type-and-effect system is also shown to be sound when translated to our developed semantics-based framework. Finally, a few practical case studies are conducted, which highlight the effectiveness of this type-and-effect system in guiding developers towards more reliable non-deterministic algorithm design. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to analyze to improve software development and maintenance. This is achieved by applying learning methods to extract relevant information from these discussions, which can then be used to create models simulating human decision-making processes. A key aspect in this context is termed 'conclusion stability,' referring to the consistency of developers' conclusions drawn from general discussion content. Building upon previous research in mining inductive knowledge, we introduce a novel approach to assess conclusion stability and propose two solutions to enhance it: (1) a statistical model grounded in non-parametric density estimation and (2) a neural network framework inspired by expert system rule induction. Our approach is applied to two real-world scenarios, namely design discussion threads on Stack Overflow and GitHub issue comments, where we evaluate its effectiveness in extracting stable conclusions across diverse developers' perspectives. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can transfer successfully to domains where only limited or no labeled data is available, while also comparing its performance against traditional topic modeling techniques. Notably, our evaluation shows that our method outperforms others in achieving conclusion stability, as evidenced by rigorous statistical analysis. This research has significant implications for practical applications, given that software developers' online discussions can be harnessed to build reliable models extracting valuable insights with minimal noise. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various domains beyond software development, including healthcare and finance, where decision-making processes often rely on the consensus of multiple experts. Ultimately, this research validates the applicability of conclusion stability in natural language based mining to extract robust decision models from diverse discussion platforms. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying structure of minimization problems, and combining this with gradient information can provide insightful insights into the geometry involved.

We investigate how the proximal gradient method discovers the Riemannian manifold structure in an informal manner, and we introduce an extension that exploits this information to enhance convergence rates when using the proximal Jacobian method.

Under certain assumptions, our approach results in a convergent sequence that remains on the manifold, and it achieves a rate of convergence of O(k^{-2/(2+p)}) when optimizing a sequence of strongly convex functions with parameters (p, \mu).

To validate our findings, we conduct numerical experiments involving image denoising and colorization, and the results demonstrate significant improvements in computational efficiency. Furthermore, we present an application of our method in hyperspectral image colorization, showcasing its potential to uncover the underlying geometry in real-world problems.

We begin by defining weakly absorbing prime ideals in a commutative ring as those prime ideals that either consist of only nilpotent elements or have a complementary set containing the unity. Our research focuses on identifying the characteristics of commutative rings with all prime ideals fulfilling this criterion, and we establish a more general definition for weakly absorbing prime ideals. Additionally, we examine specific instances of rings meeting this criterion, including certain classes of truncated polynomial rings and affine rings with restricted embedded properties. Our investigation also leads to the exploration of analogous concepts in non-commutative rings with a specific twist. Furthermore, we attempt to address a posed question by aligning it with an established problem by Gilmer and Hendry. Our work concludes with several questions for further research.

In photoelectric spectroscopy, a spectrometer is essentially an imaging device that combines various wavelengths into a single image based on their dispersion. This allows for the analysis of light sources with multiple spectral lines. By cross-correlating the resulting image with reference spectra, researchers can identify unknown light sources. Traditionally, the astrophotonic approach utilizes a glass-based spectrometer, whereas our proposal leverages the unique properties of photonic crystals and etalons to achieve the same spectral dispersion. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to leverage machine learning to enhance human drug analysis, contributing to safer and more effective medication use. Several local authorities face challenges associated with identifying and repairing road damage due to limited financial resources, which hinder their ability to deploy specialized equipment and trained personnel for road condition assessment. While advanced technologies like image processing have been shown to boost efficiency in road condition evaluation, creating and refining a centralized database capable of supporting diverse road types and environments remains a difficult task. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative approach that leverages deep learning models and a substantial, multi-national road damage image dataset to facilitate effective damage detection across different regions. To minimize data preparation time and enhance model adaptability, we also develop a transfer learning protocol utilizing synthetic data generated through a semantic fusion process. Notably, our proposed method achieves a 0.934 AUC score on the SEMANTIC STE110 dataset and 0.944 AUC score on the Indonesian dataset, surpassing the performance of models trained from scratch. Our research provides an affordable solution for local authorities to enhance their road condition assessment capabilities using image processing technology. Additionally, the generated synthetic data can be utilized to enhance the performance of deep learning models in other applications involving diverse environments, such as autonomous driving and autonomous navigation. The proposed method's source code, synthetic data generator, and dataset are available for public access at https://github.com/roadmapet RL/. The Indonesian dataset used in this study can be obtained from https://github.com/IndonesiaRDC/. The SEMANTIC STE110 dataset can be obtained from https://competitions.diognt.com/semantic-stl110/. Imitation learning seeks to develop skilled behaviors through repetitive
rehearsal, however current methods are limited by their reliance on expert
input and specific training environments. This research aims to bridge the gap
between imitation learning's potential for complex skill acquisition and the
constraints imposed by expert supervision and environmental nuances during
rehearsal. We achieve this through self-correction, enabling the learner to
internalize patterns observed across various environments, thereby producing
accurate imitation without relying on expert guidance. We present a framework
that integrates contextual information to disambiguate causal relationships between
actions and observations, and our results demonstrate successful imitation of
both simple target actions and more complex policies in disparate domains. 

Our research reveals that domain-specific training using self-correction facilitates
target imitation, despite our agent being unaware of the target action. Moreover,
we show that domain-specific training can also be achieved without expert input by
utilizing unguided observation of either the target or a compatible policy. 

Our findings suggest that imitation learning can be extended beyond target action
replication to replicate entire policies through observational learning. We
anticipate that our work will contribute to the development of more natural
forms of human-robot interaction and provide a pathway towards autonomously
acquiring complex, multi-step policies from diverse environments.

Association rule analysis is a fundamental technique used to examine large datasets, uncovering comprehensive results that ensure statistical significance but are often difficult to interpret due to their large number. We introduce two primary issues related to association rule findings: first, how to ensure every statistically significant finding can be traced back to a basic set of underlying rules with no redundant associations; second, given multiple equivalent non-redundant sets of underlying rules, what is the smallest possible size for each. We develop two algorithms addressing these questions, providing insight into the minimum necessary size of each-set even when comprehensive results are present. We also explore alternative representations of non-redundancy, focusing on eliminating sequential associations and investigate the minimum size required for each. We examine redundancy through the lens of deduction schemes, providing efficient solutions to related problems. We further investigate the redundancy associated with multiple attribute findings and introduce the concept of hyperassociation rules to address this, also exploring redundancy within binary decision tables under varying conditions. We provide a thorough comparison of our proposed methods via numerical examples. The presented methods, along with a provided implementation, can be accessed via the link to Redundity's GitHub repository. This research investigates the impact of court-ordered mental health treatment on convicted individuals with mental health disorders within the criminal justice system. Using administrative data from North Carolina, we find that participating in therapy results in a substantial, long-term reduction in recidivism rates within the next decade, particularly marked recidivism rates decreasing by 21-25%. We also discover that the benefits of therapy are more pronounced among non-violent offenders and those who complete the treatment program compared to those who drop out. Notably, we find that receiving therapy leads to an increased likelihood of receiving prescription medication for mental health disorders, suggesting that improving access to treatment may stimulate subsequent utilization of other mental health services. Furthermore, we find that the effect of therapy on recidivism rates varies depending on the specific diagnosis, with individuals diagnosed with anxiety or depression experiencing the greatest reductions in recidivism rates. Overall, our research highlights the effectiveness of court-ordered mental health treatment in reducing criminal behavior and suggests that increasing access to treatment for individuals with mental health disorders within the criminal justice system may help to decrease recidivism rates and improve community well-being. Additionally, our research underscores the value of utilizing administrative data to study the impact of mental health treatment on criminal behavior. Finally, our research provides further evidence of the significance of diagnosing mental health disorders in order to inform sentencing and treatment decisions within the criminal justice system. Based on our estimates of recidivism rates and treatment completion rates, we calculate the potential cost-benefit analysis of providing mental health treatment, and find that the benefits of treatment far outweigh the costs. Specifically, we find that providing treatment results in a savings to society of $1,300-$2,300 per person over the next decade. Finally, our research highlights several avenues for future research, including investigating alternative methods for increasing treatment completion rates and reducing disparities in the administration of mental health services. Additionally, we note that our research does not address the complex ethical considerations surrounding the use of administrative data in social science research, and suggest that these issues may be taken up in future research. Finally, we highlight several policy interventions that could improve access to mental health services and reduce disparities in the administration of services, and note that these policies could be informed by our research findings. Radio maps are being explored for their potential in accessing unlicensed frequency bands and enhancing wireless connectivity. Under the assumption that they remain relatively stable over time, their initial creation using drones can significantly benefit future applications. This research introduces an on-the-fly estimation method to update radio maps as drones move forward, leveraging their real-time signal measurements. Initial experiments using a deep learning-based model reveal that even small changes in the environment have a significant impact on radio map accuracy. Consequently, continuous radio map updating is crucial, and we propose an algorithm that incorporates information from previous time steps to refine estimation. Our results show substantial gains in accuracy compared to a baseline approach. Specifically, we observe a greater than 30% reduction in estimation error for the model's subsequent iterations. Furthermore, we investigate how different factors influence our approach and find that the proposed model performs best when the signal strength remains relatively constant. Interestingly, incorporating information from previous time steps actually hampers performance in such cases. Additionally, we note that utilizing deep learning-based models yields more accurate results than a method that solely utilizes signal strength measurements. Lastly, we note that our approach is particularly beneficial in environments where the signal strength remains relatively constant. With these findings, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective aerial spectrum surveying techniques. Ultimately, this has the potential to improve wireless connectivity and accessibility in the future. To evaluate its effectiveness, this technique is applied to real-world datasets from Twitter and Wikipedia, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional anomaly detection methods. This research delves into person verification using auditory, visual, and thermal information. We examine the effect of incorporating visual and auditory modalities, as well as the visual and thermal pair, on verification performance. Our findings demonstrate that the auditory-visual combination yields the best results, outperforming single-modal and visual-thermal approaches. Additionally, we explore the utility of applying person-specific modalities, denoted as 'appearing modes,' to enhance verification accuracy. We utilize deep learning techniques, namely, triplet network and center loss, in conjunction with an extended ResNet-50 framework to achieve this. With an audio-visual dataset comprising 1,440 videos from 32 individuals, our results show that verification accuracy is 99.5% when using both modalities, whereas it drops to 97.8% when individuals appear in only one modality. When incorporating thermal images, our model reached a 99.0% verification accuracy. Notably, our approach surpassed state-of-the-art methods using audio-visual data, as evidenced by the NIST 2018 challenge results. This research presents a novel, efficient, and robust method for person verification, which could have significant implications in real-world applications such as social media platforms, security systems, and law enforcement agencies. With the advent of multi-modal technology, our work has the potential to improve accuracy and resistance to deception in person verification. Its potential applications extend to social media, security, and the legal profession. Data and models for this research are available at https://github.com/AbhishekRaju96/Audio-Visual-Thermal-Person-Verification. Extended versions of this research will appear in the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision and the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is a difficult problem in various real-world contexts, particularly when data attributes exhibit dependencies. To address this challenge, a one-sided differential privacy model has been developed to safeguard against privacy breaches involving data attributes with dependencies. However, the existing model's primary drawback is its ineffectiveness in guarding against privacy violations affecting multiple data entities. To address this shortcoming, a novel privacy framework is introduced, which enhances the one-sided differential privacy model by reducing privacy deficits in data sets comprising dependent attributes. The proposed approach also incorporates a method to estimate privacy deficits in data utility and applies an optimization technique to balance a company's confidentiality and data utility requirements. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments using real-world data sets. The results show that this approach can successfully mitigate privacy breaches affecting multiple data entities and maintain a satisfactory level of data utility. Moreover, this approach can reduce a company's confidentiality and data utility costs while providing more accurate privacy estimates. The discovery of gas gaps at planet-forming scales in various protoplanetary disks has been reported previously. These findings have led to the hypothesis that gas gaps are created by planet formation, however the origin of one such gap in the AS 209 disk remains uncertain from existing observations. This study presents new ALMA data that supplement earlier results, focusing on the CO gap in the AS 209 disk to determine its cause. By analyzing CO's emission and depletion, as well as the nitrogen-bearing molecule DCN's emission, researchers found that CO's spatial pattern in the disk changed significantly when comparing high and low frequencies. This discrepancy suggested that CO's emission outside the gap is not simply a result of this molecule being depleted, as one would expect to see a more gradual decrease in CO emission outside the gap if this were the case. Furthermore, the ratio of DCN to $^{12}$C-O, as calculated from ALMA's high and low frequencies, showed that CO's depletion outside the gap does not explain the observed gap either. Instead, the data suggest that CO's emission outside the gap is actually comparable to that of gas that has not interacted with the planet, while CO's emission inside the gap is reduced. This reduction in CO's emission inside the gap could be attributed to CO's conversion into more stable species such as CS, as suggested by previous theoretical studies. This theory is also consistent with the observed decrease in CS emission inside the gap, as measured from ALMA's high frequencies. This study's results provide further evidence that gas gaps in protoplanetary disks are likely created by planet formation. Moreover, this research highlights the importance of considering chemical reactions in modeling planet-forming disks, as their impact on gas gap observations should not be underestimated. Finally, the data suggest that gas gaps in protoplanetary disks could be used to constrain models of planet formation, as the observed gas gap in the AS 209 disk cannot be explained by a planet that orbits within the disk's ice line. Instead, the data suggest that the planet in this system must orbit within the disk's water region, where it would need to be at least 0.6 times as massive as Jupiter to create the observed gas gap. However, this planet's mass would need to be higher, at around 5-6 times that of Jupiter, if it were to orbit within the disk's ice region, as suggested by previous studies. The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we have created the "Extensible Time-tag Analyzer" (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization, while offering exceptional performance and adaptability. Leveraging the power of multi-core processors through vectorized operations and data parallelization, ETA achieves remarkable speed, empowering users to handle massive datasets. Its modular design and user-friendly interface facilitate the configuration and reuse of analysis methods, such as etching, multi-dimensional projections, and real-time data screening, enabling seamless collaboration among researchers and enabling the development of standalone data processing tools. Furthermore, ETA's time-stamped data representation enables seamless integration with third-party software and data formats, allowing for seamless comparison with other tools and data sharing. With an open-source license, ETA serves as a versatile platform for time-stamped data analysis and visualization, where users can contribute to its continued advancement and employ it in fields like high-energy physics, biology, astronomy, and industrial quality control. Additionally, ETA's capabilities have been utilized to optimize and automate the processing of large PET data sets in medical research and bio-medical applications. Further details on the implementation, performance, and application examples are available in the article. ETA is freely available for download at https://eta-toolbox.github.io/. You can also explore ETA's functionality through interactive examples at https://ta-eta.github.io/. Furthermore, the GitHub repository for ETA is located at https://github.com/eta-toolbox/eta-toolbox/. We cordially invite you to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of ETA. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to non-smooth systems with convex state constraints. Additionally, we present a straightforward proof of the continuity estimate essential for the main result, which is derived from weak KAM theory along with an integration by parts approach. This allows us to relax the usual assumption of C^1 regularity for the cost and coupling functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of an optimal control for a canonical problem associated with this game, which can be viewed as a non-cooperative version of the Mario Truffini-Violante example. This control exhibits a singular behavior with its trajectory starting near a stable manifold's boundary, where it rapidly approaches a stationary point under weak convex control constraints. Recent research revealed a previously overlooked population of moving stars in the Milky Way, characterized by steady motion and scattered spatial distribution. Initial findings proposed these stars formed in a single entity which broke apart, resulting in the current dispersed state. We investigate whether a population of stellar "strings" in the galaxy could generate the observed characteristics, with each string comprising stars in a linear arrangement. Initially, the strings moved together en masse but, over time, individual stars began to diffuse due to random influences, ultimately leading to the present scattered state and uniform motion. Our models show that a stellar string population can easily mimic the discovered population of moving stars if the right parameters are set, specifically those affecting diffusion and the initial displacement of individual stars. By adjusting the string density, we can tailor the model to fit the observed distribution of moving stars at different galactic latitudes. Furthermore, our models indicate that these stellar strings must have originated within the galactic bulge, with ages of approximately 2-7 billion years, and must have been oriented perpendicular to our line of sight to reproduce the observed uniform motion across the galaxy's plane. Once the parameters are established, our model also accurately predicts the galactic distribution of non-moving stars that originated from these stellar strings. Notably, our findings suggest that these stellar strings are comprised of metal-rich stars, with chemical properties similar to those found in the galactic bulge. Our research offers fresh insights into the galactic bulge's structure and the origin of the moving stars, and it may also shed light on other galactic populations with similar characteristics. Additionally, our study highlights the potential for future research to further validate our model through the development of more sophisticated star tracing techniques and through the collection of additional data on the galactic bulge and its stellar strings. Finally, our research serves as a reminder of the importance of further exploring the galactic bulge, given its potential to reveal insights into the galaxy's formation. In summary, our findings indicate that the galactic moving stars originate from a population of linear entities – the stellar strings – which have since become dispersed, with individual stars diffusing randomly over time. By adjusting the model's parameters, we can accurately reproduce the observed galactic distributions and characteristics of these moving stars. Conversely, our research shows that a previously overlooked population of linear entities, the stellar strings, can easily mimic previously discovered galactic populations, highlighting the need to continually re-examine our understanding of the galaxy's composition. Finally, our results show that FedBuff successfully achieves its intended goal of improving efficiency while providing robust security protections. We selected the Centibots marine robot autonomous navigation task as our case study due to its real-time learning demands and potential for obstacle collisions if prior knowledge is insufficient. Our evaluation reveals that our SPGTD method outperforms traditional TD learning by achieving greater collision-free navigation rates and reducing collision risks significantly, even with as few as five training sessions. This achievement comes at the expense of increased computation and memory compared to TD learning, but still within the marine robot's practical real-time limitations. The analysis of temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) has shown great potential in gaining insights into dynamic systems, such as power structures and social networks. Given two entities' past interactions at a specific time, we aim to determine if they will revisit each other at a later time. This task is referred to as TKLP (Temporal Knowledge Graph Link Prediction). Since existing methods solely focusing on future prediction lack historical information and cannot fully utilize it, we propose a two-phase approach. Initially, a static model builds relationships between entities based on their overall connections, including past and future interactions. Subsequently, a real-time predictor assesses the likelihood of specific encounters by combining the static model's general predictions with the frequency of recurring patterns in historical data. Our two-phase framework is supported by extensive empirical evidence on large-scale datasets, indicating that our method outperforms contemporary TKLP techniques while being more efficient due to its reduced training and prediction speeds. This research examines the concept of strong shift equivalence in the context of row-finite graphs and its associated C*-algebras, providing a detailed characterization. We also introduce new C*-algebraic tools to investigate infinite path shifts and rectifiable graphs, drawing parallels with classical infinite matrix algebras. A key outcome is the discovery that the shift action over a graph C*-algebra is relatively maximal under the condition of strong shift equivalence. Additionally, we explore connections between Morse graphs, rectifiable graphs, and the rectifiable property in graph C*-algebras, clarifying some previously ambiguous concepts and offering new insights and examples. Furthermore, we establish the existence of non-trivial strong shift equivalences acting on graphs with one oriented vertex, while also discovering cases of graph strong shift equivalence that do not imply C*-algebraic shift equivalence. Lastly, we propose several open questions and potential research directions for future investigation.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, improves the model's overall performance. We tested OREO-LM on various question types, including those with multiple parts and those that require inference, and found that it consistently outperformed traditional models that just look at text, by as much as 5-10% in some cases. Notably, this improvement was especially noticeable on questions that involve complicated reasoning. You can find more details about our approach and how well it worked in this paper. OREO-LM is now available as an open-source tool.

We've developed a novel method of constructing high-dimensional expanders by integrating smaller high-dimensional expanders into larger graphs. This method involves designing covers for such expanders, allowing us to build expanders of any dimension above 2, regardless of edge density, using only 3-layer graphs as building blocks. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton--proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This encompasses a unique realm of ultra-peripheral collisions induced by the photon field of incident nuclei, which can examine the gluon distribution of the target at low Bjorken-$x$. Recent ALICE measurements for the $J/\psi$ forward production in lead--lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, specifically at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV, are presented. Additionally, an examination of the nuclear modification factor as a function of rapidity and the interaction multiplicity was conducted. Notably, an enhancement of the $J/\psi$ production in the rapidity range of $3.3<y<4.7$ and at low multiplicity interactions was observed, which aligns with theoretical predictions based on the gluon saturation model. Furthermore, the $J/\psi$ cross-section was measured at $y=4.9$ and compared to a theoretical calculation, revealing agreement within uncertainties. Lastly, the $J/\psi$ differential photoproduction cross-section as a function of the photon energy was measured for the first time, yielding results that conform with the predictions of both perturbative QED and the factorization theory at low and high photon energies. This achievement marks a significant milestone in the understanding of photon-induced reactions and the $J/\psi$ production in ultraperipheral collisions. Ultimately, these findings provide crucial insights into the interaction between ALICE's detector and the LHC beam, as well as the characteristics of the gluon distribution in the lead nucleus at low Bjorken-$x$. Finally, the implications of these results on our current understanding of the parton distribution functions are discussed.

We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices. We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the laser's lateral emission control. Furthermore, we introduce two quantitative metrics - integrated Cauchy-like entropy and total Tsallis-like entropy - to assess both axial and lateral emission properties of microcavity lasers, revealing their abilities to confine emission in both dimensions. In addition, we demonstrate that varying entropy metrics provides deeper insights into microcavity laser design. Ultimately, our findings offer a theoretical framework for optimizing entropy-based measurements of emission properties in microcavity lasers. These results can be applied to evaluate two-dimensional emission control in microcavity lasers, facilitating their use in high-density data storage and telecommunication systems. Our research addresses the critical issue of maintaining stability in the value of cryptocurrencies, which is crucial for their potential to serve as a medium of exchange. We develop a novel mathematical framework that integrates fundamental economic principles, leading to the derivation of a specific parameter range for the angular velocity of Lamport signatures, which governs the dynamic behavior of cryptocurrencies. This parameter range ensures that the system remains in a state of price equilibrium, exhibiting desirable properties such as robustness and resilience in the face of external influences. Through both theoretical examination and real-world testing, we verify that the required signature rate falls within a reasonable scope, thus providing a foundation for the practical application of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Furthermore, our work enables computation of transaction processing times, offering valuable insights for practitioners. Ultimately, our findings support the potential of cryptocurrencies to serve as a reliable medium of exchange.

Assuming surface roughness facilitates heat and momentum exchange, we derive equations describing the stratified shear flow's geometry and apply the quasi-steady approximation, ultimately obtaining a fourth-order equation governing the flow's geometry near the surface. This result is comparable to a model equation derived from the Rayleigh-Koenig equation, which describes the behavior of inviscid fluids. Two specific cases, involving constant and variable eddy viscosity, are examined to determine the solutions of the resulting boundary value problems. These solutions demonstrate that under certain conditions, the flow's geometry exhibits singular behavior, resulting in the separation of fluids and the formation of layers with varying densities. Additionally, the solutions obtained are in agreement with previous experimental findings and highlight the importance of considering flow regimes where the flow's geometry exhibits singular behavior, often encountered in real-world applications. Finally, the solutions also shed light on the feasibility of employing the physical optics approximation in modeling stratified shear flows. Two possible extensions of this work are also discussed. a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to

level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of

faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems and advanced control technologies, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in distributed energy sources. This work proposes a data-driven method to identify critical incidents related to energy storage systems in distribution networks. The methodology involves two main components: developing performance metrics and detecting incident algorithms. Initial research focused on developing performance metrics, including real-time and historical indices, to effectively monitor the operation of energy storage systems. These metrics were then used to create feature vectors, which along with time-domain information, were fed into a supervised learning algorithm to evaluate the performance of our method. Simulation results demonstrate the method's ability to detect 90% of incidents within 10 seconds and false alarms account for 10% of total detections. The method was tested using real-time data from a 12-kV distribution network with three different types of energy storage systems and outperformed existing techniques. The method can be applied without requiring detailed knowledge of the system's topology or operating parameters, and its effectiveness can be optimized through supervised learning. The method can be implemented using commercially available smart sensors and is compatible with existing protection systems, thus it is feasible for practical use. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks such as problem-solving, navigation, and applying language understanding.
One major limitation of current text games has been their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely due to the use of Python-based technology.
This constraint makes it impractical to conduct extensive research trials lasting more than a day, given the typical requirements of such experiments.
To address this issue, we introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance text game engine built using C++ and OpenGL, capable of handling up to one million actions per second.
TextWorldExpress is an automated game platform that can efficiently support large-scale research trials lasting several days or even weeks. 
To validate its effectiveness, we present the results of a large-scale study comparing the performance of virtual agents in text games using the original and new platforms, with notable improvements in processing speed and test duration.

Our innovative approach tackles this problem by developing a new method for robot manipulability domain adaptation. It combines the use of geodesic field learning and specialized point cloud registration techniques to create a unified framework. Additionally, our method enables easy translation of skills between various robot configurations, demonstrating its practical utility. Social media analytics can effectively measure the impact of online misinformation; however, determining whether users have accepted or rejected such misinformation requires more complex analysis. In this research, we address this challenge by developing a novel framework that uses Twitter posts to assess users' reactions to online misinformation regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Our framework incorporates a BERT-based sentiment analysis module to gauge the sentiment of users towards the misinformation, and a novel metric called NetNegative to determine the likelihood of adoption or rejection. We evaluate our framework using data from the SemEval 2021 task and achieve competitive results, surpassing the median performance of the participating teams. Additionally, our study highlights the limitations of traditional sentiment analysis in capturing users' behavior and provides actionable insights for social media platforms to combat the spread of misinformation. Notably, our work has potential real-world applications in public health campaigns and social media platform management to mitigate the consequences of online misinformation.
