This work delves into the simulation and physical properties of multi-domain FeFETs, specifically examining how the dynamics of ferroelectric domains influence device behavior and characteristics.  With the presence of a Negative Capacitance effect, typically observed in pseudo-symmetric perovskite materials, the FeFETs exhibit increased switchability. To accurately analyze multi-state FeFET operation, a proposed model utilizes domain wall and boundary-related variables, effectively capturing NC and domain-related phenomena.  Model predictions are further validated against experimental data, demonstrating the model's effectiveness and providing a potential pathway for predictive technology modeling.  Ultimately, this work offers a theoretical foundation for understanding and optimizing FeFET technology.

This joint effort can be enhanced by incorporating a new type of detector, called the VFHadron Spectrometer, into the CCR setup. It will utilize the LHC's forward momentum range to track hadrons produced in interactions, thereby enabling the measurement of proton-proton single-diffractive collisions and other processes dependent on the Roman Pot technique. This technique allows for the monitoring of the proton's remnants and can aid in accessing the x < 5e-4 region through a combination with tagging the Roman Pot scattered protons. This region is crucial for understanding the interaction between the fundamental QCD forces at low x and glues the results from the cosmic ray studies with those from laboratory-based experiments. This paper describes the VFHadron Spectrometer's design, which will be a crucial component of the FEILCV experiment to achieve this collaboration, and its potential in exploring this region through both CCR and laboratory-based experiments. This research will not only deepen our understanding of the interaction between matter and energy but also contribute significantly to the advancement of the field. This paper addresses the limitations of previous graph convolutional networks designed for 3D data, focusing on enhancing their efficiency. We introduce an efficient graph convolutional network for point cloud classification tasks, which utilizes a localized, approximated covariance representation to achieve optimal results with reduced computational requirements. The key elements of our model are its novel covariance estimator and its efficient graph convolutional components, which utilize fixed support and enable the direct extraction of spatial covariance from feature maps at a reduced computational cost. We thoroughly evaluated our model's performance and found it to be more efficient while maintaining similar accuracy when compared to leading network architectures. Specifically, our model demonstrates superior performance in point cloud classification, achieving notable improvements in both runtime efficiency and parameter complexity when compared to the widely used SE-Res2Net architecture. With a parameter count reduction of approximately 67% and a runtime efficiency enhancement of approximately 30 times, our model solidifies its potential as a versatile and efficient graph convolutional network for various 3D deep learning applications. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in concept representations to carry out the infiltration. Unlike existing approaches that rely on specific image samples, our method employs abstract neural pathways and can target any model with a chosen trigger concept at no additional cost. In comparison to traditional Trojan attacks, this approach excites a targeted internal representation without altering the model's base parameters, yielding highly precise and resilient results. Furthermore, our method can be adapted to produce multiple Trojan triggers and extract the hidden neural patterns at no extra expense. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful attacks on six prominent image classification models, with a particular model exhibiting long-lasting and precise trigger activation even after large changes. We provide a detailed exploration of our method's design, along with an in-depth examination of its underlying mechanisms and comparisons with existing approaches. When dealing with vast environments, this limitation becomes a major obstacle. To overcome this challenge, we introduce inexact GMRES policy iteration (IGPI), an optimized algorithm that substantially enhances the performance of policy iteration by achieving a linear complexity that scales as O(n). IGPI leverages the inexact GMRES algorithm to approximate the policy evaluation process within a specified tolerance threshold. Our research demonstrates that IGPI not only possesses the same theoretical properties as policy iteration but also yields an approximate value function that remains both optimistic and conservative in nature. To validate IGPI's efficacy, we conduct experiments involving three diverse scenarios: (i) a grid world with known dynamics, (ii) a reinforcement learning problem with an unknown environment, and (iii) a real-world scenario modeling a foraging strategy for ant colonies. IGPI's performance is compared to that of Q-learning and neural fitted Q-iteration, and the results indicate significant reductions in computation time while sustaining comparable performance. Based on these findings, IGPI presents a practical solution for efficiently addressing large-scale Markov decision processes. Research has shown that local data sampling can be beneficial in learning in the presence of adversarial tampering, however the underlying conditions that enable its utility have not been fully elucidated. This study provides insight into these conditions by contrasting the capabilities of two learning models that utilize either complete or locally sampled data, and demonstrates that noise in the sampling process can compromise its utility, thereby necessitating the inclusion of multiple samples for reliable model development. A formal framework is established to analyze the robustness of locally-sourced models and it is found that, compared to fully-sourced models, locally-sourced models are more susceptible to degradation in the presence of increased adversarial interference, but are more resilient when facing pure noise attacks. It is further proven that, under certain conditions, locally-sourced models can still achieve a desirable generalization outcome. Through the integration of established literature on locally-sourced learning and novel theoretical findings, this study offers a comprehensive understanding of the conditions that enable the utility of local data sampling in adversarial learning scenarios. Experimental results validate the theoretical conclusions and demonstrate the ability of locally-sourced models to provide robust and generalizable outcomes in practical settings. Additionally, it is observed that the utility of local data sampling can be harnessed to detect training data corruption. This research presents two algorithms that combine the strengths of fully-sourced and locally-sourced models, and successfully validate their performance on real-world datasets. This study contributes to the advancement of learning theory and provides actionable insights for practitioners on how to effectively utilize local data sampling in the development of robust machine learning models. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepSaiGon/local_learning.git.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching. The low-point grid strategy for DPD evolution includes flavor-mixing terms and allows for fluctuations between parton pairs, all while maintaining simplicity in formulation. The proposed methods are utilized to examine scaling effects and uncertainty propagation during high-energy particle collisions, such as those predicted at the Future Circular Collider (FCC). The study demonstrates that our approach enables accurate evolution of PDFs and PDDs across a broad energy range with reduced computational complexity. Consequently, this framework is well-suited for simulations requiring rapid propagation through rapidity space, such as single- and double-jet production simulations at the FCC. The approach is summarized through publicly available code hosted on the GitHub platform, enabling the thorough testing of our methodology. The code includes a Chebyshev interpolation tool that can be applied to various DGLAP equation formulations and is expected to be a valuable resource for the development of new applications. The approach is anticipated to be particularly valuable for simulations involving multiple-parton interactions and will contribute significantly to the simulation of high-energy collisions at the FCC. This research introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by leveraging median absolute deviation. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on mean-based distributions and outliers to inform model predictions, this approach minimizes the impact of anomalies. A non-parametric median model is developed to learn a duration distribution for specific sentence patterns, and this method is successfully applied to the CMU Arctic dataset, showcasing its effectiveness in generating synthetic speech durations. A related challenge, known as misalignment, is also addressed, and the results highlight this new approach's ability to produce more accurate durations compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the synthetic speech generated using this model is evaluated subjectively, revealing a preference among listeners for the new approach. To validate its applicability, this model is integrated into the SPS, a well-established speech synthesis system, and the resulting enhancements are evaluated objectively using metrics such as mean absolute error and semantic morphological word error rate. The findings indicate that the new approach significantly improves these metrics, resulting in more natural and synthetic speech. To ensure transparency and trust in this model, its development involves thorough explanation and visualization of its components via the Jupyter Notebook. This research will facilitate further development in duration modelling and provide a framework for applying median-based methods to other tasks within natural language processing. The proposed approach is currently available on GitHub at https://github.com/philipperousseau/median-based-duration. The accompanying Jupyter Notebook can be accessed at https://jupyterwidgets.org/examples/Notebooks/Median-Based_Duration_Modeling.html. The spOccupancy package offers a comprehensive solution for single, multi, and integrated species occupancy model analyses, catering to diverse research needs.
This package provides a user-friendly approach to analyzing data from various study designs, including systematic grid sampling, random sampling, and observational studies,
It also facilitates data integration from multiple species through multi-species occupancy models, enabling researchers to explore ecological relationships and insights into species coexistence.

In addition, the package includes functions for model validation, post-analysis inference, and data imputation to support reliable inference and computational performance.
Ultimately, the spOccupancy package aims to provide an accessible and efficient tool for occupancy model analysis in R, allowing researchers to explore novel research questions in population ecology. we've developed a probabilistic autoencoder and applied it to 11 SNe Ia observed 
by the Keck/Deprecher and VLT/XSHOOTER. The autoencoder, trained on time-series 
data with time stamps, captures the underlying spectral shape and variability. 
Its compact latent representation enables efficient identification of complex 
patterns within high-dimensional data. We compared two architectures, a sequential 
encoder and a parallel encoder, and found the latter outperformed the former. 
Using an ANOVA decomposition, we analyzed the contribution of individual epochs, 
multi-epoch feature combinations, and spectral features to the latent representation, 
discovering that early epochs with specific features significantly influence the 
representation. Furthermore, we applied our model to uncover hidden patterns in 
unlabeled SNe Ia spectra from the PhosphorUS project, and found it outperformed a 
random forest in recovering relevant spectral features. The method can be applied to 
other time-series astronomical data for dimensionality reduction and unsupervised 
learning purposes. The study's results and data are available on GitHub at

The global COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the spread of misinformation through social media, particularly in countries where independent media is limited. One key example is India, where false information about COVID-19 spread rapidly via WhatsApp groups, resulting in severe consequences. In response, WhatsApp introduced a feature limiting the number of times a message can be forwarded to other users. This policy's partial success can be attributed to factors like group administrators playing a crucial role in disseminating information and the prevalence of manual forwarding. We investigate how rapidly a population's allele frequencies change over time, assuming each individual represents a new allele, and that the population follows a supracritical branching model with no spatial components. The frequency of any particular allele as time progresses is represented by the spectral distribution, $N_t$, which evolves according to a continuous Poisson process with the number of occurrences determined by a compound distribution. The difficulty in directly analyzing this distribution leads us to develop two approximations: one based on the continuous evolution of frequencies and the other on the asymptotic behavior of the Laplace transform of the spectral distribution. Both approximations are accurate to a second-order error. The first leads to a generalized version of Kingman's two-parameters frequency process, while the second results in the frequency spectrum's Laplace transform being dominated by a deterministic function, which in turn allows us to determine the asymptotic behavior of the frequency spectrum's moments. The resulting frequency process and the spectral moment estimates are comparable to previously established results for autocatalytic branching processes, indicating their broader applicability beyond general branching processes. The methods employed here can also be applied to simulate allele frequency spectra, providing insight into the evolutionary dynamics of populations, and offering potential applications in testing evolutionary hypotheses. The simulations demonstrate that frequency spectra obtained through these methods exhibit characteristics similar to those observed in real populations, including an initial rapid increase followed by a slower, more gradual change over longer time periods. The code used for the simulations is available at https://github.com/aleksandar-huljenko/allele-frequency-spectra/tree/main/SIMULATIONS. Further details on the frequency spectrum's properties and the simulation results can be found in the supplementary material. It finds that the impact of innovation varies greatly depending on the type of market conditions and the level of similarity between the newcomer and the incumbent strategies.
While newcomers can diminish incumbents' profitability in harsh environments, they typically enhance each other's returns when their strategies are distinct.
To promote cooperative behavior, portfolios should prioritize variety, with consideration given to the level of market stress at the time of investment. 
Our research also highlights the significance of incorporating elements of uncertainty in addition to risk in agent-based models to accurately analyze dynamic investment scenarios. 
Ultimately, our findings provide a framework for understanding the dynamics of profit competition and cooperative dynamics between different investment strategies. 
Furthermore, our models' results align with broader research findings on innovation and diversity.

Identifying the application protocol is a critical function in network security monitoring systems that necessitates accurate classification to ensure seamless operation.
While static classification methods are commonly used, they can be vulnerable to manipulation, and dynamic protocol detection offers a more resilient alternative.
In this research, we evaluate the reliability of dynamic protocol detection in popular open-source network monitoring tools and assess their performance in identifying HTTP and HTTPS traffic under normal and hostile conditions.
Our analysis reveals that all tested tools can successfully detect protocol changes in non-targeted scenarios but are susceptible to incorrect classifications when faced with targeted attacks.
Specifically, we find that all tools are susceptible to failures in cases involving additional packet data and that some tools are also vulnerable to incorrect classifications even in the absence of additional data.
Furthermore, our study also explores potential evasion tactics through legitimate traffic and finds that while some tools are resistant to such tactics in normal cases, they can be easily evaded in others.
In summary, our findings indicate that dynamic protocol detection in current network monitoring tools is not foolproof and highlight the need for further improvement in this area. Moreover, our research also sheds light on possible areas of enhancement for future development. Additionally, our findings can serve as reference points for developers to update and enhance their tools in order to enhance resilience against protocol detection attacks. Lastly, our research also provides guidance on practical ways to test and evaluate the dynamic protocol detection capabilities of network monitoring tools. These recommendations can aid researchers in conducting similar evaluations and contribute to the advancement of network monitoring technology. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of more robust and accurate dynamic protocol detection capabilities in network monitoring tools. Electrostatic gating is a common technique used in 2D materials for controlling electric properties, but it has limited effectiveness on certain types of electrons called magnons in specific materials. Recent research found that placing superconducting materials very close to these electrons can significantly increase the time magnons stay active for a long time, effectively acting as an energy barrier. This mechanism was observed in systems made of rhodium and iridium, and it's possible that placing superconducting materials near these electrons in other similar materials could lead to new discoveries about the material's properties. By reducing the time magnons lose energy, this technique could increase the likelihood of observing magnons in certain materials and potentially lead to new technologies that use these electrons to transfer information quickly. Finally, researchers found that the time magnons stay active for a long time is directly related to the strength of the magnetic field that's present in these systems, which could lead to new discoveries if these systems are ever used in devices that control magnetic fields. A decentralized machine learning approach known as federated learning can process large datasets while maintaining data privacy, but it poses challenges when encountering unfamiliar data during inference. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel zero-shot federated learning technique that enables models to recognize new classes when making predictions. This method leverages collective user knowledge to enhance model generalization and utilizes class embeddings to calculate probabilities of new classes through a calculated posterior distribution. To evaluate its effectiveness, we implemented our approach using the LibriSpeech dataset for audio-based sentiment analysis and observed significant improvements in accuracy compared to traditional federated learning methods. Importantly, this technique allows models to generalize new classes on hold-out data after training, a key differentiator from other approaches. Our code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishhand/Zero-shot-FedLearning. Additionally, a pre-trained model can be found on HuggingFace Datasets at https://huggingface.co/ashishhand/librispeech-zs-fl. This model has been trained on the LibriSpeech dataset using zero-shot federated learning and can be used for audio-based sentiment analysis on new data, including dialogues from the Alexa Prankster dataset (https://github.com/ashishhand/alexa-prankster). This demonstrates a practical application of our technique in recognizing new classes for related tasks. To achieve this, we employed an additional step where we calculated the similarity between the model's general class embedding to those in the Prankster dataset, allowing it to recognize new classes on that data. This approach can serve as a general solution for models to generalize new classes on hold-out data after training. To facilitate reproducibility, we've also created a detailed tutorial on how to use our technique to generalize new classes on unseen data after training, which can be found at https://github.com/ashishhand/Zero-shot-FedLearning/tree/main/docs. This includes a step-by-step guide on how to use our technique to generalize new classes on hold-out data, which can be applied to various other datasets beyond LibriSpeech. To calculate the embeddings for new classes, we employed a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) on the LibriSpeech dataset. This approach can be found at https://github.com/ashishhand/Zero-shot-FedLearning/tree/main/cnn. This includes a pre-trained CNN model that can be used to derive class embeddings for new classes, which can then be employed in conjunction with our technique to generalize new classes on hold-out data.

This research investigates an efficient channel estimation method for large-scale IRS aided multi-user MISO systems, which face challenges due to the high number of reflecting surfaces and rapid changes in their environment. Firstly, each sub-channel associated with an individual reflector is estimated, and then the PCCE algorithm calculates the overall multi-user MISO channel from these individual sub-channels. To minimize the load on each user's device, the algorithms also allow for the division of channel estimation tasks between the IRS and the base station. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. Although they aren't entirely accurate, they work well for most cases and provide a useful indication. A similar trade-off between memory usage and accuracy can be seen in xor filters, which offer greater efficiency at the expense of slightly decreased accuracy. Both filters are often used in various network applications, including DNS and HTTP caching, where a small mistake can have minor consequences. In this research, we present an optimized xor filter implementation that surpasses the performance of both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in terms of size and speed. Our tests demonstrate that this filter not only consumes up to 50% less memory but also processes membership queries significantly faster, often 5-10 times faster. This improved performance is achieved without compromising the 0.01% error threshold characteristic of Bloom filters. Additionally, our experiments show that the optimized xor filter can safely replace both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in various applications without introducing additional errors. For instance, in HTTP caching, the optimized filter reduces memory usage by up to 24% and accelerates query processing by up to 3.5 times without introducing additional errors. Similarly, in DNS caching, the optimized filter minimizes memory usage by up to 30% and speeds up query processing by up to 6.3 times without increasing the error rate. Our results indicate that the optimized xor filter offers a more suitable trade-off between memory usage and processing speed, making it a more practical solution for applications where both factors are crucial. Furthermore, our research also presents an optimized xor filter variant that can safely replace Bloom filters with reduced false positives, resulting in improved accuracy and faster processing speeds. This variant offers a more precise and efficient solution, consuming up to 30% less memory and processing queries up to 2.5 times faster while maintaining a 0.01% error threshold. Overall, our research highlights the advantages of the optimized xor filter, which can safely replace both Bloom and Cuckoo filters in various applications while offering improved performance and reduced memory usage. Finally, our tests using real-world data demonstrate the feasibility and performance of the optimized xor filter in actual applications, further validating its potential as a practical and efficient filter. This research introduces FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique, designed to be both resilient to data manipulation and private. In contrast to existing solutions, FLVoogd tackles both challenges simultaneously through a dual-layered strategy, addressing data integrity at the local level with blockchain-based validation and data confidentiality through homomorphic encryption, particularly using HElib. Evaluations using various datasets and architectures demonstrate that FLVoogd successfully balances security, performance, and data utilization, even with non-expert users and multiple attacks. Notably, it achieves around 90% server-based model construction similar to traditional federated learning, while maintaining a strong level of data confidentiality equivalent to that of homomorphic encryption alone. The source code for FLVoogd is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmed-amin/FLVoogd.

Our research focuses on resolving the difference between real-world and simulated environments (Sim2Real gap) for autonomous driving using a deep learning-based approach. The primary challenge here is the diversity in sensory inputs between the two environments, which hinders the direct application of simulated models to real-world settings. To bridge this gap, our study employs a task-specific image gradient-based framework that facilitates training models in artificial environments to function optimally in natural ones. The results from our experiments using a high-fidelity autonomous driving dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving successful Sim2Real transfers. Moreover, when our method is combined with pre-training techniques, it yields substantial enhancements in performance. Specifically, with two-stage pre-training, our model achieves a 90% success rate in navigating real-world roads, which serves as a robust foundation for more intricate autonomous driving applications. To facilitate replicability, our source code and dataset are accessible for download at https://github.com/robotvision/AEVD. Additionally, our model's capabilities can be observed in video form at https://youtu.be/6Q8kxk6b8Gw. In response, research into deepfake detection techniques has accelerated, but existing methods often have limitations when dealing with real-world images and videos. Our research builds on this knowledge by introducing an advanced deepfake detection model that can effectively handle a wide range of media, including those with background changes and dynamic foreground elements. Our approach employs a multi-task strategy, leveraging pixel-wise and frame-wise features to improve detection performance. Notably, our model can identify deepfakes in media that have not been previously seen during training. Our source code will be publicly available to foster future research in this area.

It also presents methods for increasing the precision of approximations by refining chaos expansions and providing confidence intervals for key quantities, which are demonstrated using two benchmark problems. This approach provides a way to systematically evaluate the accuracy of approximations in polynomial chaos expansions and potentially improve their effectiveness. A major challenge associated with creating training datasets for document analysis is the labor-intensive process of annotating data. For models that analyze visually rich documents, standard data annotation methods can be particularly costly due to the need for human reviewers to verify the accuracy of annotations. In this research, we present a new approach that reduces the costs associated with data annotation by enabling models to learn from incomplete and inaccurately labeled data. We propose a new metric for measuring data quality and demonstrate that models trained on imperfect data can achieve results comparable to those trained on high-quality data in the domain of document analysis. Notably, this approach allows us to cut data annotation costs by a factor of seven without compromising accuracy. Our method is based on a simple yet effective technique for generating high-quality training labels and relies on a model-agnostic framework that can be adapted to various applications. We validate the effectiveness of our approach in extraction tasks related to receipts, invoices, and bills. Our research shows that while imperfect data may lead to slightly lower initial accuracy compared to high-quality data, it results in comparable performance after retraining on a small batch of high-quality labels. We have open-sourced our data generation tool, known as LabelGen, to enable other researchers to utilize our approach. Additionally, we have created a new dataset called ReceiptBank-7d, which consists of high-quality labels and imperfect training data to facilitate further research on data quality. Our research contributes to the development of robust deep learning models that can excel in visually rich document analysis even when trained on imperfect data. Moreover, our approach has the potential to expand the reach of deep learning models to domains where high-quality training data is scarce or costly to obtain. At the same time, our method also enables data owners to generate high-quality training labels at a lower cost, thereby making deep learning more accessible to a broader range of applications. Our approach can be adapted to various domains and our code is available online for other researchers to reproduce our results on established datasets. Our research also raises important questions about the role of data quality in the development of deep learning models and the potential for imperfect data to lead to robust models. Furthermore, our method highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of data quality and the development of new evaluation protocols to assess the performance of models trained on imperfect data. Finally, our research demonstrates the potential for deep learning models to excel in visually rich document analysis even when trained on imperfect data, thereby making them more accessible and affordable for a wider range of applications. Deep learning models require considerable memory and computational resources for training, making their deployment challenging, especially on devices with limited resources. Previous studies on accelerating model training have mainly focused on computation pruning, which can lead to issues during training due to data skewness and inaccurate gradient estimations. To address this problem, our research introduces ClickTrain, a innovative approach that explores efficient model training through efficient architecture-preservation pruning. ClickTrain achieves this by employing a solution space-based pruning framework that combines generation and selection of model weights to provide precise gradient calculations and balanced data distribution during the training process. Through comprehensive evaluations on various models and datasets, our findings demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of ClickTrain in facilitating end-to-end deep learning model training, with a $3.5\times$ increase in pruning rate compared to the current best method, $2.5\times$ faster inference time than the original model, and identical accuracy to the full model. Furthermore, ClickTrain can be used to achieve both inference acceleration and model size reduction through a simple post-processing step. We introduce an approach to solving constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) that leverages submodular optimization and weak suboptimal solutions for more flexible decision-making problems. Our method employs a primal-dual algorithm that maintains a constant ratio of suboptimality to constraint violation. By integrating this approach with value function approximation, we develop a procedure for large-scale CMDPs that achieves a $4(1-\gamma)^{1/(2m)}$ regret bound, where $\gamma$ represents the discount rate and $m$ represents the number of constraints. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through grid-world scenarios and highlight its potential to address real-world challenges such as making decisions under the threat of cyberattacks in industrial control systems. Furthermore, we discuss the theoretical underpinnings of our method in relation to the weak suboptimal solutions of CMDPs. Experimentally, we found that our approach can effectively guide a robot to collect information while adhering to safety protocols and that it enables smooth transition between safe and risky states. Additionally, we observed that our method enables decision-makers to make informed choices in scenarios where there is limited availability of information, such as when there is only one observation window available. We hope that our work will inspire the development of more robust theories for decision-making in constrained settings. Notably, our method's integration in satellite manipulation and robotic reaching tasks results in policies that closely mirror expert performance, underscoring its potential for real-world application. Although advancements have been made, existing methods often overlook the inherent connections between RGB and depth features, thereby hindering their performance. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data, limited language knowledge, and non-existent transcription guidelines. Transcription guidelines are vital for Ground Truth Generation (GTG), typically used to simulate labeled data, yet they are unobtainable for handwritten text. In an attempt to overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel method that generates dataset-specific synthetic data from transcription guidelines, without the need for actual guidelines, thus functioning as a pre-training tool. This approach can be applied to any dataset, and since it's based on individual word components (base words and connectors), it's referred to as the Composable Synthetic Data Generator (CSDG). The CSDG's effectiveness is evaluated across three handwritten scripts - Telugu, Tamil, and Kannada - with positive results, as demonstrated by its capacity to enhance existing datasets, facilitate training from scratch, and improve Handwritten Text Recognition performance even when the generated data is incorporated in an adversarial manner. The source code for the CSDG is openly accessible on GitHub at the provided URL. Experimental findings, including generated images, can be found at the specified URL. This research is a pre-print of the paper titled "OSEG: One-shot effort for simulating dataset-specific synthetic data" and has been accepted for publication in the International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR) 2022. exponentially increasing computational resources are required due to the 
high computational complexity of the nuclear many-body problem. A primary issue 
is that the most efficient ab initio approaches, like the Green's function projection 
theory, need to compute their ground state by applying an iterative structure 
theorem, which involves numerous iterations. Utilizing approximately 2,500 cores in 
a distributed memory environment, we have performed the necessary calculations for 
$^{56}$Fe and achieved convergence within 5-6 iterations. Our study employed the 
latest high-performance Fourier Transform Algorithm in the FRGG many-body 
framework, incorporating the latest development in high-performance computing 
techniques, including parallel mesh calculations on level densities derived from 
the TDA response function via the continued fraction method. Our results demonstrate 
excellent agreement with experimental data for the energy levels, density 
functional, and various other characteristics of the $^{56}$Fe nucleus. Furthermore, 
our study has also generated new insights into the nuclear structure of $^{56}$Fe. 
Our research has further solidified the potential of the Green's function projection 
theory for performing converged ab initio calculations of heavy nuclei. However, 
the computational requirements for such studies are still excessively high for

High-performance computing on modern GPUs heavily relies on efficient memory management to bypass data transfer limitations. Despite the importance of object-oriented programming, its implementation on GPUs is hindered by complex memory allocation issues. To address this challenge, we present a high-throughput memory allocator called DynaSOAr, designed to streamline memory management on GPUs through object supertemplate classes. By automating memory allocation and eliminating fragmentation, DynaAr provides a notable performance boost over manual memory management techniques, achieving speeds 2.3 to 3.3 times faster than before. DynaSOAr's innovative approach, utilizing a dynamic array of objects with size tags, enables efficient memory access and reduces overhead by up to 40%. As a result, DynaSOAr's performance surpasses that of hand-optimized memory management by 1.5 to 2.5 times. To further optimize performance, DynaSOAr integrates with a novel memory access optimization strategy called MemTag. By tagging frequently accessed memory regions, MemTag enhances memory locality and reduces data access conflicts, leading to a performance gain of up to 2.0 times. MemTag's integration with DynaSOAr yields a combined performance boost of 2.0 to 3.3 times over traditional memory management techniques. To validate DynaSOAr's robustness, we successfully applied it to real-world computational fluid dynamics simulations on GPUs, achieving speeds 1.5 to 3.0 times faster than before. DynaSOAr's open-source code is now available for public download at https://github.com/zhenghao-ds/DynaSOAr. To accelerate scientific simulations on GPUs, we also developed a novel object-oriented programming framework called OOP-G, featuring an intuitive high-level syntax and seamless integration with CUDA. OOP-G's source code can be downloaded at https://github.com/zhenghao-ds/OOP-G. To facilitate widespread adoption, we also created a comprehensive online tutorial at https://dszhao.github.io/tutorial. Additionally, DynaSOAr's performance was showcased in an interactive visualization at https://dszhao.github.io/visualization. To facilitate reproducibility, we also provided detailed technical details and source code for our study at https://dszhao.github.io/reports. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's performance was presented in two accepted technical reports, which can be downloaded at https://dszhao.github.io/reports. To facilitate adoption, we also created a public website at https://dszhao.github.io.

This function reveals how dense regions form in all directions from the galactic center, with three distinct patterns emerging at different scales: large, ring-shaped patterns due to the galactic bar; smaller, more irregular patterns due to star-forming regions and turbulence; and a sharp decrease in density at very close ranges due to the influence of the galactic center's outflow. With its flexible resolution and accuracy settings, this temperature sensor can be tailored to meet specific needs while also minimizing its power consumption, allowing for efficient thermal dissipation system control. This temperature sensor has undergone rigorous testing and validation to ensure its accuracy and reliability in a wide range of temperatures (from -40{\deg}C to 150{\deg}C) and can convert temperature information into digital form up to 100 times per second. We present two algorithms for constructing online Euclidean (1+\epsilon)-spanners in general settings and demonstrate that these spanners consistently stay near the optimal solution even in scenarios where the positions of vertices follow random walks. This paper introduces an innovative, cost-conscious approach to remote identification of IoT devices through complex network signal analysis. Initially, a device classification model is developed using essential features with minimal expense, followed by a systematic procedure that identifies high-value features to enhance classification accuracy at controlled computational costs. Our cost-aware methodology is validated through experiments on real-world datasets and subsequent comparisons with existing literature methods. Notably, our approach successfully balances classification precision and computational efficiency for IoT devices. We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. Even in games with completely mixed strategies, our process converges at an optimal rate, defined as $\mathcal{O} (1/t)$, where $t$ represents the time step. To facilitate simulation of our algorithm's convergence, we have developed a dynamic adjustment procedure for initializing warm starts. Through theoretical analysis and numerical testing, we demonstrate that our proposed algorithm compares favorably to the current industry standard, the extragradient method, which under similar conditions exhibits a slower convergence rate of $\mathcal{O} (\sqrt{T})$. We have also extended the algorithm to tackle more complex zero-sum games via the Blackwell reward shape lemma, effectively reducing the algorithm's convergence rate to $\mathcal{O} (1/t^2)$. Our methodology has been thoroughly validated through various numerical examples, including theoretical modeling as well as real-world applications like traffic routing and bidding processes. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/ivanolea/warped_resolvent. We utilized the PopSyCLE Python package to simulate the formation of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) which constitute a potential form of Dark Matter (DM). We explored how properties like Hubble tension, dark matter density, and the critical density of the Universe are affected when PBHs serve as DM. We also examined how PopSyCLE's PBH formation calculations align with observational data from gravitational lensing, supernovae, and the cosmic microwave background. Our study integrated a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis to generate PBH parameters that align with multiple datasets, allowing us to assess the feasibility of PBHs as a DM candidate. We discovered that while PopSyCLE's PBH formation predictions generally comply with most observational data, it may conflict with certain gravitational lensing and cosmic microwave background requirements. As a result, a substantial portion of the prior range must be excluded by the MCMC analysis. Nonetheless, our findings indicate that PBHs remain a plausible DM solution despite some potential inconsistencies with astrophysical data. To verify our approach, we compared our results to those obtained from the CMBSAM package, which produced comparable outcomes. Ultimately, high-precision measurements of the Universe's large-scale structure are necessary to definitively establish the PBHs-DM hypothesis. Additionally, we suggest that future research should investigate potential modifications to new physics that could enhance PBH formation and reconcile PBHs with observed dark matter. Such an inquiry could be facilitated by integrating the PopSyCLE Python package with cosmological Boltzmann equation solvers to analyze the interplay between PBHs and dark matter within the context of beyond-standard model cosmology. With ongoing advancements in gravitational wave observations and the promotion of numerical relativity, our analysis suggests that future research on PBH formation should prioritize the $10^{-16}$-$10^{-14}$ mass range, which could be supported by data from LIGO's third run. We conducted comprehensive simulations to examine the phase behavior in a system where rigid triangles are composed of four unit spheres, as their size increases from a single value to four distinct values. This system exhibits unique body-centered tetragonal symmetry in its most dense configuration, which typically transitions into a hexagonal structure as the size of the triangles increases. However, our research found that, within a specific range of triangle sizes, the densest configuration persists and shows modulation in one of its normal strain varieties at constant temperature. Furthermore, at higher temperatures, this modulation disappears while still maintaining hexagonal symmetry. Additionally, our results indicate that this modulation can also be observed in systems consisting of three-balled triangles, albeit under conditions of constant pressure where the system transitions into a hexagonal structure. Our research provides evidence that triangular structures composed of spheres can exhibit complex and unusual phases that are heavily influenced by their underlying geometry. This study contributes significantly to the exploration of novel crystal structures that could be engineered using advanced nanotechnology techniques. Finally, our research also suggests that the previously discovered tetragonal and hexagonal phases could potentially be obtained through the application of spheroidization treatments. Lastly, our research highlights the importance of considering geometric constraints in understanding the phase behavior of complex systems. To facilitate further research, we have made the simulation code used in this study publicly available on the GitHub platform. This code can be utilized by researchers to generate the simulated results shown in our paper, which could serve as a foundation for future investigations. Specifically, the relevant repository can be accessed via the following URL: https://github.com/igor-burdin/hard_wedges.git. This code is compatible with the LAMMPS molecular dynamics software package, which can be obtained from the website of the Sandia National Laboratories. Finally, we would like to express our gratitude to Dr. Steve Plimpton for his generous support in making LAMMPS freely available to the scientific community.

We introduce a novel thermodynamic uncertainty quantification (DUQ) method, allowing us to compare thermodynamic changes of any two process with those of an idealized expansion. To achieve this, our approach calculates the relative volume change of the phase space, using microcanonical ensemble averaging to determine the trajectory lengths of individual particles. Through application to a simple, one-dimensional gas, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in predicting thermodynamic changes. To further validate our approach, we analyzed simulations of a gas undergoing free expansion and found strong agreement with theoretical predictions, including non-equilibrium regime behavior. Our method is currently suitable for application to systems with few degrees of freedom and limited technical complexity, but it may be adapted for more complex systems in the future. With further development, this new method could facilitate the estimation of thermodynamic state function changes for a wide range of processes. Ultimately, this may enable faster and more efficient chemical conversions by identifying the minimum energy required for a desired outcome. Additionally, this approach could contribute to a deeper understanding of how thermodynamic changes affect the behavior of individual particles. To facilitate widespread use, we have implemented our method in a publicly available Python package called pyDUQ. This package includes functions for calculating the relative volume change and determining Hamiltonian trajectories, along with various tools for simulating free expansion and other processes. With pyDUQ, researchers can quickly and easily apply our new approach to their own systems, simply by defining their Hamiltonian. By providing a user-friendly interface for calculating thermodynamic state function changes, pyDUQ is enabling researchers to access the functionality of CANEPAT, a popular tool for simulating free expansion and other chemical reactions. This collaboration between pyDUQ and CANEPAT is an important step towards making our new method even more accessible and convenient to use. By combining the capabilities of these two tools, researchers can now leverage the power of pyDUQ to determine thermodynamic state function changes, while still utilizing the workflow and settings that they have established within CANEPAT. This seamless integration of pyDUQ and CANEPAT is a key achievement that reflects the flexibility and adaptability of our new approach. By providing a range of different tools and interfaces, we have created a comprehensive system that enables researchers to apply our new method in a wide range of contexts. This system is based on the fundamental principle that the length of a Hamiltonian trajectory should be seen as an inherent property of the system, rather than something that needs to be determined through simulation or other forms of analysis.

We've investigated solitary waves called nanoptera in two preloaded systems: a woodpile model with weak nonlinear interactions and a diatomic chain composed of differently sized particles. When isolated nanoptera form, their shapes match the original particle configuration. When two nanoptera collide head-on, they combine into one nanoptera, with possible phase shifts depending on the initial conditions and any impurities present. Collisions that don't involve particle overlap result in nanoptera passing through each other, with their shapes determined by the relative velocities and distances between them. In the woodpile model, we found that even small nonlinear effects can prevent nanoptera translating like classical particles, while in the diatomic chain, we observed non-trivial oscillations in the gaps between particles during collisions. Additionally, the nanoptera's energy remains conserved over many iterations, with any deviations occurring due to the system's finite size and ending within 1% of the expected value after many iterations. Notably, the nanoptera's characteristics can be adjusted by changing the pressure applied to the system. Our research also includes a special case where one of the nanoptera is at rest, with the other moving freely, and finds that the non-trivial oscillations in the diatomic chain decay at a rate inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the particles. This research provides a mathematical explanation for the experimentally observed decay of solitary waves in granular chains. Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching in G that, when combined with the matching complement of K_G, results in the edge coloration of the complete graph K_G. This notion was first introduced by Alon and Carrafero in 2003, and have since been extensively studied by various mathematicians. A graph that possesses this pairing is known as pairing-friendly. A specific type of graph that exhibits this pairing-friendly characteristic is the quartic circulant graph under consideration here. This paper delves into the examination of another class of graphs, the accordion graphs, which are also pairing-friendly. It investigates the Hamiltonicity of these graphs as well as their perfect matchings, and demonstrates that they are isomorph with the aforementioned quartic circulant graphs. The research further presents methods of constructing accordion graphs based on polynomials with particular properties and determines the parameters under which these constructions are possible. Nonetheless, current models fall short in artistic stability - their outputs frequently deviating from intended artistic styles. This shortfall hinders models' capacity to capture intricate artistic characteristics, which are deeply rooted in the models' latent space. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the concept of semantic stability, where we endeavor to maintain specific artistic elements like brushes and colors during image generation. To accomplish this, we develop a novel framework that identifies and extracts distinct semantic features from a set of reference images, which are subsequently incorporated into the diffusion process using our proposed steering method. To facilitate feature incorporation, we also introduce a framework for training latent space classifiers. Our novel approach surpasses existing artistic generation techniques and achieves remarkable results, as evidenced by our comprehensive evaluations and the created demo artwork. In response to this challenge, researchers have recently proposed various deep learning architectures, but thus far, there remains a noticeable gap in the accuracy of predicted weather forecasts compared to actual measurements. Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers focus on one-way node interactions, yet ignore bidirectional patterns that may hold crucial information. This study introduces Finding NeMo, a competition that challenges participants to identify real fraud cases within a large transaction network by examining two-sided node connections. The problem is framed as a machine learning task and participants are encouraged to submit their approaches to this feature network learning problem. This year's competition features three datasets from Indian banks and two evaluation metrics to assess node centrality-related aspects of the network. Additionally, the winners will be selected based on a community-rated approach. The paper outlines the methodology and provides sample code to replicate the results, enabling interested researchers to participate in the NeMo competition. Furthermore, the paper highlights the distinction between preserving network properties and improving a machine learning model's performance, exemplified through the competition's findings. Our research has significant astrophysical implications, with potential applications in the study of compact binary mergers, white dwarf stars, and the behavior of black holes in general. Through thorough testing, we observed that our method surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks in terms of preservation of the subject's identity and overall visual clarity. Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on complex datasets that are read-only, lead-long, and distributed across multiple locations. As datasets grow in size, various processing pipelines are applied to them for analysis, which generates substantial IO and computation-driven latency. To mitigate this issue, several acceleration methods have been proposed, but they often fail to account for the distinct characteristics of certain scientific datasets, leading to inefficient solutions. As a result, general-purpose acceleration methods may not effectively apply to specific datasets, while tailored approaches might not be adaptable to future, yet unknown, scientific data sets. To bridge this gap, we suggest a new framework focused on creating dataset-specific performance models, which can be developed using a simplified profiling process and utilized to inform the design of new dataset processing systems, ultimately leading to better performance. Our approach is demonstrated by building performance models for two prominent scientific datasets, Chandra and Pan-STARRS, and using them to design an optimized system around the file system, which results in significant speed-ups of up to 6.3 times in analysis latency for these datasets. Our findings emphasize the importance of considering specific characteristics when designing systems for large-scale scientific data, which should guide future research and development. Moreover, our profiling methodology can serve as a standard tool for evaluating the performance of existing scientific data sets, which can in turn be used to evaluate the performance of various processing pipelines and guide the development of efficient analysis workflows. Lastly, our study provides a concrete example of applying machine learning as a tool for classifying and solving real-world scientific data challenges through transfer learning. By applying our profiling framework to other scientific data sets, we can develop new, dataset-specific performance models and design optimized systems around them. Furthermore, our work can facilitate collaboration among researchers by providing a common language for evaluating the performance of different scientific data sets, which can be used to identify common characteristics and develop more general and efficient acceleration methods for scientific computing applications. To this end, we have made our profiling framework and simulation environment publicly available to support these efforts. Our code can be found at: https://github.com/ahmedsafwat/dataset-profiling. Our study breaks down the GCNN component, providing an accessible and mathematically grounded explanation for its convolutional part and demonstrating how it aligns with traditional matched filtering used in remote sensing and graph analytics contexts. This clarity empowers researchers to modify GCNN to suit specific application requirements. Furthermore, we highlight the similarities between GCNN's matching approach and well-known aggregation methods in graph analysis, such as the Gibbs sampling technique, thereby facilitating cross-domain knowledge transfer. To illustrate the general applicability of our findings, we modify GCNN to analyze synthetic and real-world hyperspectral image data across various platforms. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at the provided URL. Ultimately, this research aims to disseminate the concepts behind GCNN to a broader remote sensing community audience. Experimental results show that with a clear understanding of GCNN, substantial improvements can be achieved in practical applications within remote sensing and other graph-related domains. Specifically, our tests on real-world hyperspectral image data yielded a 3.0% enhancement in NSSR (Normalized Spectral Signal Ratio) metric when evaluated on the relevant PCC (Pixel Correlation Curve) criterion. Given the numerous real-world applications of remote sensing, this improvement translates to increased efficiency in other graph-based domains as well. In summary, our study offers a groundbreaking explanation for GCNN, paving the way for researchers to leverage this model in various domains and achieve improved results in practical applications. Additionally, our research highlights the potential for deep learning models to be informed by theories in remote sensing and graph analytics, thereby facilitating knowledge transfer between previously distinct fields. This work can serve as a model for similar efforts to disseminate the concepts behind other deep neural network components, thereby promoting cross-domain collaboration and innovation. Lastly, our study demonstrates the practical value of theory-driven deep learning models in real-world applications, thereby validating the long-standing research goal of deep learning modeled after real-world processes. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains, however its effectiveness significantly hinges on the quality and abundance of training data. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that leverages a pre-trained parser ensemble to enhance its own performance on data scarce languages and domains. The approach involves two key modifications to traditional self-training: it utilizes deep contextualized representations and adaptable dependency graphs for enhanced syntactic structure prediction. Moreover, we introduce a simple yet effective strategy to mitigate syntactic errors introduced by the parser ensemble during self-training. The proposed method is evaluated across multiple languages and domains, and the experimental outcomes demonstrate its capability to improve results significantly. It is noteworthy that our approach even surpasses the baseline supervised parser ensemble in several cases, and in some scenarios, it outperforms other complex semi-supervised parsing methods. Ultimately, self-training emerges as a practical and effective solution to address data scarcity in dependency parsing. All experimental code and datasets are available for reproduction of results at https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/DCST.

The flow of electrical current in "smart" devices relies on semiconductors, which produce essential light in our daily lives through emission. Nonetheless, the majority of semiconductors are not used for this purpose due to a lack of efficiency; they either emit in the wrong part of the spectrum or not at all when they should. The key to improving technology lies in discovering new semiconductors with optimal properties. The search for improved semiconductors has also led to the discovery of exotic states of matter that have piqued the interest of researchers. The 5d transition metal iridium plays a crucial role in generating these exciting states of matter. Recent findings suggest that certain materials containing iridium are on the verge of developing "topological quantum errors," a phenomenon that occurs when multiple quantum states collide in a 3D structure. In software systems, the operational environment is distinguished from their internal workings by the configuration space, which encompasses external variables like user input and system settings. This research delves into the internal characteristics of software systems through their compile-time attributes, referred to as compile-space, and investigates a novel approach: utilizing specialization based on runtime configuration information to reduce compile-space variability. Our study involves three case studies with open-source code and five evaluation criteria, which yield substantial benefits in reducing compile-space size and simplifying configuration processes. Notably, our findings demonstrate that compile-time optimization can shrink the compile-space by up to 80% in some instances without compromising system functionality. This pioneering study opens doors for further research into the relationship between compile-space and operational environments, potentially leading to more efficient compilation methods and optimized system performance. Overall, our results suggest that incorporating more compile-time information can produce more accurate and refined compile-space profiles, thereby enabling innovative solutions to manage and reduce operational environment variability during the coding process. These solutions could also be applied to other domains and used in tools to automate the customization and tailoring of systems for diverse external conditions. Our source code and data are available for reproduction of our experimental results at https://github.com/ahmedamr92/Config-Specializer. Recently, there has been a surge in interest in cross-lingual model sharing, which allows us to utilize knowledge from a proficient "source" language to enhance "target" language performance. Although this concept has been around for a while, it has been limited to specific models, which are trained using a particular architecture. In this research, we introduce a novel approach that enables the transfer of representations across languages and models. We develop a method that leverages neural task representations as weak supervision, allowing us to enhance the proficiency of any given natural language processing model in a target language, given a corresponding model in the source language. Our approach is built on a weak supervision framework called supervised attention, which enables us to translate task-specific knowledge from the source language into the target language. Through our experiments, we demonstrate that this method achieves substantial improvements in various benchmark datasets for NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and part-of-speech tagging, across a range of models, including BERT and RoBERTa, and across multiple language pairs, including English and both Spanish and Indonesian. We also conduct an in-depth analysis of our method's efficacy and make our code available for reproducibility. Furthermore, we create a new dataset called CTSR, which comprises neural task representation annotations for over 1000 sentences in both Spanish and Indonesian, enabling the transfer of knowledge across these languages. This dataset is highly diverse, with annotations that are both coarse-grained and fine-grained, and it is accompanied by an automated evaluation framework that assesses the quality of model transfers. We also release our model weights, which achieve state-of-the-art performance on various target language datasets, for both the source and target languages. In particular, our method achieves a 3.5 and 2.5 F1-score improvement over the baseline models on Sentiment Analysis for Spanish and Indonesian, respectively. Similarly, our method achieves a 2.5 and 1.5 F1-score improvement over the baseline models on Named Entity Recognition for Spanish and Indonesian, respectively. To address this challenge, we have developed a new approach, BasicVSR++, which focuses on reducing these initial artifacts through a novel alignment technique that realigns frames before they're used in the prediction process. This modification allows the model to learn more accurate long-term predictions. When compared to the previous approach, BasicVSR++ demonstrates improved performance across various metrics and video encoding schemes, achieving even higher VSR standards when encoded in a professional format. When evaluated under the same encoding conditions, the previous approach only sees a slight improvement. BasicVSR++ achieves this through a combination of a stronger model design and the previously mentioned alignment technique. As a result, the model can predict frames up to five frames ahead while maintaining high video quality, a feat previously unheard of in the field. BasicVSR++ has also seen success in other related tasks, such as video deblurring and video denoising, outperforming the competition in these areas. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. To accomplish this, we first define norms related to u's Dirac operator, namely ℝⁿ+1. We subsequently prove the theorem by demonstrating the function u/(|u| + ϕ) satisfies specific conditions within the specified regions, where ϕ represents an appropriate approximation of u within those areas. Notably, the proof relies on an initial inequality derived from the Rellich-Kondrachov theorem to bound the L² norm of u's gradient. Furthermore, we extend Hadamard's theorem to specific polynomial monogenic functions, providing a concrete example for its applicability. Additionally, we discuss potential generalizations of this theorem to functions with more complex singularities. Finally, the paper's last section explores a converse to the theorem within the context of monogenic functions near a regular point. The study culminates by highlighting connections to other notable theorems, including Liouville's and Myers' in the context of smooth functions. The research presented here builds upon earlier works by V. Monard, M. A. A. Agostinelli, and M. A. Caldeira, among others. We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, previously proposed as simplified models for certain types of turbulent behavior. We establish that the 2D version of this map has two distinct invariant sets with maximal entropy, which can be represented by sequences from the set of integers that follow the rules of Dyck paths, under specific conditions. This finding enables us to demonstrate that there is no limit to how closely another system with maximal entropy can approach the entropy level of the heterochaos map, over sufficiently large observation periods, even if it starts arbitrarily far away. In addition, we define the entropy associated with the 3D version of the map, using the language of simplicial complexes with certain geometric properties, and confirm that it has only one invariant set with maximal entropy. We also show that the maximal entropy associated with the 2D heterochaos map can be broken down into two distinct components, one related to the scaling properties of its noninvertible components and the other related to its unique directional expansion behavior. This analysis provides new insights into the structure of the set with maximal entropy, now known as the Dyck system, and reveals a previously overlooked aspect of its properties. We also explore connections between the generalized baker map and other well-known systems with maximal entropy, particularly the interval exchange map, under specific conditions. Finally, we propose that the system with maximal entropy associated with the 2D heterochaos map, now known as the Dyck system, may serve as a model for understanding certain types of turbulent behavior in physical systems. We also suggest that the system with maximal entropy associated with the 3D version of the map may provide a suitable model for understanding certain types of turbulent behavior in physical systems with more than 2D spatial complexity. These model extensions are crucial in ensuring the stability of the missing mass in the universe, a phenomenon known as dark matter. As a result, there is a growing need within the particle physics community to identify the most effective experimental strategies required to explore the universe at its most fundamental level. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the potential strategies for future collider experiments to uncover the intricate world of scalar particles. The research focuses on the most popular theoretical models featuring multiple Higgs bosons, such as the SM2HDM, KMSS, and inert doublet model, as these models offer the most compelling explanations for the observed Higgs-like signal and dark matter phenomena. These models exhibit distinct characteristics, such as invisible Higgs decays, flavor-changing neutral currents, and scalar coupling modifications, which can be effectively investigated through in-depth analyses of various production and decay processes at hadron colliders and precision photon colliders. The research presents detailed numerical simulations of these phenomena, along with the development of optimal observables and likelihood-based analysis methods to precisely identify the underlying scalar particles through accurate separation of signal and background processes. This research introduces the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model, an enhanced autoregressive generative network, designed to produce raw audio data more efficiently than its predecessor, VoiceNet. By integrating Pitch-dependent Dilated Convolution Neural Network (PDN) technology into WaveNet, the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model significantly reduces the number of parameters required while preserving its intricate detail reproduction capabilities. Evaluations using the VCTK dataset reveal that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model surpasses VoiceNet in terms of sample quality across various pitch levels and outperforms VoiceNet in terms of computational speed, with both metrics being highly significant. Additionally, the model demonstrates resilience in the face of parameter pruning, producing high-quality audio even after parameter reduction. Notably, the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model's performance in raw audio generation exceeds that of more advanced text-to-speech systems like Tacotron 2 and Tacotron 2 with VITS. Moreover, the model's audio recordings are comparable to those of professional human speakers in terms of mean opinion score. Finally, the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model's synthesized audio recordings also surpass those of VoiceNet in terms of mean opinion score. Specifically, the model excels in producing raw audio data at various pitch levels while maintaining its robustness against parameter pruning. Furthermore, the research presents an open-source implementation of the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model, inviting fellow researchers to build upon this framework in the future. In particular, the researchers suggest that the model's technology could be adapted to generate other types of periodic data, such as electrical signals. Finally, the researchers plan to expand upon this model in a forthcoming paper, which will focus on using this framework as a pre-training component to enhance raw audio data detection capabilities in acoustic event detection systems. This potential enhancement was identified during an initial evaluation of the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model using the US8K dataset. Specifically, the results revealed that the model could potentially increase raw audio data detection accuracy by a significant margin. Therefore, the researchers aim to build upon this framework in a future study. Furthermore, the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model's open-source implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengyinwei/Quasi-Periodic_WaveNet. Recommender Systems are indispensable to assist users in selecting items that cater to their personal tastes, given the overwhelming number of choices available. While Collaborative Filtering has proven effective in addressing the data scarcity issue, it often neglects to exploit item grouping patterns that are inherent in the user-item interaction data. Our research introduces BCF, a novel CF approach that leverages both individual user preferences and shared patterns among items to enhance recommendation accuracy. The bifocal architecture of BCF comprises two key modules: the user-bicluster module, which identifies and isolates unique user groups, and the preference assignment module, which tailors these groups to individual users. The incorporation of locality-aware and adaptive methods in the preference assignment module addresses the issues of sparse and subjective user feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed BCF approach surpasses state-of-the-art CF methods on real-world datasets, thereby validating the significance of item grouping patterns in enhancing recommendation accuracy. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the model's architecture and bicluster-based modules reveals the individual contributions of user-specific preferences and item grouping patterns to the overall accuracy. Our findings and models have been made accessible for public evaluation. Additionally, a video summary is available at https://youtu.be/6Q6k0xkxw4U. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhaozh/biclusterCF. BCF is also available as a cloud API at https://recommenderai.com/recommender/biclusterCF. BCF is compatible with TensorFlow and Keras, allowing for seamless integration into existing CF pipelines. The datasets employed in our research comprise movie and book recommendations, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/zhaozh/biclusterCF/tree/main/datasets. Our research has led to the development of BCF, an open-source recommender system that can be accessed at https://recommenderai.com/recommender/biclusterCF and executed on Google Cloud at https://cloud.google.com/ai-platform/unified-ml. BCF is an adaptable solution that can be applied across diverse domains and scales due to its model simplicity and model size compactness. Consequently, BCF is suitable for deployment on edge devices and mobile apps, thereby enhancing user experience and facilitating personalized recommendations on mobile devices. The effectiveness of BCF in addressing data scarcity and item grouping pattern exploitation has been empirically validated through our experiments. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the model's architecture and bicluster-based modules has been conducted to elucidate their individual contributions

Lastly, we propose two novel activity indicators and compare their robustness to established ones, particularly in the context of long-baseline observations. This research lays the groundwork for utilizing these activity proxies in the study of solar cycles and other phenomena in the Sun's activity patterns. This research has the added benefit of enhancing our understanding of the Sun itself. The theory of shadows serves as an extension to bicategories, allowing for the computation of relative traces that take into account 2-categorical structure. This extension is reflected in the concept of shadows being bicategorical traces through the establishment of a type of Baez-Dolan Lurie correspondence, where we demonstrate that formation of shadows acts as a functor from the category of bicategories to the category of shadows, achieving a generalization of the theory of traces in monoidal categories to the realm of bicategories, and revealing a theoretical framework in which higher algebraic concepts can be evaluated. This abstract presents a fundamental approach to understanding shadows as an extension to bicategories, and illustrates their similarity to traces in monoidal categories. Furthermore, we show that this concept is consistent with the theory of topological bicategories, and that it furnishes an effective method for calculating relative traces with regard to 2-categorical structure. This calculation is exemplified in the computation of $\pi_2(S^2)$, where we show that it equals the shadow bicategory of the point, formed through a functor that maps the interval to the point. This result is derived as a consequence of the theory of shadows being bicategorical traces. Furthermore, we establish that topological bicategories constitute a type of shadow bicategory, and that these concepts constitute a theoretical framework in which higher algebraic ideas can be evaluated.
