Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of neural tone mapping in producing detailed and visually appealing images from overly bright raw data, achieving results comparable to traditional manual methods. However, neural tone mapping's reliance on paired training data limits its application to new scenes, and its computational efficiency also poses a problem. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new method that extracts scene-specific style information from image pairs and applies it to unpaired scene images to produce more natural-looking results. To achieve this, we developed a new neural network that can perform both global forward and inverse tone mapping, extracting a universal style profile from image pairs and using it to regulate the tone mapping process through an adaptive adjustment mechanism. Through our experiments, we show that our method outperforms previous approaches in producing detailed and visually appealing results, and our analysis confirms its computational efficiency as well. Ultimately, we successfully created a new tone-mapped image from a scene that was not included in our training data. To verify the global applicability of our method, we created an interactive visualization demonstrating its effects. To facilitate future research, we will publicly release our code and data. Additionally, we will showcase our results in a demo format. Please see https://sulcitech.github.io/ToneMap for more information. (From: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00444)

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where experts were asked to predict the emotional impact of audio-visual content on elderly viewers. Building on previous research, we enhanced existing models through two key approaches: Firstly, we incorporated multi-head attention into the two-dimensional transducer to increase data utilization. Secondly, we optimized the training protocol by introducing a frame overlap during end-to-end training, thereby bridging the gap between the predictor and the decoder. Notably, our model achieved an average mean absolute error of 0.1046 across all provided datasets, securing the top rank in the LoveU competition with a 20% improvement over the runner-up model. The source code for this project has been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/loveu-challenge/CVPR2022_AQTC_TSDN.

As snowfall accumulates, the interaction between falling particles and surface roughness can lead to uneven deposition, causing certain areas to receive more snowdeposits. Artificial intelligence that incorporates active inference is gaining traction as a brain-inspired paradigm for decision-making, however, its application has been limited to simulated environments due to computational constraints of its original Bayesian formulation. We have adapted this framework into a deep learning structure, known as deep active inference, that overcomes these limitations while retaining the essence of its original theory. We have successfully integrated the resulting model into a self-directing system for an autonomous robot navigating a physical environment with unknown layout. Notably, this model is capable of generating informative actions that refine its understanding of the environment. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through experiments at two different levels of uncertainty. The findings highlight the ability of our model to effectively explore and learn about its environment in a dynamic setting. Furthermore, we have found that the actions it takes are not only efficient but also aligned with real-world active inference principles. We believe that deep active inference presents a promising solution for creating more adaptive and data-driven robotic systems. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepActiveInference/deep_active_inference_robot. A video showcasing the results can be accessed via https://youtu.be/6Q8xk6e4kUk. Additionally, the pre-trained models used in the experiments can be downloaded from https://deepactiveinference.github.io/models/robot_dai.zip. We invite researchers to replicate our work and build upon our findings. We envision that deep active inference has the potential to revolutionize various applications by introducing a more adaptive and brain-inspired approach to decision-making. Given its generalizability, deep active inference can be applied across a broad range of domains including robotics, computer vision, and audio processing. We are excited to see the numerous possibilities that deep active inference can bring to the table! In real-time particle physics experiments such as the LHCb Upgrade, real-time data processing is crucial. To achieve this, we employ a technique called sparse data compression based on a novel autoencoder architecture. By utilizing a dual-head approach after initial 3D data transformations, we successfully compressed raw experiment data and accurately reconstructed it in avionics systems, resulting in a significant reduction of data volume and associated latency. Notably, while maintaining the same level of precision, our method compresses raw experiment data by approximately 30% in one case and 40% in another. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the capability of our model to dynamically adjust its compression level in response to changing data rates. The efficacy of our sparse data compression method via autoencoder has been thoroughly validated using simulated particle physics data. To ensure seamless deployment in real-time processing systems, we have also developed an online strategy for determining the optimal compression level. Lastly, we examine the relationship between temperature and density for these galaxy clusters within the framework of Finzi's gravity model. We discovered that this relationship can take on two distinct forms, depending on the sign of the clustering parameter, with one form mirroring the relationship predicted by Newtonian gravity. We conducted these analyses and obtained our results using data from the MaxiPlanck/SDSS catalog, which includes 42 galaxy clusters. A previously underappreciated ability to move along vertical and overhanging surfaces has been observed in Pacific Lamprey, allowing it to climb from its birthplace to its feeding grounds by adhering to rough surfaces with its suction cup-like mouth. This unique capacity is now being studied to develop novel robotic solutions that could access previously inaccessible areas with potential applications in search and rescue operations. This research focuses on creating a simple yet effective robotic system that mimics the lamprey's motion dynamics by using a basic model with a built-in adhesive module. The findings show that the underlying dynamics responsible for the lamprey's ability to climb can be replicated using a robotic system similar in design. The success of this collaboration indicates promising possibilities for creating robots that can effectively navigate overhanging environments. With further advancements, these robots could potentially use their adhesive capabilities to lift heavy loads, offering new possibilities in robotics. The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios. This work lays the groundwork for applying these solutions to a broader range of astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the Guderley problem and its relevant mathematical concepts due to their instructional value. Finally, we briefly discuss the practical implications of these solutions in the contexts of supernovae and white dwarf stars. This research was motivated by the need to address uncertainty and variability in the density of a compressing substance, which was not adequately addressed in previous studies. As a result, this paper offers a more general and applicable solution to the Guderley problem than existing works, which were primarily concerned with uniform or decreasing density scenarios. Furthermore, we expand our analysis to include scenarios with multiple power law changes in density, which may occur naturally due to the presence of layers or shells in a given system. This is particularly relevant to astrophysical systems, such as stars and planets, as well as laboratory settings, such as gas cylinders, where such variations in density may be artificially created. This research has potential practical applications in understanding and analyzing various phenomena involving shock waves and changes in pressure and density. These scenarios include supernovae explosions, the collapse of stars, and shock waves in gases with varying densities and temperatures. Additionally, this work may contribute to the development of more accurate and generalized models for the Guderley problem that can be applied to a broader range of astrophysical and cosmological events. One potential solution to address this issue involves explainable AI (XAI), which aims to enhance user understanding of the computations made by deep neural networks. Although XAI research has gained momentum, the inherent challenges of its field are hindering progress in implementing practical solutions. One key area of improvement is the current limited consideration of human perspectives, which are crucial for effectively tackling the complexities of XAI. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial for determining the required treatment strategy, from non-intervention to surgical removal and further histological examination.  Establishing a polyp's histological characteristics involves analyzing the histopathological features of a biopsy taken from the polyp.  These analyses aim to identify the type of lesion (e.g., adenoma, hyperplasia) and the level of dysplasia present (low, moderate, high).  Creating an automated system for making these diagnoses could enhance clinical efficiency and provide patients with better care.

A comprehensive dataset called UniToPatho has been developed to support the development of an automated system for diagnosing and determining the level of dysplasia in colorectal polyps.  This dataset consists of 13,041 individual images, along with their corresponding labels, obtained from 104 whole-slide preparations of colorectal polips.  The images were captured using two different types of microscopes and were annotated by three experienced pathologists.  The dataset's images were selected using a patch-based extraction method to facilitate training machine learning models.  The UniToPatho dataset is accessible at https://git.unipr.edu/hst/UnitoPatho.

This research introduces MrSARP, a novel deep generative prior-based approach for enhancing the resolution of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images. MrSARP is based on a hierarchical autoencoder that models raw SAR data upsampled by a factor related to the system's wavelength. By initially ignoring the previously mentioned upsampled values and only focusing on a low-resolution representation of the image, a prior model is developed that strongly encourages sparse representations. When high-resolution images are reintroduced, the prior model is refined to prioritize authentic SAR data production, which effectively acts as a regularization technique for the SAR image recovery process. Experimental results from various platforms, including a Digassp-4100 system with real data and the S-band radar data from the Airborne Synthetic Aperture Radar (ASAR), demonstrate that MrSARP significantly outperforms other SAR image upscaling techniques in terms of resolution and detail. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined classical-optimization classical-qubit strategy to obtain approximate solutions for challenging combinatorial issues.  Within this framework, key concerns are determining the optimal Q-angle set.  This study introduces a method using a modified Bayesian approach to determine these Q-angles.  This BQAO approach is initially evaluated on the Planted Partitioning Problem, where traditional optimization methods fall short, especially in diverse problem instances.  Our research shows that the BQAO method consistently yields accurate solutions across various problem cases.  Key findings include accurate solution rates of 90% or higher for problems with up to 16 qubits and depend only on the problem definition, not the qubit count.  Moreover, the BQAO method outperforms a prior Bayesian approach and offers improved solution quality over its classical-opt optimization counterpart by at least 68%.  This breakthrough quantum algorithm now exhibits enhanced performance and greater practical value.  Our research also includes a crucial observation regarding the Bayesian cost function's properties, which may lead to further research opportunities.  This finding indicates that the cost function is minimized when its derivative equals zero, a valuable insight that may contribute to future research.  Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/JulianKasberger/BQAO.
